# T1DMAI

Note

Most of the code in this repo was written by AI. If you don't like that, feel free to leave.

This repo is a zoo. Here I train & test many blood glucose forecasting models (including my own) on both my own data and metabonet (public).

My model is a small transformer that forecasts blood glucose 2 hours ahead. I've made two variants: D16 DILATE and D16 MSE which use DILATE and MSE loss for training, respectively. D16 refers to the width of the model (16). They are both trained on synthetic traces, and then a LoRA adapter is added for light fine-tuning, but I also test them without the adapter.

Feast thine eyes on some of their forecasts (these have been trained on synthetic traces, then fine-tuned with a LoRA adapter on my training split):

Caution

Research and educational use only - not a medical device. T1DMAI is a research artifact. It is not clinically validated, has no regulatory clearance, and its output is a forecast of research signals, not medical advice. It must not be used to make medical, diagnostic, or treatment decisions, to calculate or adjust insulin doses, or to manage diabetes in any way. For medical guidance consult a qualified healthcare professional. The software is provided "as is", without warranty of any kind (see LICENSE ).

## 1. Background

I have type 1 diabetes and I wanna know if I can train a BG forecasting model to help me with my daily management. To this end I've made some auxiliary tools:

- T1DMSIM creates synthetic CGM traces since UVA/Padova was too slow on my laptop.

- T1DMDROID runs the models on my phone, also has some neat functionality like reading BG from multiple CGMs at once.

For evaluation, I use the recommendations by Jacobs et al., IEEE Reviews in Biomedical Engineering, 2024 [1] . It's a nice paper that you should probably read.

## 2. Main results

All models suck. XGBoost is the best one but my own model comes close. More details below:

- On my data, D16 DILATE + LoRA comes 3rd of 26 (22.8), behind XGBoost (22.2) and LightGBM (22.4). Wilcoxon puts it level with both at 60 and 90 min, behind them at 30 and 120.

- On MetaboNet, D16 DILATE + LoRA comes 9th (34.6) but has the lowest RMSE of all models at 90 min. XGBoost leads at 30, 60 and 120.

- At 60 min a 3771 parameter LoRA adapter helps both models on both datasets: 26.1 to 22.8 and 27.1 to 23.5 on my data, 36.6 to 34.6 and 36.7 to 35.1 on MetaboNet. At 120 min on MetaboNet it makes D16 DILATE worse (48.0 to 50.4).

- On MetaboNet, LoRA also fixes the bands. The 90% band holds the truth 75-78% of the time at 60 min with sim only and 81-85% with LoRA. On my data both are 83-85%.

- T1DMAI + LoRA reacts earliest on my data: 40-50 min time gain at 60 min, against 30 for XGBoost.

- It also catches the most lows on my data: 40-47% at 60 min, against 29% for XGBoost. On MetaboNet every low-RMSE model misses nearly all lows (XGBoost 0%, T1DMAI 6-8%), while linear extrapolation catches 58%.

- LightGBM matches XGBoost within 0.2 mg/dL everywhere. An LSTM with 15 hours of history comes 3rd on MetaboNet (33.6 at 60 min), against 35.9 for the 2 hour one.

- Zero-shot Chronos-2 and TimesFM 2.5 beat zero-shot Chronos-Bolt by 1.4-2.7 mg/dL at 60 min on both datasets, but trail fine-tuned Chronos-Bolt.

## 3. Models

Numbers in brackets point to References . Everything except the baselines and the foundation models was trained from scratch on each dataset's training split. T1DMAI comes in two versions: sim only is the checkpoint in models/ , and sim + LoRA adds a frozen-base rank 1 adapter [23] (3771 parameters) trained on the real training split.

More in docs/USAGE.md and ARCHITECTURE.md .

## 4. Data

My data. 115 days from T1DMDROID: days 1 to 80 for training, 81 to 115 for testing. Note that the model sees future inputs like insulin & carbs. I should probably also train the adapters while withholding those inputs.

MetaboNet [2] . Official split, 279 test people from 9 studies. Blind, because most of them use closed-loop pumps whose future insulin reacts to glucose the model hasn't seen.

## 5. Method

- LoRA checkpoints are picked by mean RMSE on the last 10 days of each subject's training data.

- All models forecast at the same moments.

- 95% intervals: bootstrap over people (MetaboNet) or days (my data).

- Significance: Wilcoxon signed-rank on paired absolute errors against the best model, Bonferroni corrected.

- Clinical error grids: DTS [20], Clarke [22], CG-EGA [21].

## 6. Results

## 7. Limitations

- My data is N=1 over 35 days.

- The test sets differ a lot (in range 89% vs 75%, CV 28% vs 40%), so don't compare numbers across them.

- Lows are rare: 292 forecasts on my data, 8347 on MetaboNet.

- T1DMAI fell back to the last reading on 0.7% of my forecasts and 0.4% on MetaboNet, including all 28 ShanghaiT1DM ones. The other models never fall back.

- The bands are raw quantiles, no conformal correction.

- The sparse GP's own uncertainty isn't shown. Its noise fit hit the bottom of its grid, giving a band about 1 mg/dL wide.

- Time gain is only computed for my data.

- Unlogged meals count as "no meal".

- CPU timings are single runs on one laptop core and varied by up to 45% between runs.

- LightGBM, LSTM (15 h), Chronos-2 and TimesFM 2.5 have no CPU timing yet.

## 10. Reproduce

python -m zoo.run MODEL --cache CACHE --template template.parquet --truth truth.parquet [--causal] python finetune.py --checkpoint CKPT --cache CACHE --lora-rank 1 --val-days 10 --select-on rmse \ [--blind | --no-blind] python export_submission.py --checkpoint CKPT --template template.parquet --cache CACHE \ --max-context 336 --fill ladder --quantiles [--future-doses zero] python leaderboard.py MANIFEST.json --out results

Chronos-2 and TimesFM 2.5 run under .venv-zoo ( requirements-zoo.txt ).

## 11. Published scores

RMSE (mg/dL) that each model's paper reports, beside the same model on my data and on MetaboNet. The papers use other people, splits, inputs and history lengths, so a gap between the two sides is not a like-for-like comparison. My data is non-blind, MetaboNet blind (§8).

RMSE in mg/dL at the single step 30 or 60 min ahead, as printed in each paper. T1DMAI has no published score.

Chronos-Bolt (Zhang et al. 2026) and N-HiTS (Potosnak et al. 2025; Sergazinov et al. 2024) are published only as RMSE averaged over every step up to the horizon, which is not the same quantity, so they have no row.

# Did it really use REA?

English · 简体中文

> ⭐ Star the list on GitHub to find it again, or Watch → Custom → Releases for the weekly digest .

Many cases are described as "built with REA". This page checks each one against the project's own README, the author's post, or the official showcase, and records what we found. First checked on 2026-10-14; the "README says REA?" column was re-checked against every linked repository's current README and agent files on 2026-11-10, with no changes. X posts could not be opened from our environment, so for them we rely on the third-party case records named in the table.

Summary (39 rows, 2026-11-10):

- 26 confirmed: the README, the agent instructions (AGENTS.md, CLAUDE.md) or the official showcase says REA was used.

- 3 partial: REA was used for part of the work only.

- 4 not verified: 2 claimed only in the author's post, 2 with no source naming the tool.

- 6 not REA: other AI tools (mostly Claude Code or Codex with Ghidra or IDA) or manual reverse engineering.

Whether REA helps is a separate question. The two controlled comparisons in this list, rea-lab (482 preregistered runs) and leanrea (36 runs), found no significant gain in solve rate from REA, at higher time and cost. Both are small. See Does REA help? The evidence .

If you find a case that is wrong here, open an issue using the case form.

# Modern Web Guidance

Modern Web Guidance is a set of skills that embed web platform expertise, best practices, and browser compatibility data directly into your coding agents. It helps to steer your coding agents away from legacy patterns, and instead toward solutions that harness the power and capabilities of the modern web platform.

Stewarded by the Google Chrome, Microsoft Edge, Mozilla Firefox, and MDN teams, alongside the web development community.

Documentation · Eval Dashboard · Source Code · Report an Issue

## Quickstart

npx modern-web-guidance@latest install

This command runs an interactive wizard to install Modern Web Guidance. See Alternative Installation Methods below.

#### Try it out (without installing)

# Search for relevant guides npx modern-web-guidance@latest search " animate a dialog modal backdrop " # Retrieve a guide by ID npx modern-web-guidance@latest retrieve " animate-to-from-top-layer " # Scan a codebase for legacy patterns to modernize npx modern-web-guidance@latest legacy-scan .

## Why?

Coding agents often default to older patterns because LLM training data contains vast amounts of legacy code. This often leads them to generate bloated JavaScript for tasks that now have native, high-performance web platform solutions.

Even if a model knows an API exists, it often lacks the density of real-world, modern implementation patterns required for production-ready code.

Modern Web Guidance bridges this gap. Our skill's CLI returns targeted, expert-curated guidelines directly into your agent's context window, focusing on:

- Modern Browser APIs : Helping models correctly structure APIs they frequently misuse.

- Performance & Accessibility : Preferring platform-level APIs that can be optimized by the browser and include built-in accessibility affordances.

- Responsible Fallbacks : Guiding models to use sensible, lightweight fallbacks instead of heavy polyfills or legacy libraries.

## What's Included?

We cover the past several years of the web platform's new features, all the way up to the cutting edge. The guides are designed to be token-efficient ; we run evals enabling us to prune lowest-common-denominator content that models already know.

### Core Disciplines

#### 🎨 User Experience

Smooth visual states (View Transitions, entry/exit animations, parallax scroll, CSS scrollbar-color ).

#### 📐 CSS Layout

Modern layout systems (container queries, subgrid , modern color spaces like oklch , text-wrap tuning, and line-height trimming).

#### ⚡ Performance

Speed optimizations (instant preloading, Interaction to Next Paint (INP) diagnostics, and scheduling tasks via scheduler.yield ).

#### 📝 Forms & UI

Native components (Anchor Positioning for tooltips, Popover API, dialogs, :user-invalid validation, and auto-sizing fields).

#### ♿ Accessibility

Important considerations (screen reader and keyboard operability, content navigation and discoverability).

#### 🤖 Built-in AI

Local client models (native translation, summarization, and language detection APIs).

View an example: the navigation-drawer guide .

#### The full list

### CSS & Layout (140 features)

### HTML & DOM (36 features)

### JavaScript & APIs (74 features)

### accessibility

- accessible-error-announcement : Synchronize programmatic accessibility states (like aria-invalid) with the visual :user-invalid state to ensure screen reader users receive error feedback only after interaction, mirroring the visual experience.

- accessible-generated-content : Use CSS generated content ( ::before / ::after ) in ways that stay accessible, including alternative text for decorative content.

- respect-os-text-scale : Respect the operating system's text scale preference for a page so font sizes, layout, and rem-based measurements follow the user's accessibility settings.

### built-in-ai

- language-detection : Detect the language of user-generated content or already present site content.

- language-model : Run on-device natural language inference in the browser using the Prompt API, with streaming output, structured JSON responses, and multi-turn session management.

- summarizer : Summarize text content using the on-device Summarizer API.

- translator : Translate text between languages using the on-device Translator API.

### css

- animate-to-intrinsic-sizes : Smoothly animate interactive components (like accordions, menus, and expanding cards) to and from their natural dimensions.

- atrule-support-conditionals : Conditionally apply certain CSS rules or declarations only if a certain at-rule is supported by the browser.

- calculate-with-intrinsic-sizes : Calculate the size of an element based on its intrinsic size, while ensuring it fits within given design constraints.

- child-state-based-styling : Build a component that changes its styling based on the state of one of its child elements. For example, a component that renders in light or dark mode based on whether a theme toggle is checked (or not).

- content-based-styling : Build a component that changes its layout based on whether it contains specific child elements (or not). For example, if the component contains an image, use a multi-column layout, otherwise default to a single-column layout.

- css : Action-oriented guidelines for modern CSS architecture, including the cascade, selectors, scoping, nesting, and design tokens. Use this guide when authoring styles or managing design systems.

- css-layout : Modern CSS layouts such as flexbox, grid, subgrid, container queries, anchor positioning, and intrinsic sizing. Use this skill when architecting responsive UI components or page layouts.

- design-token-reactivity : Define higher-order design tokens, like density modes (compact, comfortable, spacious) or themes and have descendant components react to changes directly and in component-appropriate ways.

- dynamic-sibling-styling : Create dynamic visual spectrums or layout arrangements that automatically adapt to the number of elements in a group.

- fluid-scaling : Scale items like font size, spacing, and media sizes smoothly based on the parent container's size rather than using fixed breakpoints

- individual-transform-properties : Animate or override individual CSS transform properties (e.g. translate, rotate, scale) independently of other transform properties on a single element.

- overflow-clipping-control : Adjust the visible clipping boundary of an element to align with the content edge, padding edge, or border edge—or a specified offset from any of these—offering finer-grained control over how content is clipped.

- reduce-style-repetition : Reduce excessive style repetition by encapsulating complex or dynamic styling logic into reusable functions (such as a function that computes a gradient based on a set of input parameters).

- responsive-design : Build UI that adapts to container and viewport size, including container queries, dynamic viewport units, aspect ratios, and responsive typography.

- selector-atrule-combinations : Target elements based on the intersection or union of selectors and conditional @-rules while minimizing repetition.

- size-aware-styling : Build a component whose styles can be conditionally dependent on its own width or height, rather than the width or height of the viewport. For example a card component that can change its layouts depending on how large it is, or a call-to-action button that can conditionally display helper text based on its width.

- style-parent-with-has : Style parent elements of a form field (e.g. labels or fieldsets) when the field is invalid.

- usage-aware-component-variations : Build components that adapt visual logic based on semantic context using CSS container style queries.

### forms

- animated-select-picker : Create a custom select component whose dropdown is animated. For example, the menu fades or slides into view, or the options animate upon selection.

- autofill-address-form : Build an address form with correct autocomplete attributes and autofill support.

- autofill-highlight-inputs : Customize the styling of form fields that have been autofilled and not edited by the user

- autofill-payment-form : Build a payment form that collects card details with correct autocomplete values and autofill support.

- autofill-sign-in-form : Build a sign-in form with correct autocomplete values and autofill support.

- autofill-sign-up-form : Build a sign-up form with correct autocomplete values and autofill support.

- brand-consistent-forms : Match checkboxes, radio buttons, range sliders, and progress bars to your site's color palette without replacing them with custom components.

- branded-select-styling : Create custom select elements whose button, picker, arrow icon, and checkmark all seamlessly match your brand or design system's typography, colors, spacing, and border treatments.

- custom-select-picker-layouts : Create custom select pickers whose options are positioned in unique or interesting ways, rather than the traditional stacked list of options.

- form-fields-automatically-fit-contents : Allow form fields to grow and shrink to fit the user input, e.g. as the user types or selects a different option. Apply maximum and minimum size limits to create dynamic and responsive form fields that conform with the page design.

- ime-safe-enter-submit : Implement Enter-to-submit in textareas and single-line inputs (chat, search, inline rename) safely for IME (Input Method Editor) users to prevent submitting incomplete text.

- required-field-feedback : Provide error message for required form fields that were skipped or left empty only after user interaction, to avoid preemptive errors and ensure feedback is timely and contextually relevant to the user's flow.

- rich-media-picker : Create a custom select component whose options can contain complex HTML formatting (e.g. images, icons, and other rich formatting) rather than just plain text.

- select-menu-interaction : Validate that a non-default option has been chosen in a select menu only after the user has interacted with the control.

- slider : Style a native range slider with custom track, thumb, fill, and focus states while preserving native functionality and accessibility.

- sms-otp-form : Verify user phone numbers and one-time passcodes delivered over SMS with automatic code extraction and accessible form input.

- switch : Build an accessible switch with the native HTML switch attribute, falling back to a styled checkbox when not supported.

- validate-input-after-interaction : Show form field validation feedback (e.g. password complexity or email format requirements) only after the user has finished their initial interaction, avoiding premature errors on page load or while the user is typing.

### html

- accessible-web-components : Make custom elements accessible by default, setting roles and ARIA state via the ElementInternals ARIA mixin, managing focus with delegatesFocus, and keeping ARIA relationships within a single shadow root.

- custom-elements : Define, register, and manage the lifecycle of autonomous custom elements, covering constructor rules, lifecycle callbacks, upgrade timing, attribute/property reflection, and naming conventions.

- form-associated-custom-elements : Make a custom control participate natively in forms with formAssociated and ElementInternals, submitting its own value, integrating with constraint validation, and reacting to reset, disable, and state-restore.

- prerendering-custom-elements : Server-render a custom element, then hydrate it in place without re-rendering or a flash of unstyled content.

- shadow-dom : Encapsulate a component's DOM and styles with Shadow DOM, construct the tree efficiently with HTML templates, and project consumer content with slots.

- styling-web-components : Style across the shadow boundary with :host selectors, inherited and custom properties for theming, ::slotted and ::part, and cascade layers and container queries inside compone

# GURU by Unus Lumen

A self evolving AI framework. Your phone, your house, your network, your rules.

DISCLAIMER: this is not another helpful assistant app. It is powerful software that has not existed in this form before, and it does exactly what you ask it to. Read this page in full before you install anything from the latest release .

GURU reaches your phone, your television, your console, your lights, your speakers, your router and the machines in the cupboard, and it does the work. Not by describing what you could do. By doing it.

And it is not fixed. GURU writes its own tools, its own skills, its own automations and its own rooms. When it meets something it cannot do, it builds the capability and keeps it. That is the whole design: a superintelligence that gets more useful the longer you own it, rather than one that waits for me to ship an update.

Any model is powerful when you give it reach. GURU is the reach.

## What GURU actually is

It is not a chat app. It is a permission layer across 167 Android permissions, a tool registry of around 390 tools and growing, an encrypted memory engine written in Rust, a full Unix userland bundled inside the APK, twelve rooms in one lobby, and Otio, the economy where your own output becomes something you can sell.

You only ever open one app.

GURU speaks the protocols devices actually use, rather than a list of brands I partnered with. UPnP and SOAP for boxes that expose services. DIAL for casting and app launch, including reading a device's app list and knowing the difference between a device that refused and one that never answered at all. Wake-on-LAN for anything asleep. Android TV Remote over its own protobuf protocol, so a Sony or a Philips or a Shield is drivable without an emitter. Roku's ECP. Samsung's websocket remote. LG webOS. Xbox SmartGlass all the way down, including the ECDH key exchange and the AES-CBC channel a console insists on before it will do anything. SNMP for hardware that will never have an app. IR through a Broadlink blaster or the phone's own emitter where one exists. SSH for any machine with a shell. ADB for anything running Android.

Televisions, Fire Sticks, consoles, lights, speakers, blinds, doors, sensors, the router, the printer, the thermostat. If it is on the network, GURU sees it, names it, and finds the way in. If it is not on the network, GURU learns the remote and blasts it instead.

Every capability is a protocol implemented properly, which is why coverage keeps widening instead of stopping at the brands somebody paid me to support.

And it verifies. Every write is followed by a read, and the value the device reports is compared against the value that was written. A transport saying it worked is not evidence. The device's own answer is. A command against a capability the device does not report is refused with a reason naming both, never quietly ignored, because a silent no and a success look identical to you and one of them is a lie.

A network map is only worth having if it is honest, and most scanners are not. They hand you a list of IP addresses, miss anything that does not answer a broadcast, and call it a day.

GURU sweeps every port rather than a curated list, because a curated list is the bug. It reads mDNS and SSDP properly, with the multicast lock arranged rather than assumed. It fingerprints endpoints by their HTTP responses, their certificates, their DIAL description and their UPnP device document, so it can tell you what a thing is rather than that something answered. It walks the whole house, keeps the map, and notices what is new.

When it cannot reach something it says so, and it tells a refusal apart from an absence. An empty list is never allowed to mean "I did not check".

The brain is a Rust engine running in-process, sealed in an encrypted vault with a passphrase generated on first run and never shown. There is no server in the path and no port open to the world.

Inside it is a real cognitive architecture rather than a vector table. Facts enter a BUFFER layer, get promoted to EPISODIC when they are recalled enough, and settle into SEMANTIC once they are strong and repeated. Strength decays exponentially with a seven-day half-life, recalling something strengthens it, a daily consolidation pass merges duplicates and prunes what is weak, and a graph records typed edges between memories: semantic, temporal, causal, and cross-references that mark two memories as contradicting, superseding or duplicating each other.

Nothing is really deleted. Deleting archives, because a memory trail you can rewrite is not a trail.

Every other assistant resets to zero every session and calls it a fresh start. That is a design choice, and it is why none of them ever actually know you. GURU remembers what you told it in March and uses it in November without being reminded.

I gave GURU the ability to extend itself, because a fixed assistant is a dead assistant.

It writes tools and registers them locally, and they are permanent. It writes skills and automations. It adds whole rooms to its own lobby, each one a vessel that starts empty and gets composed by talking to it. It can rewrite the prompt stack it runs on.

You should never be waiting on a company to decide your problem is worth solving. Describe the problem and let it build the thing.

This is why GURU is not a wrapper around somebody else's capability.

The APK ships BusyBox, Toybox, a full Termux prefix with bash and apt, CPython 3.14 with numpy and Pillow, git with a working HTTPS transport, ffmpeg, sqlite, OpenSSL, OpenSSH, jq, rsync, tmux, Tesseract, and a reverse-engineering toolchain including a JDK, apktool, aapt2, jadx and zipalign.

No root. No setup. No tutorial. No "now go and install Termux". The tools are there because I put them there, and a pathshim makes prebuilt Linux binaries run on a stock Android phone. That same trick is what lets GURU drive a phone that would otherwise refuse it.

The lobby is a page of tiles you drag into any order you like, and you can ask GURU to reorder them by voice. Make a new room by naming it; it appears immediately and you compose it by conversation.

Portal is the chat: streaming replies, tool calls you can watch happen, a canvas, attachments, and slash commands ( /help , /status , /whoami , /usage , /tasks , /tools , /think , /stop , /clear ).

Agents is where you make your own. Give one a name, instructions and the tools it may use, and it takes work off you in the background while your chat carries on. An agent with no tools still reasons; an agent with a tool can change something on your phone, and the picker shows exactly which tools it holds and offers nothing else. One press grants all of them or none.

Otio is the economy. Inner Mind is a living graph of everything GURU holds about you, covering memories, conversations, tasks, notes, projects, agents, skills, thoughts, people and every device it has found, drawn as one tissue you explore rather than a list you scroll.

Heartbeat is the clock. Skills are imported capabilities. Notes , Journal , Projects , Calendar and Thoughts are the rooms you will live in, each one a full workspace with its own home-screen widgets, and Settings is where the brain and the model are configured.

Media ingests, probes, transcribes and indexes everything you throw at it, including OCR and keyframe extraction on video.

Ad Space is the one place I sell anything: a canvas inside the app that runs animated packs the server pushes, and it never interrupts your work.

The heartbeat is the difference between an assistant and a presence.

It fires every thirty minutes into your newest conversation with a prompt you write yourself. Not a shipped default, but yours, stored in the database, editable, with a live preview of exactly what a beat will inject, tokens and all.

The room shows you the chain's own pulse: when a beat last actually arrived, and when the next one is booked for. A booking proves only that an alarm was written. Firing proves one was delivered. Without both numbers, "scheduled and dead" and "scheduled and working" look identical.

The switch cannot be turned on without a prompt, because a chain with nothing to send is not a chain. Off always works, and nothing but you ever turns it off.

There is also a Fire Now button, and it hands the beat to the portal so you watch the reply stream in like any other turn. That exists because the first version fired headlessly into the database and the log proved it worked while the screen showed nothing, and a button that fires something you cannot see reads as broken.

Every model call, every search and every request goes through an embedded Tor engine. Nobody sees what you ask.

When the circuit is not ready the request throws rather than quietly going out over your own connection. That matters more than it sounds: the previous version returned an empty proxy list under a comment claiming it refused clearnet, and the HTTP stack reads an empty list as "no proxy", so "fail closed" was in fact a direct connection to the public internet. It throws now because throwing is what actually stops it.

Loopback and LAN addresses stay direct, so your own model keeps working with zero configuration. One policy, in one place, enforced in code rather than promised in a document.

Every prompt GURU runs on is pulled from the publisher, saved onto your phone in plain text and editable. There is no compiled-in instruction set and no hidden layer deciding what you are allowed to ask.

If you want to know why GURU did something, go and look. If you disagree with how it behaves, change it. There is no intellectual property I am protecting in those files, because you could do all of this yourself if you tried hard enough. I did it first, and you are welcome to it.

## Otio

Otio is where everything you make with your GURU turns into something you can own, sell, or share. It is not an app store, and it is not a second-hand marketplace bolted onto a chat app. It is three layers, and only the first one is live.

Layer one, the creator market. You sell whatever you build: skills, tools, agents, masks, and also games, websites, apps, books, NFTs, services and any other digital thing you make. That list is deliberately open. I have named the kinds I have thought of and I am not going to pretend that is the whole of it.

What ships today is the agent market, because agents are what exist so far. The rest of the layer is the same machinery with more item types in front of it.

Layer two, the data marketplace. This is the one I care about most and the one that does not exist yet.

The idea is that GURU stops other apps farming your data, the way a VPN would, and absorbs that traffic itself instead. You see your own captured data, categorised and readable, and you decide what, if anything, to sell. The buyers are the companies already buying that data today, except they buy it straight off you instead of off big tech.

That is the same complaint GURU started from, turned into a business instead of a grievance. Right now the deal is you get spied on for free. Layer two is me offering a version where you get paid. It gets switched on when there are enough backers to do it properly, because it is a big job and I will not ship a half version of it.

Layer three, the social network. A decentralised social layer inside the app, used by both you and your GURUs. Least specified of the three, because it comes last.

Identity is a wallet, not an account. No sign-up, no login, no email capture, no profile the server can attach to a person. You trade under a pseudonym and the server never learns your name.

The money is held by Unus Lumen. I take the funds, hold them, and pay creators out to their accounts. It is not per-transaction settlement and it is not on-chain, and I would rather say that plainly than let anyone assume a decentralised payout that does not exist. The split is 80 percent to the maker, 20 percent plus payment cost

https://github.com/Kiln-AI/harness-tuner.markdown:
### Tune your agent's harness: tools, prompts, skills, model and hyperparams

A real production agent, after tuning: 2.5x fewer failures, 6x cheaper, 2x lower latency. Measured on held-out data, on a smaller model. It's a multi-turn agent with over 200 tools.

Better models move the frontier. A tuned harness gets you above it.

## What it tunes

Most optimizers tune the prompt. Harness Tuner tunes everything around the model.

- Tools. The biggest win we see. Your tools probably wrap APIs written for code, not for agents. It rewrites them for the agent: smaller responses, better descriptions, no repeated calls. When a script should do the job, it writes a new code tool.

- Prompts and skills. It cuts contradictions, adds the requirements nobody wrote down, and moves long instructions into skills that load only when needed.

- Model and settings. It tunes thinking level, temperature and the rest. It keeps your model by default. Allow other models at start-up, or optimize for speed or cost, and it also searches models and providers.

- RAG, fine-tunes and sub-agents. It attaches, swaps or drops the ones in your project.

It tries different methods, not just different words: one big prompt or skills, RAG or a skill, many small tools or one general one.

## How it works

- You set the goal and steer. Optimize for quality, cost or speed. When it cuts cost or latency, it holds quality. Tell it what to focus on and what not to touch, in plain English.

- Many goals, not one number. Bring all your evals. It tracks every one.

- Fix one thing at a time. Each experiment runs only the evals it targets, so trying an idea is cheap. Before anything is promoted, it's checked against every eval. Nothing regresses quietly.

- A graph, not a line. Experiments branch from any earlier version, often from several parents, and the winners merge back.

- Train, val and test, enforced in code. Agents only ever see train. Val decides promotions. Test is never read, so the number you report is one it never optimized against.

- Several winners, your pick. It finds the best quality, the cheapest at good quality, a balanced option and the fastest. Compare them side by side in Kiln .

- Runs on the coding agent you already use: Claude Code, Codex or OpenCode, on your existing subscription.

- Works with Kiln . Our free app tracks every experiment and shows the trade-offs side by side.

## Optimize the demo project

Copies a small moderation task, which ships with the tuner, into a new folder, adds it to Kiln, and tunes it: 624 labelled forum posts, and an eval. The baseline prompt doesn't know the forum's house rules, so there's plenty to find and fix.

> Requires adding an OpenRouter API key to Kiln. The harness-tuner run will cost about $2.

uv tool install harness-tuner harness-tuner --demo

## Quickstart

uv tool install harness-tuner harness-tuner

It walks you through the rest: starting Kiln (or getting it from kiln.tech ), then picking the project and task to tune. Your agent needs to be a task in Kiln, with evals. Kiln can walk you through creating both.

It works in waves until the budget or the clock runs out, wraps up, then writes a report and prints where it is. Details: docs/your-own-task.md .

## What you need

- Kiln , on the same machine. The CLI walks you through installing and starting it.

- An agent, with evals. Kiln can walk you through creating both.

- A coding agent you already use: Claude Code (the default), Codex or OpenCode. The tuner's agents run on your subscription.

- Your model provider keys, stored in Kiln. Used for running the agent being tuned, and evals.

- uv , to install it.

Missing something? docs/install.md has a check and a fix for each requirement.

Harness Tuner is free and open source, but it needs LLM API calls. See docs/costs.md for details.

## Works with Kiln and Seahaven

Tuning an agent takes more than a loop. Kiln and Seahaven have the rest:

- Evals that say what good looks like, as many as your product needs.

- Synthetic users that hold multi-turn conversations, the same for every candidate.

- Synthetic worlds for agents that change data. Every run gets a fresh copy of the world, and evals grade what the agent actually did, not what it said it did.

## FAQ

Prompt optimizers tune the prompts inside a program. Harness Tuner tunes the whole agent you already have: its tools, skills, prompts, model and settings, against every eval you care about.

In a way, that's what it does, with the rigor and scale built in:

- a code loop runs the process, so it can't get off track

- real experiments, each one tracked

- batches of experiments planned and run in parallel

- many evals, each tracked on its own

- cost control: experiments run only the evals they target, winners merge, and ideas that aren't working stop early

- val and test sets withheld from the agents

- skills that guide your coding agent through each step

A tuned harness is easier to deploy (no GPUs, off-the-shelf models), easier to update when new product requirements come up, quicker to move to the latest model releases, and cheaper. Kiln supports fine-tuning too, and the tuner can use your fine-tuned models in advanced cases.

A model router picks a model for each request, based on how hard it guesses the request is. Harness Tuner makes the task easier for the model, by giving your agent the tools and instructions it needs. That often lets every request go to a cheaper model, and it improves quality in ways a bigger model doesn't.

It doesn't touch your original tools. It writes wrappers: small code tools that call your existing tools and reshape what goes in and out. A wrapper can trim a response to the fields that matter, loop over a set of results, fold many calls into one, or do the math so the model doesn't have to. Your tools keep their current signature, so nothing outside Kiln changes.

Kiln builds you evals that use synthetic users. Each eval item sets a persona, a goal and a number of turns, and a model plays the user. The simulated user is the same for every candidate, so comparisons are fair, and its cost is tracked separately from your agent's.

Experiments call your agent's tools, so they need an environment where those tools can run. The best option is a synthetic world for your evals, built with Kiln Seahaven . It gives you a safe, reproducible and highly parallel place to run them.

The tuner's agents only ever see the train split. Val is used only to decide which candidates get promoted. Test is never read by the tuner: you run it for your final report, so the number you quote is one it never optimized against. This is enforced in code, not asked for in a prompt.

Run the tuner again and pick the new model at start-up (or allow any model). It checks the new model against every eval, re-tunes the harness for it if needed, and builds on everything it learned in earlier runs. Upgrading becomes a routine run, not a project.

Harness Tuner runs on Kiln , our free app. Kiln provides:

- Evals: creating and running them ( Kiln evals ).

- Experiment tracking: the provenance of every experiment: what it changed, and which experiments it came from.

- Views of the results: a Compare view to compare experiments on evals, cost and speed, and an Experiment Graph view to see how the tuning progressed.

- Harness history: every experiment's harness is kept, for future experiments and comparisons.

It depends on the scope of the project. A small agent with a small eval can cost a few dollars. A large agent with hundreds of tools can cost several hundred. You set a budget for the model calls through Kiln (your agent CLI's own usage is not counted) and a time limit, and it stops starting new work when either runs out.

Harness Tuner does several things to keep costs down:

- Targeted experiments: each experiment runs only the evals it's trying to improve, and stops early when an idea isn't working.

- No wasted runs: if your evals can't detect a real win, it says so before spending anything.

- Subscription agents: the tuner's own agents run on your existing Claude Code, Codex or OpenCode subscription. It uses some of your quota, but that's usually much cheaper than per-token billing.

Evals need direct API access and can't run on a coding agent subscription, so their tokens bill to your provider keys in Kiln. Details: docs/costs.md .

## Docs

- How it works : the whole loop, with a diagram.

- Install : every requirement, with a check and a fix for each.

- Concepts : waves, experiments, splits and the promotion gate. Read it before your first run's report.

- Your own task : what your task needs, and how the first run starts.

- CLI reference : every command and flag.

- Objectives and models : what to optimize, and which models it may use.

- Costs : estimate a run before you start it.

- Limitations : what it doesn't do. Read it before planning a long run.

- Architecture : the wave loop, the gate, measurement, memory and the sandbox.

- Agents : the ten agent roles and what each one does.

- Agent CLIs : how it runs on Claude Code, Codex and OpenCode.

## Contributing

See CONTRIBUTING.md .

## License

Harness Tuner is MIT licensed .

The Kiln name and logos are trademarks of Chesterfield Laboratories Inc.

# Select

Run your company with AI agents that earn their autonomy.

Agents of any kind — developers, marketers, support, sales — work in an organization you design. Every result is checked by code against a delivery contract, and an agent stops needing your approval only once its verified record shows it can — per task type, revocable at any time.

> Status: 0.2. Accounts, guided setup, local IMAP/SMTP mail tests, routines and the verification loop are covered by end-to-end tests. Docker images build and the Compose stack starts successfully in Ubuntu GitHub Actions CI. Real model API calls have not been verified yet: see Limits .

## Why Select

Multi-agent orchestrators let you decide in advance what agents may do alone. Select replaces that guess with evidence:

- Delivery contracts. Each task type has a YAML contract. The system runs its checks itself and keeps a receipt — contract version and hash, every check, the evidence. A model never declares that a check passed.

- Autonomy earned per agent and task type. Supervised → sampled → autonomous after a streak of verified successes; back to supervised at the first blocking failure or human correction.

- Limits the score never overrides. Payments, contracts, taxes and hiring are always supervised, in code.

- An honest counter. The share of work finished without a person is always shown next to the rate of errors people found afterwards.

- No invented numbers. Every value carries its source; a quantity that is not in the customer's e-mail fails verification.

Both diagrams are SVG and can be reviewed or edited directly in the repository.

## What it does

These four come from the end-to-end test run against local IMAP and SMTP test servers ( E2E_SCREENSHOTS_DIR ); the others are the demo company. All are real captures.

## Explore the interface

These are real Playwright screenshots of Select running locally with fictional demo data . No external model provider or mailbox is connected in this capture session.

## Quickstart

Requirements: Docker Desktop (Windows, macOS) or Docker Engine with Compose (Linux).

git clone https://github.com/Kirby54/Select.git select cd select ./start.sh # Windows: .\start.ps1

The script writes .env with random secrets (keep a copy), starts the containers and opens http://localhost:3000 , where the first visit creates your account. Without the script: cp .env.example .env , set the secrets, docker compose up --build .

No API key yet? Open the demo company from the account menu and press Run demo week .

Five-minute guide: docs/getting-started.md . Development setup without Docker: docs/installation.md .

## How autonomy works

Default promotion thresholds are 20 and 50 verified successes in a row — starting hypotheses to calibrate, not proven values . An e-mail to an address that never wrote to you always goes to a person. Details: docs/autonomy.md .

## A contract

id : support_reply version : 1 title : Support reply risk : medium required : [to, subject, body] checks : - id : recipient_from_message rule : provenance # the address must be the one that wrote to us params : { fields: [to] } - id : no_unauthorised_promises rule : forbidden_phrases params : { field: body, phrases: ["refund", "discount", "guarantee"] } approval : mode : by_autonomy external_action : send_email

More in docs/verification.md .

## Architecture

Next.js 16 web app → FastAPI API → PostgreSQL 16, with a worker on a durable PostgreSQL job queue that runs agents, reads mailboxes, sends approved e-mail and fires routines. select-verify is a separate Python library with no database or network access. See docs/architecture.md and the interface's design system .

## Security

Agents never hold a permission to send, pay or sign; the server applies the approval rules and sends. External content is treated as data and checked against stored sources. Passwords use Argon2id; sessions live in an HttpOnly cookie with an anti-forgery header; provider keys and mailbox passwords are encrypted. Read docs/security.md and docs/deployment.md before opening Select to a network.

## Tests

make test # Python verifier/API tests on PostgreSQL plus frontend unit tests make e2e # Playwright UI scenarios against a running stack

e2e/complete.spec.ts (4 more scenarios) runs on a password-mode stack with the local mail servers of scripts/dev-mail.py : first owner, guided setup, a real IMAP mailbox, an e-mail triaged, routed, quoted, approved and sent once over SMTP (the .eml file is checked), a weekly routine seen from a New York browser on Paris time, and an invited colleague joining.

## Verify a real model (optional)

The CI tests use network doubles, not real provider keys. Before connecting production data, use the explicit live-provider probe with your own test credentials . It sends a harmless fixed JSON-generation prompt and reports whether the chosen model returns the expected result. It never stores the key or accesses company data. Real-provider compatibility is not yet certified by the maintainers.

## Benchmarks

None published yet. The protocol ( autonomy-bench : same tasks and models, autonomy rate and undetected-error rate side by side, compared with a single agent and with Paperclip) is in bench/README.md . Until it runs, Select makes no comparative claim. Feature parity is tracked honestly in docs/parity.md .

## Limits

- Provider calls have not been exercised against real paid-model APIs (no keys in CI). An Ollama-compatible localhost HTTP stub is used to test the full worker, deterministic verification and approval pipeline; it does not execute a real model.

- Docker : GitHub Actions builds both images, starts PostgreSQL, API, worker and web with Compose, and reaches the API health endpoint through the web proxy on Ubuntu. The start.sh script itself was tested with a stand-in Docker CLI; real macOS/Windows installations and start.ps1 have not been exercised in CI.

- Mailboxes were tested against local IMAP and SMTP servers, not yet at a real provider. No OAuth: Microsoft 365 and Outlook.com cannot connect yet; Gmail needs an app password.

- Agents write text and structured results through model APIs. Code-change proposals can be checked for basic diff structure and sent to mandatory human review, but no repository code is edited, executed or pushed by Select. There is no isolated Claude Code or Codex runtime yet. See review-only code proposals .

- Attachments are not read; quotes are sent as e-mail text, without a PDF.

- No e-invoice : the invoice draft is not an XRechnung or ZUGFeRD file and is never presented as compliant. Businesses exempt from VAT ( franchise en base ) are not handled properly yet.

- No single sign-on, two-factor authentication, plugins or sandboxed code execution.

## Documentation

Five minutes · Installation · Provider probe · Configuration · Mail · Agents · Autonomy · Verification · Workflows and routines · Architecture · Deployment · Security · Troubleshooting · Design system · Français

## Contributing

Start with CONTRIBUTING.md . Good first contributions: a new contract for a task type you know, or a new deterministic rule — each with one accepted and one rejected example.

## Roadmap

- Verify with real model keys and real mailboxes; keep Docker startup, recovery and tests green across supported environments.

- Coding-agent runtimes: run Claude Code or Codex in a code workspace, verify with the project's tests, approve the exact diff.

- Run without Docker (embedded database), like a one-command install.

- Quote PDFs, attachments, OAuth mailboxes, VAT-exempt businesses.

- Run autonomy-bench and publish the raw results.

## Licence

The application ( apps/ ) is licensed under AGPL-3.0-only ( LICENSE ). The select-verify library is licensed under Apache-2.0 ( packages/select-verify/LICENSE ) so that other tools can adopt delivery contracts freely.

## Support

Questions and ideas: GitHub Discussions. Bugs: GitHub Issues. Vulnerabilities: privately, see SECURITY.md .

# agent-access-review User access reviews for AI agents. It finds every agent and MCP server an organization runs, works out what each one can read, write, execute and send, tests that access against 12 controls, and produces the packet an auditor expects: a reviewer sign-off sheet, hashed evidence, and OSCAL assessment results mapped to NIST 800-53, SOC 2, NIST AI RMF and the OWASP Top 10 for LLM Applications. > In one sentence: the quarterly "who has access to what?" review that companies already run for employees, applied to AI agents. > Real-world case study: what you get by copying the MCP configs from official READMEs : 8 of 9 unpinned, 7 of 9 with unreviewed write/send/execute access, and an exfiltration path once they're combined. ## Quick start (2 minutes) You need Python 3.11+. No cloud account, API keys or network access. pip install agent-access-review agent-access-review demo demo reviews five example agents and writes the packet to review-demo/ . Open review-demo/access-review.md , or just read the sample report here without installing anything. Then review your own setup: Secrets in your configs are masked before anything is written, so the output is safe to share. ## Problem Every SOX and SOC 2 program runs quarterly user access reviews: list who has access to what, have an owner confirm it's still needed, revoke the rest, keep the evidence. AI agents now hold the same kind of access (API tokens, database connections, shell access, mailboxes), and almost nobody reviews them: - No owner, no approval. A developer adds an MCP server to their Claude Desktop or Cursor config and the agent instantly has their GitHub token and home directory. No ticket, no approver, and it never appears in an access review. - Over-broad by default. Setup guides tell people to grant the whole home directory, the full-control repo scope, or tenant-wide *.All Microsoft Graph permissions. - Secrets in plain text. MCP configs routinely hold raw tokens and database passwords. - A new attack path. An agent that can read sensitive data, read content an attacker wrote (a GitHub issue, an email, a web page), and send data out can be prompt-injected into leaking that data. No traditional access control looks at that combination. Agents are non-human identities. They need the same joiner/mover/leaver and recertification controls as people, plus a few that are specific to AI. ## What it checks Each control is defined once in controls.yaml and cross-walked to every framework, so one test produces evidence for all of them. The mappings are my own judgment and should be checked against official crosswalks before being relied on in a real audit. ## The AI-specific risk: exfiltration paths (AAR-09) Traditional access reviews look at one permission at a time. For AI agents, the danger is a combination : an agent that can read sensitive data, reads content an outsider wrote, and can send data out. Each leg is harmless alone. Together, one prompt injection hidden in an email, ticket, issue or web page can instruct the agent to leak the data. # Mintigate demo (offline)

Offline demonstration — simulated agent, simplified demo runtime. Proprietary Mintigate Runtime not executed.

This folder is a small, deterministic demonstration that you can read in full and run on your own computer. A simulated agent proposes three fixed changes to a synthetic two-file fixture. A simplified demo runtime decides on each change in a temporary copy of the fixture, and an independent check confirms what happened.

## What it shows

Each decision is recorded with the SHA-256 of the target before and after, in a report.

## What you need

- This folder, as received.

- Node.js 18 or later. Nothing else: no package to install, no Git, no Claude Code, no SDK, no network access, no account and no model call.

## Run it

Open a terminal in this folder (on Windows, PowerShell or Windows Terminal) and run:

node mintigate-demo.mjs

The demo takes no option. There is no live mode.

## Exit codes

## What it writes

- Each run creates a new folder .output/run-<date>-<random>/ in this folder. Earlier runs are never changed.

- The fixture is copied into workspace/ inside that new folder, and the changes are made there only. The shipped fixture/ folder is never written.

- At the end of the run, even after an error, the demo removes the files and folders of that workspace/ one by one. It removes nothing else.

- What remains is one report: .output/run-<date>-<random>/report.json . It holds the decisions, the audit records, the hashes, the checks, the negative controls, the clean-up count and the hashes of the demo files that were used. It contains no absolute path of your computer.

Nothing is written outside .output/ , and no setting of your computer is changed. To remove everything, delete this folder.

## How the checks work

smoke-test.mjs does not use demo-runtime.mjs to judge the outcome. It copies the fixture, reads the files itself, computes their hashes and compares them with the expectations in scenarios.json :

- the decision of each scenario;

- for the applied change: exactly the expected line changed, and nothing else;

- for the other two: the target is unchanged, or was not created;

- the hashes in each audit record match the files;

- every protected file and every file outside the scope is unchanged, no file was created or deleted, the shipped fixture is unchanged, and the temporary copy was removed.

It then runs negative controls: deliberately wrong expectations or observations, such as expecting the refused change to be applied or pretending that the protected file changed. Each one must make a named check fail. If a contradiction went unnoticed, the run ends with code 1.

## Files

## Limits

- The agent is simulated: its three proposals are fixed in scenarios.json . No model is called.

- The runtime is a simplified demo runtime of a few rules: a folder or file scope, a list of protected files, and exact text replacements. It is not the proprietary Mintigate Runtime, which this demo does not contain or execute.

- The demo works only on its own synthetic fixture. It does not run on your repository, does not watch or intercept your tools, and has no approval command.

- It is not a benchmark and measures no performance.

## Licence

The MIT licence in LICENSE applies to the files of this kit only.

### Try a deliberate mismatch

In a separate copy of the demo, open scenarios.json . For protected-file-change , change expect.decision from PENDING_APPROVAL to APPLIED , then run:

The demo should exit with code 1: the protected change still requires approval, and the independent check rejects your altered expectation. Inspect the generated report.json to see the decision, failed checks, and file hashes.

You control this local demo and can change its policies or code. It illustrates governance rules; it does not protect against its own administrator.

## Beyond the demo

This demo illustrates scoped changes, human approval boundaries, and audit records using a deterministic agent and a simplified runtime.

Mintigate is being developed to help developers govern real agent workflows. This demo does not execute its proprietary Runtime or connect to a live model.

Explore the project, current evaluation results, and limitations: https://mintigate.com

# Laplace’s Scissors

English · 한국어

Source · Issues · Discussions

Rotate an LLM’s output matrix to compute edits while preserving protected answers.

Rust · Triton · CUDA / HIP · Readout rotation

Quick start · Commands · Implementation and tests · Math and design

Laplace’s Scissors computes rotation edits for an LLM’s original output matrix. probe constructs numerical inputs from model weights and traces directions with weak output discrimination, cancellation across layers, and the associated weight coordinates. diagnose uses cases with expected answer strings to find plane or joint rotations that repair failed answers while protecting successful ones. Each objective and protection condition is checked with actual GPU outputs. Scaling analysis applies the same edit policy across checkpoints to measure deviations from a reference curve and the amount recovered.

flowchart LR A[Original checkpoint] --> B[Observe hidden states] B --> C[Protected readout rotation] C --> D[GPU validation] D --> E[Accepted proposal] E --> F[Generate or export]

## Commands

## Quick start

### Environment

Prepare a Rust toolchain, a Python environment that can import Triton 3.8, and a CUDA or HIP driver. Python provides the Triton compilation bridge. Rust handles model loading, tokenization, execution, edit computation, and result storage.

export LAPLACE_CACHE= " ${XDG_CACHE_HOME :- $HOME / .cache} /laplaces-scissors " export LAPLACE_PYTHON=python3 cargo build --release

.cargo/config.toml places Cargo build artifacts outside the project. LAPLACE_CACHE stores models, kernels, and run results. Select the backend and device index with LAPLACE_BACKEND=auto|cuda|hip and LAPLACE_DEVICE . Set LAPLACE_DRIVER_LIBRARY for the driver library path, or ROCM_PATH / HIP_PATH for the ROCm SDK. The HIP backend also checks the selected Python environment for the rocm-sdk-core package. Device names and execution targets come from the driver.

### Fetch a model and prepare inputs

cargo run --release -- fetch Qwen/Qwen3-0.6B cargo run --release -- inspect Qwen/Qwen3-0.6B --out " $LAPLACE_CACHE /graph.json " cargo run --release -- cases --count 12 --seed 7 --out " $LAPLACE_CACHE /cases.jsonl "

Model inputs accept organization/model , organization/model@revision , a Hugging Face model URL, or a local safetensors model directory. Hub inputs are pinned to a commit SHA, with SHA256 recorded for each file. Use --revision to select a revision and HF_TOKEN for authentication.

Check an answer from the original model:

cargo run --release -- generate Qwen/Qwen3-0.6B \ --prompt ' What is 2 + 2? Reply with the number only. '

### Case format

Write custom cases as JSONL. expected is the zero-based index of the correct entry in choices . The choices specify the expected answer; the model generates an answer string for prompt . See the example below and the example JSONL .

{ "id" : " sum " , "prompt" : " What is 2 + 2? Reply with the number only. " , "choices" :[ " 3 " , " 4 " , " 5 " ], "expected" : 1 , "oracle" :{ "sum" : 4 }}

The original chat template builds the prompt, whose token prefix stays fixed. The expected answer is encoded separately and followed by EOS to form the target token sequence. The answer body must survive a tokenizer round trip exactly. When the original generation ends with EOS and exactly matches the expected string, every prefix of that generation is protected. For failed cases, each target answer token and EOS must score above every competing token in the vocabulary.

## Compute and apply edits

Numerical probes · Answer repair · Checkpoint export · Scaling analysis

### Numerical probes · probe

probe takes model weights and an execution graph. Seeded selections of embedding rows form numerical prefixes, a reference vector, and an orthonormal basis. Two vectors with the same norm as the reference vector are injected directly at the decoder input. Responses are compared with Jeffreys divergence, the symmetric KL divergence between output distributions. A weak direction has low output discrimination between equal-sized injections under the recorded numerical input distribution. Model acquisition for this command loads safetensors and configuration files.

cargo run --release -- probe Qwen/Qwen3-0.6B \ --directions 12 --prefix-length 3 --seed 7 --probe-angle 0.05 \ --max-angle-degrees 3 --coordinates 12 --intervention-fraction 0.1 \ --out " $LAPLACE_CACHE /runs/probe " cargo run --release -- probe Qwen/Qwen3-0.6B \ --inputs " $LAPLACE_CACHE /runs/probe/inputs.json " \ --proposal " $LAPLACE_CACHE /runs/probe/proposal.json " \ --out " $LAPLACE_CACHE /runs/probe-replay "

--directions sets the maximum dimension of the search basis constructed from weights. The actual dimension follows the hidden width and the rank of embedding differences. --prefix-length sets the number of numerical vectors before the injection position. --probe-angle is the spherical angle used to construct the two inputs, in radians. The minimum eigenvector of a small response Gram matrix proposes a direction; measurements through the actual decoder compare its divergence with that of the existing basis directions.

Residual branches from the selected pair of runs provide signed layer contributions. The branch with the largest negative contribution supplies --coordinates weight coordinates and attention-head totals. --intervention-fraction controls diagnostic interventions that change each selected coordinate’s magnitude in both directions. Each intervention reruns from the fixed numerical prefix. Signed contributions and measured intervention effects are recorded separately. --coordinates 0 performs layer tracing; --intervention-fraction 0 performs divergence tracing and protected rotation.

The edit is a readout rotation that protects the original output matrix’s row Gram matrix, the midpoint of the two hidden states, and reference and control states. --max-angle-degrees , --max-edit-norm , and --tolerance set bounds on angle, weight change, and protected-output error. Among three candidates within the angle bound, the program saves an edit that increases measured divergence and satisfies the protection tolerance. Candidates apply actual GPU rotation and readout to observed hidden states. --inputs loads saved inputs; protected_hidden can hold additional protected vectors from the same model. Adding --proposal reruns the saved input pair through the full decoder.

Probe outputs are manifest.json , inputs.json , trace.json , transport.json , report.json , status.json , and an accepted proposal.json . Replay also records replay-frames.json . Results include input and model hashes, actual hardware and precision, divergence, layers and weight coordinates, preservation errors, numerical residuals, and execution counts by stage. Proposal version 3 stores the divergence objective and injection-input hash. Reapplication verifies weight and execution-configuration hashes.

### Answer repair · diagnose

cargo run --release -- diagnose Qwen/Qwen3-0.6B \ --cases " $LAPLACE_CACHE /cases.jsonl " \ --max-planes 8 --max-angle-degrees 120 --margin 0.05 \ --max-new-tokens 64 --context 2048 --time-budget 20m \ --out " $LAPLACE_CACHE /runs/rotation " cargo run --release -- generate Qwen/Qwen3-0.6B \ --prompt ' What is 2 + 2? Reply with the number only. ' \ --proposal " $LAPLACE_CACHE /runs/rotation/proposal.json "

--max-planes sets the number of rotation planes to investigate. --max-angle-degrees bounds the rotation angle, and --margin sets the minimum logit gap between each target token and every competitor. --tolerance bounds each protected-output change divided by 1 + |original logit| ; its default is 0.00002 . The inequalities include a numerical allowance derived from this tolerance and the observed logit magnitude. For each plane, merged forbidden intervals yield the angle with the smallest weight change. Candidates are checked with actual GPU readout in order of weight change.

After checking plane candidates, a joint response computation adjusts multiple targets together. --joint-steps sets the number of adjustment steps and defaults to 12; setting it to 0 runs the plane candidates. --joint-rank sets the maximum joint rotation basis dimension and defaults to 64. --max-angle-degrees also bounds the joint rotation’s largest principal angle. --max-edit-norm bounds the Frobenius norm of the output-weight change. Acceptance requires the full-vocabulary margin, protected-output tolerance, target answer and EOS, and preservation of originally successful generation paths.

Joint search computes and shares the output basis and cost Gram matrix once. When twice the response count is smaller than the rotation dimension, it solves the Cayley system in that smaller space. Candidate scores use the compressed output basis on the GPU. After search, a rotation completion minimizes weight change while preserving observations. The original GPU readout checks that the completion stays within angle and cost bounds and preserves every prefix’s token choice, satisfied margins, and protected-output tolerance. completion in candidates.json records costs before and after completion and whether it was applied. computation in report.json records compressed-output and original-validation call counts and timings by computation stage.

--max-new-tokens bounds generated tokens, including EOS. --context must accommodate the prompt plus that generation allowance. Omitting --cases generates symbolic problems using --count and --seed . Diagnosis uses the original template with thinking disabled. generate --thinking selects the thinking format.

The time budget starts with model loading after file acquisition and covers computation and attribution. The output directory contains manifest.json , status.json , baseline.json , candidates.json , report.json , and accepted proposal.json and attribution.json files. Reports record the model revision, input token paths, weight dtypes, hardware, measured validation values, and square-root and readout call counts. Status values are complete for completion, partial for budget expiration, and failed for execution errors.

A proposal contains either orthonormal plane vectors and a half-angle coordinate, or an orthonormal joint basis and a small orthogonal matrix. At runtime, the final hidden vector is rotated before multiplication by the original output matrix. In models with shared embeddings, rotation applies at readout calls. Reapplying an answer-repair proposal checks hashes for weights, configuration, and tokenizer files, plus the output-operation contract. generate --proposal reads proposal versions 1, 2, and 3.

#### Output-row attribution

--attribution-rows sets the number of output rows to report and defaults to 6. For each row, results include high-contribution coordinates, the loss after reverting that row’s edit, the total contribution sum, and integration error. Contributions follow the specified straight-line readout intervention path and retain negative values. Setting the option to 0 saves the generation proposal and validation results.

### Checkpoint export · export

export saves a new checkpoint with the proposal applied to the output matrix. It preserves original tensors and writes the edited lm_head.weight in FP32. It unties embedding and readout weights and saves configuration, execution graph, and shard index files. The output matrix uses CPU F64 block multiplication; original-model loading and contract checks use the shared model runtime. Run the exported model using its directory path.

cargo run --release -- export Qwen/Qwen3-1.7B \ --proposal " $LAPLACE_CACHE /edits/proposal.json " \ --out " $LAPLACE_CACHE /exports/qwen3-1.7b-edited " cargo run --release -- generate " $LAPLACE_CACHE /exports/qwen3-1.7b-edited " \ --prompt ' What is 2 + 2? Reply with the number only. '

materialization.json records the original revision and hashes, applied proposal, measured weight-change norm, and FP32 storage rounding e

# Infinix — Local Autonomous Agent for Windows and Linux

> ⚠️ Project Status: ABANDONED / BASE FOR COMMUNITY. This project is no longer actively maintained by the original creator. The codebase is released as an open-source foundation for anyone to fork, improve, modify, or build upon. The only requirement: your derivative work must also remain free and open-source (GPL-3.0).

> Original Creator: Moonyeep - Built with Manus AI, based on ZeroScript architecture

Infinix is a local autonomous AI agent for Windows and Linux, controlled through supported browser-based AI chats. Its local bridge provides endpoint diagnostics, workspace tools, browser automation, shell access under a selectable capability profile, and hierarchical multi-agent delegation. No separate model API key is required for browser providers.

## 📢 About This Project

This project was created by Moonyeep using Manus AI , built upon the ZeroScript architecture. The original creator has abandoned this project and is releasing it as an open-source base for the community.

Why release this?

- The project works but needs significant improvements

- Looking for capable developers to take this base and make it better

- Fork it, modify it, rebuild it - do whatever you want

- Only requirement: Your derivative work must remain FREE and OPEN-SOURCE (GPL-3.0)

- No commercial use without keeping it open-source

Roblox Studio is an optional integration. When enabled, Infinix can also control Studio through its MCP server; the general local agent does not require Roblox Studio.

Eight AI providers are supported: DeepSeek (chat.deepseek.com, recommended), ChatGPT (chatgpt.com), Google Gemini (gemini.google.com), Kimi (kimi.ai, Moonshot AI), GLM (chat.z.ai, Z.ai), Qwen (chat.qwen.ai), Arena (arena.ai, a multi-model playground) and Meta AI (meta.ai). On ChatGPT, screenshots and image input are turned off on purpose: the free tier limits files and images on a separate quota from messages, so vision would only work part of the day. Gemini and Kimi can be unstable: Gemini tends to stop using the Roblox tools in long sessions, and Kimi sometimes uses its own native tools instead of the Roblox commands. On Arena, use Direct mode (Infinix only supports Direct; it blocks Start in Battle / Side-by-Side / Agent modes). DeepSeek is the recommended provider.

> 💬 Discord community: Join here for help and discussions.

> Also known as: Free Claude Code alternative, Free Codex alternative, OpenClaw without API key, Infinix Roblox, Infinix free download, Roblox ChatGPT agent, Roblox DeepSeek agent, Roblox Gemini agent, Roblox Kimi agent, Roblox GLM agent, Roblox Qwen agent, Roblox Arena agent, Roblox Meta AI agent, Roblox Studio AI automation, Luau AI, MCP Roblox, lemonade alternative free, lemonade.gg alternative, free Roblox AI agent, free lemonade roblox alternative

## ⚠️ Infinix is Free Beware of Paid Copycats

Infinix is 100% free and open-source. It always has been, and it always will be. There is no official paid version, no subscription, and no sign-in required to use the extension.

If you come across a site or extension using the Infinix name that asks for payment or account creation, it is not this project. The only official links are the ones listed at the top of this README.

## How it works

AI chat in browser <-> Infinix Extension <-> local Bridge -> endpoint/workspace tools and optional MCP integrations (including Roblox Studio)

The extension runs inside a supported chat page and connects to the local bridge on the same PC. The bridge provides enabled local diagnostics, workspace and process tools; the extension provides browser automation. Roblox Studio is optional and its tools appear only when that integration is enabled.

## Multi-agent teams

The supervisor can delegate bounded tasks to providers authorized at startup. Each worker runs in an inactive tab in a minimized dedicated Infinix team window with a separate per-tab ToolRegistry, so provider pages do not take focus or remain visibly open. Workers use the Basic profile and read-only diagnostics/workspace tools, including source search and Git inspection; they do not inherit terminal access, browser control, file writes, remediation, or the supervisor's Amplo permissions. Delegating children requires explicit allow_children and is bounded by the session concurrency setting and a three-level depth limit. Spawn slots are reserved before asynchronous tab creation, preventing parallel requests from exceeding the configured limit. Worker startup can take up to two minutes before a handshake timeout, and status remains starting until the provider is ready. Tool results are returned through the same result envelope as other extension tools so the supervisor receives the assigned task ID, rather than an empty {} response. Supervisor/worker messages are routed through the local bridge with direct-parent/child checks; message retries are idempotent only when the original sender and content match. agent.team.status preserves its direct-child response by default and can optionally return include_descendants=true with a bounded hierarchy and state counts. Hidden tabs continue to run where the browser allows it, but browser or OS suspension can pause them.

Reliability requirements for slow provider startup, hidden-tab execution and bridge-mediated team messaging are tracked in MULTIAGENT_RELIABILITY_REQUIREMENTS.md ; some items still require implementation.

## Software development workflow

For repository work, the local agent can load root AGENTS.md / CLAUDE.md guidance and common project manifests with workspace.context , search literal source text with workspace.search , and inspect local changes using git.status and bounded git.diff . File reads support bounded line ranges. The recommended flow is to inspect repository guidance and existing changes first, search call sites before editing, make focused changes, add targeted tests, run relevant checks, and review the resulting diff. These additions provide repository context and code navigation; worker agents remain read-only and should return findings/evidence to the supervisor.

Core regression tests: python3 -m unittest discover -q . Extension tests: run node over each zeroscript-extension/test-*.js file from the repository root.

## Reusable skills

The package includes 12 task skills for endpoint diagnostics, incident response, browser automation, software development, testing, study, secure downloads, Linux privileged operations, research, data analysis, administrative assistance and multi-agent delegation. See skills/INDEX.md . The agent should load only the relevant skill and references; these guides do not grant permissions or override the active profile.

## Setup

Linux is supported with Chrome/Chromium or Edge and the start_agent.sh launcher. The launcher automatically prepares Python dependencies; see INSTALL_LINUX.md.

On Linux, the Amplo session can use the terminal.run_as_admin tool when sudo is available. If needed, the OS desktop opens its askpass authentication dialog. Enter the password there—not in the chat. It is passed directly to sudo, never to the model or Infinix logs, and is not stored by Infinix; the system may cache sudo authorization until its normal timeout.

📺 Setup tutorial on YouTube covers every step below.

### 1. Download the zip and install the extension

Download the latest zip from the Releases page and extract it. The zip contains both the Bridge and the extension folder.

On Linux, Chrome/Chromium and Edge are supported. To load the extension:

- Go to edge://extensions (Edge) or chrome://extensions (Chrome)

- Enable Developer mode (top right toggle)

- Click Load unpacked

- Select the zeroscript-extension folder from the extracted zip

### 2. (Optional) Connect Roblox Studio

Open Studio and load a Place, then enable MCP (first time only):

- Click Assistant AI in the top bar

- Click ... (top right of the Assistant panel)

- Click Manage MCP Servers

- Click Enable Studio as MCP Server

Not sure where to find these options? The video tutorial shows exactly where to click.

### 3. Run the Bridge

Windows: double-click start.bat inside the extracted folder.

macOS: double-click MacOS_Start.command inside the extracted folder. The first time, macOS will show a security warning ("could not verify... free of malware") - this is normal for any script downloaded outside the App Store, click Done, then go to System Settings > Privacy & Security, scroll to the bottom, and click Open Anyway. You only need to do this once.

Linux: open a terminal in the extracted project folder and run chmod +x start_agent.sh (if needed), then ./start_agent.sh . It creates a local virtual environment, installs websockets, and downloads Python 3.12 into your user directories if the system only has an older Python (e.g. Ubuntu 20.04). It does not use sudo or change system packages. See INSTALL_LINUX.md.

Keep the terminal/window open while using Infinix. The General Agent does not require Roblox Studio; enable the Studio MCP server only when you want Roblox-specific tools.

### 4. Start a session

Go to https://chat.deepseek.com (recommended), https://chatgpt.com , https://gemini.google.com , https://www.kimi.ai , https://chat.z.ai , https://chat.qwen.ai , https://arena.ai or https://www.meta.ai and open a new chat. The Infinix bar appears above the input box. Click Start session. Type what you want to build.

Only works on chat.deepseek.com, chatgpt.com, gemini.google.com, kimi.ai, chat.z.ai, chat.qwen.ai, arena.ai and meta.ai - it will not work on any other site. If the AI starts answering in plain text instead of acting, remind it to use the commands or start a new session.

### 5. Watch the setup tutorial

Watch the setup tutorial on YouTube
