Octomind is a CLI-first AI coding agent runtime. It gives an LLM real access to your repo — reading and writing files, running shells, searching code, delegating to sub-agents — through MCP tools. The same session engine works interactively , piped through stdin , as a background daemon , over WebSocket , or as an ACP sub-agent inside another agent's stack.

# Interactive octomind run developer:general # Piped — CI, scripts, automation echo " Explain the auth module " | octomind run developer:general --format plain # Daemon — keep it alive, talk to it from another terminal echo " watch the build " | octomind run --name watcher --daemon --format jsonl octomind send --name watcher " run the test suite "

## Why Octomind?

Most coding agents assume a human is watching the screen. Octomind is built for the work that keeps going after you leave.

- Policy as code, not approval popups. Deterministic guardrails — pre-call guards, post-result hooks, post-turn validators — live in TOML and scripts, so they work in CI, daemons, and scheduled runs.

- Proven on real PRs. It solved 24 of 25 held-out tasks at lower cost than the closest competitor. See the benchmarks .

- Ready-made specialists. octomind run developer:general pulls a packaged agent (prompt, model, MCP servers, tool permissions) from a tap . Publish your own with one repo.

- Sessions that stay sharp. Adaptive compression keeps long tasks moving while retaining task knowledge and the live exchange.

- Any model, any budget. Use Octomind Cloud or your own key (OpenRouter, Anthropic, OpenAI, DeepSeek, Ollama, and more), pick a model per role, and set spend thresholds per request and per session. A request over its threshold stops; at the session threshold a terminal session asks y/N before continuing, while a non-interactive octomind run stops with exit code 75.

- One config. Models, tools, roles, guardrails, budgets: all TOML, no framework code.

## Quick Start

1. Install (macOS, Linux):

curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/muvon/octomind/master/install.sh | bash

On Windows, in PowerShell:

irm https: // raw.githubusercontent.com / muvon / octomind / master / install.ps1 | iex

On macOS, you can also install with Homebrew:

brew install muvon/tap/octomind

2. Get model access. The fastest path is Octomind Cloud, which includes models and needs no configuration:

octomind login

Prefer your own provider key? Skip login and export one (also OPENAI_API_KEY , ANTHROPIC_API_KEY , DEEPSEEK_API_KEY ), then follow Model access to point the config at it:

export OPENROUTER_API_KEY= " your_key "

3. Run a specialist in your project:

cd ~ /your/project octomind run developer:general

You're now in a session with an agent that can read your code, run commands, and edit files. The interface is a plain line prompt with markdown rendering — no TUI to learn, so it works over SSH, in tmux , and in CI logs. The first time you run a specialist, it may install its tools and ask for credentials.

> developer:general comes from the default tap muvon/tap , not your local config. Plain octomind run starts the config's default role, assistant:concierge .

Try the recorded bug-fix demo : two failing tests, an agent fix, and an independent test rerun.

## Benchmarks

Measured on octobench against 25 tasks harvested from merged pull requests across Python, PHP, Rust, C++, and JavaScript. Each agent works in the pre-fix repo; held-out tests from the merged fix decide pass or fail. These are the published July 30, 2026 results, not a measurement of this checkout.

- The harness matters. opencode used the same model and endpoint; octomind solved 24 vs 19 at roughly half the cost. All four agents ran stock invocations with no tuning, so this measures the whole harness, not individual features.

- Worst-case pricing, still ahead. glm-5.2 ran without prompt caching while Opus billed ~97% of context re-reads at cache rates — and octomind still led on solves, cost, and wall time.

- Reproducible. Per-case table, artifacts, and reproduction guide: BENCHMARK.md . Background: blog post .

## Guardrails: Policy as Code

Drop a .agents/guardrails.toml in your repo. The runtime enforces it deterministically, with no code to compile and no plugin to install.

# Pre-call deny — block a class of calls before they execute [[ guard ]] match = " shell(command=^rm \\ s+-rf?) " message = " rm -rf blocked. " # Conditional rule — only fires after the agent ran git status this session [[ guard ]] match = " shell(command=git push) " when = [ " +shell(command=git status) " ] message = " Review changes before pushing. "

Hook and validator script examples: Guardrails guide .

## Five Ways to Run It

The same session engine, exposed however your workflow needs it.

Need machine-readable results? Pass --schema schema.json to constrain the final response to a JSON Schema (requires a model with structured-output support). See Structured output .

## Features

### Specialists

octomind run developer:general # general dev, language skills auto-activate octomind run doctor:blood # blood-test interpretation specialist octomind run lawyer:sg # legal specialist

Running a specialist fetches its manifest from the tap registry, installs any required binaries, resolves credentials, starts the right MCP servers, and then opens the session.

Build and register your own:

octomind tap init yourteam/my-tap # scaffold, validate, git-init, and register locally octomind tap yourteam/my-tap # on another machine, after publishing to GitHub

The octomind- prefix is added automatically: yourteam/my-tap maps to the repository yourteam/octomind-my-tap .

## Installation

The install script detects your OS and architecture (Linux and macOS on x86_64/aarch64) and installs to ~/.local/bin/ . Pass --install-dir <DIR> or set OCTOMIND_INSTALL_DIR to override. On Windows (x86_64/aarch64), install.ps1 installs to %LOCALAPPDATA%\octomind\bin and adds it to your user PATH ; it honors OCTOMIND_INSTALL_DIR and OCTOMIND_VERSION too. install.sh still works from Git Bash or MSYS2.

Command not found? Add the install directory to your PATH :

export PATH= " $HOME /.local/bin: $PATH "

Building from source requires protoc ; see Building from source for per-OS prerequisites.

Verify:

octomind --version octomind config # generate the default config octomind run # start your first session

Shell completions: octomind completion <bash|zsh|fish|elvish|powershell> .

### Model access

Octomind Cloud — octomind login (device-code sign-in, like gh auth login ) stores a gateway key locally. The default config already uses octohub:auto . Learn more .

Bring your own key — set the provider's environment variable ( OPENROUTER_API_KEY , OPENAI_API_KEY , ANTHROPIC_API_KEY , DEEPSEEK_API_KEY , …) and point the model tables at it. The supervisor and compression profiles also default to octohub:auto , so update all three:

[ model ] name = " openrouter:google/gemini-2.5-flash " [ supervisor . model ] name = " openrouter:google/gemini-2.5-flash " [ compression . model ] name = " openrouter:google/gemini-2.5-flash "

Provider details and per-role overrides: Providers & models .

## Configuration

Config lives at ~/.local/share/octomind/config/config.toml on macOS and Linux, and under %LOCALAPPDATA%/octomind/config/ on Windows. Set OCTOMIND_DATA_DIR to override the data root.

octomind config --show # view current config octomind config --validate # validate config

Override any value for a single run with -c :

octomind run -c supervisor.enabled=false

Full reference: Configuration reference · Environment variables .

### Session commands

Full list: Session commands .

### Telemetry

Octomind reports anonymous usage: which commands, tools, and models are used, plus timings, token counts, and error kinds. It never sends your code, prompts, file paths, tool arguments, or environment values. Opt out in any of three ways:

export DO_NOT_TRACK=1 # the cross-tool standard, honored first export OCTOMIND_TELEMETRY=0 # for subsequent commands in this shell # or set `telemetry = false` in config.toml

Exact field list: Telemetry .

## Documentation

Full index: doc/README.md · Hosted: octomind.run/docs .

## Contributing

The most impactful contribution isn't code — it's specialist agents. A cardiologist publishing doctor:medications . A tax attorney publishing lawyer:us . A security researcher publishing security:owasp . One TOML file, and everyone facing that problem gets a specialist-grade AI.

- How to write a tap agent

- Open issues

Code contributions are welcome too. Set up the hooks and run the gate before you push:

pip install pre-commit && pre-commit install make dev # fmt + clippy + test

Commits follow Conventional Commits . Full guide, architecture overview, and code conventions: CONTRIBUTING.md · internals: Architecture .

Community participation follows our Code of Conduct . Report vulnerabilities privately using the security policy .

https://github.com/Ninnix/lokey.markdown:
Lokey is an Android keyboard with local word prediction, dictation and translation. The models run on your phone. Writing a message does not require an account, a subscription or a connection to an inference service.

The keyboard is native Kotlin and Android Canvas, with a C11 bridge to the inference runtimes. It supports 39 languages , eleven keyboard families, and a few small models chosen for work that belongs on a phone.

## Screenshots

## What you can do

- Get up to three complete-word suggestions, ranked from model probabilities.

- Hold Enter to dictate; slide up to keep recording or left to cancel.

- Translate into another app's text field with LFM or Qwen, using the same text model that supplies prediction and autocorrection.

- Use native script layouts, accent menus and bundled input converters.

- Change key colors, save designs, create layouts, and choose recorded switch sounds and haptic feedback.

- Keep copied text in a local clipboard, with pinning and deletion controls.

Swipe typing, adaptive letters and autocorrection are optional and start off. Keyboard height starts at 100%. Settings you have already chosen are preserved.

## Start here

Lokey requires Android 9 or later and an ARM64 device . Download the signed APK from Releases , open Lokey, and follow setup to enable and select the keyboard. Choose your language and download the models you want. Ordinary keyboard input works without downloading a model.

The interface follows Android's language setting. Android 13 and later also provide a separate app-language setting. Keyboard layout and model language remain separate choices. See supported languages .

## Models

Lokey uses one active text model for prediction, autocorrection and translation, and one speech model for dictation. An LFM-only installation uses LFM for all three text functions; Qwen is not required. Automatic chooses this pair for your language and hardware. Supported Qualcomm Hexagon devices can use the NPU; CPU execution remains available. Model files are downloaded separately from the app.

MODELS.md explains selection, formats, memory reuse and limits.

## Build

Use JDK 17 or later, Android SDK 37, NDK 28.2.13676358 and CMake 3.31.6.

./gradlew :app:assembleDebug

The APK is written to app/build/outputs/apk/debug/app-debug.apk . The build guide covers runtime checkouts and optional Hexagon support. The release guide covers signing and distribution.

## Privacy

Prediction, translation and speech recognition run locally. The app has no advertising or analytics SDK. Clipboard history, settings, custom designs and speed-test records use Android's private app storage.

Model downloads contact Hugging Face and its delivery providers, which receive network request information such as your IP address. Text and microphone audio are not part of those requests. Opening an external link or sharing a result uses the app you choose.

Read the privacy policy and the developer Data Safety disclosure .

## Status and documentation

Lokey is beta software. Device checks cover the OnePlus 15 and POCO F3; performance and model quality vary with the phone and language. Interface translations still need full native-speaker review.

- Keyboard use and customization

- Supported languages

- Language and keyboard mapping

- Models and inference

- Building , testing , and releasing

## Credits

Lokey uses the Loina core , llama.cpp , and whisper.cpp forks. Their exact revisions are pinned in runtimes.json .

Models, dictionaries, recordings, icons and artwork have their own licenses. Attribution and license texts are bundled in the app, under Models → Models & inference credits and Feel → Input & design credits, and in the assets directory .

## Contributing and license

See CONTRIBUTING.md for correctness checks, performance comparisons and useful bug reports. Application code is released under the MIT license . Third-party runtimes, model weights and bundled assets retain their own licenses and notices.

Run smarter agents. Use fewer tokens. Our code review bill went up 36x this year. Now a review costs us 18 cents. See how ↓ Quickstart · Case studies · Tour · Templates · Deploy · Docs AgentRun is an open-source platform that supercharges your agents. It adds self-improvement, durable execution and a control plane on top of your favorite agent harness. Your agents become smarter, more fault tolerant and use fewer tokens with every run. An agent's Learning tab: what it kept, and what changed since. Demo data from the console's recorded fixtures. ## Case studies Code review. Greptile started charging a dollar a review in March, then our agents took off, and our bill went from $180 a month to $6,451. So we built our own reviewer on a cheap model and tuned it on our own PRs. It costs 18 cents a review, and on 30 PRs it had never seen it caught 1.6x the real bugs Greptile did. How we built it · Tune one on your repo Merchant codes. We let Opus figure out how to classify merchants, then handed what it learned to a cheap model. Same job, $0.89 down to $0.12 a merchant. How it works · Do it with your own job ## Why AgentRun Agents are great at figuring things out. The problem is they figure out the same things over and over. Give an agent a job it has done a hundred times and it rediscovers the same API, rereads the same docs and rebuilds the same plan, and you pay for every token of it. Bring your agent on the harness it runs best on: Claude Code, Codex, OpenCode or pi. AgentRun does everything around it: - It learns the work. After each run, the agent keeps what will help next time: a note, a skill, or a workflow that does the job without the loop. The next run starts from there. - It never loses a run. Every run lives in one store. Kill the server mid-run, start it again, and the run carries on. Give each agent the computer the job needs: a sandbox, a Linux desktop, an Android phone or a browser. - You stay in control. Approvals, spend caps and one console for every agent: what needs you, what failed, what's running and what it cost. You don't build the plumbing: provider integrations, recovery, run tracking and learning are all here. Run it on your laptop with one command, in one container, or as a server with runners. Apache-2.0. ## Start in three steps You need Node 24.22.3 or newer, on macOS or Linux. - Start it. npx @parcha/agentrun It starts the server and one runner on port 7340 (or the next free one), keeps everything in ~/.agentrun , and opens the console in your browser. Start it. npx @parcha/agentrun It starts the server and one runner on port 7340 (or the next free one), keeps everything in ~/.agentrun , and opens the console in your browser. - Add one model key. In the console, set a password, then add a key under Settings → Model keys . One OPENROUTER_API_KEY gives every harness a model. An Anthropic key runs pi and Claude Code; an OpenAI key runs pi, Codex and OpenCode. - Run your first agent. Open Templates , apply KYB due diligence , and start a run with a company's name and website. It needs nothing but your model key. When it finishes, the run's Report tab has a due diligence report with a verdict and every claim cited. Then open the agent's Learning tab to see what it kept for next time. Rather have your coding agent do it? Tell it: Read agentrun.ai/SKILL.md and set up AgentRun for me . If Docker is running on your machine, new agents get a Docker sandbox with a shell. Its image builds on first use, which takes a few minutes, and the console says when it's ready. Without Docker, agents still read and write files, but get no shell. Want your own server with a URL? Deploy it to Render in one click. ## Take the tour Workflows that make the call. A step can ask a fast typed question, see how sure the answer is, and pick a route. Here the model leans approve at 0.61, below the workflow's 0.75 bar, so the case goes to review. Every agent in one place. Mission Control opens first: what needs you, what failed, what's running and what it cost, by day, by harness and by tool. Every agent is an API. Start a run from the Playground, then copy the same request into your code. You stay in control. An agent can stop and ask you, and the run waits until you answer. ## Agents that learn the work Turn it on with "learning": true in an agent's definition. At the end of every run, the agent gets one more turn to say what it would keep. AgentRun checks it, grades it, and commits the keepers to the agent's own git folder. The next run starts from there. flowchart LR start["Run starts from
the agent's main"] --> work["Run does the job"] work --> propose["Last turn proposes
notes, a skill, a workflow"] propose --> check["Code checks,
then one grader"] check -->|kept| commit["Commit to main"] commit --> start - Notes are short markdown files, one fact each, in Claude Code's memory format. - Skills are how to do a job again, and only a run that finished the job can write one. - Learned workflows run as one tool call on any harness, under the run's own cap and tool permissions. Once a learned skill has served 3 runs, the next run is asked for that job as a workflow draft, and a draft is dry-run before it's kept: no model is asked and no tool runs. The agent's Learning tab shows every note, skill and workflow and the log of changes, and each run shows which notes it was given and opened. Retire anything there, or with npx @parcha/agentrun learning retire and the note's ETag. Git keeps the history, so a retired note can come back. Each agent has a learning folder: plain git with one branch, main . A run reads the index of active notes in its instructions and gets the learned skills beside its own. Code checks every proposal first. An item that breaks a rule of its own (a size or count limit, its name, its shape) is left out and the rest goes on. A secret or a hidden character anywhere in the answer, a file outside the folder, a deletion or a full index drops the whole answer, since no item of it can be trusted. Then one grader judges what it says, and AgentRun commits what passes. A risky rule waits for your OK. A rule the run found in a page or a pasted email, or a note that holds an account number, is dropped. Once an agent's notes outgrow the learning budget, each run gets the ones that bear on its first message, whole, and a line for each of the rest. A run that only ran a learned workflow isn't asked what to keep. ## Workflows A lot of agents don't need to be agents. Write repeatable work as a typed workflow: tool calls, model steps and fast typed decisions (yes or no, pick one, a score, each with its confidence), with an agent to fall back on when a case is unclear. AgentRun runs it as an agent's revision, under the agent's tool permissions and a cap like any run, and a trigger can start one. An illustration of the control flow in examples/support-answer.mjs , not a recording of a model run. Watch any workflow run node by node, pause it and resume it, and read every decision and why it was made: A workflow is a JSON document of typed steps: { "v" : 2 , "name" : " read-site " , "schemas" : { "In" : { "type" : " object " , "required" : [ " website " ], "properties" : { "website" : { "type" : " string " } } }, "Page" : { "type" : " object " , "required" : [ " ok " ], "properties" : { "ok" : { "type" : " boolean " } } } }, "input" : { "schemaId" : " In " }, "output" : { "schemaId" : " Page " , "path" : " home " }, "root" : { "node" : " chain " , "steps" : [ { "node" : " call " , "label" : " Read the home page " , "via" : " tool " , "tool" : " web_fetch " , "args" : { "url" : " {website} " }, "out" : " Page " , "as" : " home " , "deadline_s" : 60 } ] } } Steps can call tools, run a model, ask a fast typed question, branch on the answer, map over a list in parallel, loop a bounded number of times, call other workflows, or hand the hard case to an agent. Save one as an agent's workflow field; npx @parcha/agentrun workflows validate checks it first. The workflow language also runs on its own inside your app, with a TypeScript builder . ## Runs that survive Every agent, revision, run and step lives in one store. Stop the server mid-run and start it again, and the run carries on. With several runners, another runner picks up a dead runner's runs once their 30-second lease runs out. A finished step is never run again; a write a crash cut off mid-call is marked interrupted rather than retried, so you can check it. ## You stay in control - Approvals. Each tool is allowed, asks you first, or is denied. A call that asks waits on the run's page until you answer. "Never ask" lets an agent run unattended, and a deny set on the server still holds over it. - Spend caps. Give a run a cap and it pauses there instead of failing, and tells you the least it needs to go on. A cost AgentRun can't price reads "unknown", never $0. - Questions. An agent can stop and ask you, and the run waits until you answer. - One console. Each run has a live Timeline, its files and, for a browser, a screen you can take over. ## Templates Five ready-made agents. Apply one in one screen, make it yours, and measure it with its own eval cases. Each template is one folder: the agent's instructions, its skills, its rules and its eval cases. Templates → Apply grants nothing until you tick each MCP tool yourself. npx @parcha/agentrun template eval DIR runs a template's eval cases as real runs on a throwaway server and grades them. Template packages has the folder format. Want a template to know your code? Tune a template on your own code walks through the loop we ran on code-review . Triggers start capped runs on their own: schedules, signed webhooks and GitHub pull request events. ## Harnesses and computers Harnesses. Name one in the agent's definition with harness . Approvals, caps, computers, triggers and learning work the same on each. npx @parcha/agentrun server capabilities says which harnesses your server runs. Computers. An agent gets a computer with one setting. It gets the tools for that kind and nothing else, and changing the computer changes nothing else about the agent. computer : kind : sandbox # none, sandbox, desktop, phone or browser provider : daytona # one you connected in Settings → Computers (none takes no provider) Every kind but none names its provider. An agent with no computer setting gets the Docker sandbox where the server has Docker, and no computer otherwise. Remote computers bill through your own account with the vendor. - Keys. Add a vendor's key once in Settings → Computers . Your server seals it and shows it only as set or missing; it never enters the agent's computer. Test connection makes one read at the vendor and starts nothing. - The run's files. By default a run's folder lives on your server and the Docker sandbox mounts it. Turn on an Archil disk in Settings and the folder lives there instead, so a Daytona, Modal or E2B sandbox mounts the same folder. Those three run only with an Archil disk, and with Archil on the Docker sandbox is refused. - Watching and taking over. A browser run streams to the run's Screen tab through your own server, never through a vendor link. Take the controls, then hand them back. The agent can also stop and ask you to take over, for a login or a captcha. - Proof. Each provider has a conformance suite for its kind. Run it against the vendor yourself, from a checkout after npm ci && npm run build : npm run conformance -w @parcha/agentrun-computer -- --provider docker --kind sandbox . @parcha/agentrun-computer is the protocol underneath: one small daemon in every computer and one provider per vendor. ## How it fits together flowchart LR you["Console · CLI · API"] --> server["Server"] server --> store["One store
SQLite or Postgres"] runner["Runners"] -->|claim runs| store runner --> hands["Hands
run folder + computer"] - Server. Serves the API at /v2 and the console. It writes [truncated]

## 🖥️ Live Dashboard Showcase (4K Retina)

All 22 core modules are captured from live production ( chatty.personaliai.com/dashboard ) in crisp 4K Retina (3840×2160) resolution, representing real hydrated application state:

## ✨ Features

- 💬 Embeddable Chat Widget — One <script> tag, streaming SSE replies, crisp vector Shadow DOM rendering on any site with zero CSS bleed.

- 📚 RAG Knowledge Hub — Deep semantic retrieval powered by PostgreSQL pgvector , HNSW indexing, and hybrid lexical/vector search.

- 🛠️ Autonomous Tool-Calling — Schedules real meetings (Google Meet, Microsoft Teams, Zoom), qualifies leads, and checks calendars.

- 🔑 Bring Your Own Key (BYOK) — Free-tier Gemini by default, or per-bot OpenAI/Anthropic/Groq with AES-128 encryption.

- 🤖 81-Tool FastMCP Server — Control the entire dashboard programmatically from Claude Desktop, Cursor, or Codex via OAuth 2.0 / API Keys (including complete Voice Agent configuration, screenshot telemetry, and autonomous workflows).

- 📊 5-Pillar Scorecard — Independent A–F performance auditing across Conversion, Deflection, Accuracy, Reliability, and CSAT.

- 🎯 Proactive Campaigns — Behavioral triggers (exit-intent, time-on-page, scroll-depth) with timezone-aware cadence planning.

- 🐳 One-Command Self-Host — docker compose up , point to Supabase, and launch in 60 seconds.

### Campaign Telemetry Ledger

Campaign configuration is persisted in chatty_campaigns . Widget deployments record impression , click , and conversion events through POST /api/widget/campaign-events with bot_id , campaign_id , and an optional idempotency_key (safe for retries). Recomputed analytics are accessible via GET /api/bots/{bot_id}/campaigns/{campaign_id}/analytics .

Campaign drafts support a validated schedule_config ( once , hourly , daily , or weekly with IANA timezone). POST /api/bots/{bot_id}/campaigns/audience-suggest generates bounded segments, intent thresholds, and rationales before saving. Delivery channels include web, email, WhatsApp, and SMS. Safety policies support overnight quiet hours ( quiet_hours: {"start": "22:00", "end": "08:00"} ). The background worker python -m app.workers.campaign_scheduler claims Redis idempotency keys for 24 hours to prevent duplicate dispatches. Provider-backed steps are expanded only for leads with explicit marketing consent and are then filtered by the same segment , returning_only , and min_intent_score rules used by the widget; qualification signals may be persisted in chatty_leads.custom_fields by an AI flow. Provider jobs additionally claim a hashed recipient/campaign frequency-cap key atomically before sending; cap hits are recorded as intentional suppressions, not retries. Each queued provider job carries its deterministic delivery key into the worker, which upserts queued , sent , failed , or suppressed state in chatty_campaign_deliveries ; campaign analytics reports delivery success rate and channel breakdown without exposing recipient addresses. Apply migration 20260930130000_campaign_delivery_ledger.sql before enabling provider campaigns in a new environment. Email delivery uses configured Resend or OneSignal credentials; unconfigured channels fail closed.

### Flow Builder Safety & Deterministic Dry-Runs

The AI Flow Architect endpoint ( POST /api/flow/generate ) requires authenticated users with settings permission. Prompts are bounded to 4,000 characters, and generated graphs are validated for unique node IDs and resolvable edge references. Dry-runs enforce execution step budgets to prevent runaway loops and store immutable graph snapshots for deterministic replay. Webhook/action mappings use a safe {{input}} and {{context.path}} resolver; exact-value mappings preserve JSON types and unresolved fields are surfaced in the trace rather than silently sent.

Published widget flows execute their control nodes too: delay is capped at five minutes, condition accepts only the declarative input == , != , contains , starts_with , and ends_with grammar, and loop has a 100-iteration hard ceiling plus an explicit done , complete , or exit route. A webhook node is dispatched through POST /api/widget/flow/webhook , not from browser JavaScript. The API reloads the current active flow and permits only the selected published node's config.url (or config.webhook_url ), posts a bounded mapped body, adds an idempotency key, disables redirects, and pins DNS through the SSRF guard. Browser-supplied destinations, headers, and methods are never accepted. A webhook can set bounded max_attempts (1–5), backoff_ms (0–5,000), and timeout_ms (500–30,000); only connection errors, timeouts, and 5xx responses are retried. Use labeled success / true and error / failed / timeout edges to make the outcome path explicit. Operators can inspect an immutable run snapshot and trace at GET /api/bots/{bot_id}/flow/runs/{run_id} before replaying it.

## 🔌 7-Channel Omnichannel Hub

Chatty provides native, industrial-standard bidirectional messaging across all major customer conversation surfaces from a single, unified workspace. Messages from every platform normalize into an internal event pipeline, allowing automated flows, the AI brain, and human operators to interact seamlessly.

### Key Architectural Highlights

- Zero-Latency Ingestion Queue: Webhook endpoints perform HMAC verification and return HTTP 200 OK in <40ms, preventing Meta and TikTok from triggering exponential 3-second webhook retry storms while the AI reasons.

- Smart UI Normalization: Interactive buttons automatically adapt across channels (rendered as native inline keyboard grids on Telegram, sliced to 3 quick-reply buttons on WhatsApp and TikTok, and transpiled into numbered text options like Reply [1] or [2] for SMS).

- 24-Hour Messaging Window Enforcement: Tracks last_inbound_at on Meta channels to prevent API rejection codes ( 131047 ), automatically falling back to pre-approved WhatsApp Business templates when the window expires.

- TCPA Compliance Interceptor: Deterministically halts automation and registers opt-outs when users text regulatory keywords ( STOP , UNSUBSCRIBE , CANCEL , QUIT ).

- Non-Destructive Secret Store: Credentials and webhook verify tokens are stored in an encrypted PostgreSQL JSONB envelope ( omnichannel_config ), ensuring updates to one channel never wipe keys from another.

## 🗺️ Visual Flow Builder Engine & Conditional Runtime

Chatty includes a visual node-based conversation engine built on @xyflow/react . You can design rigid conversational paths for high-stakes business logic (lead qualification, appointment scheduling, promotional campaigns) and let the AI brain handle open-ended questions.

- Time-Conditional Branching: Condition nodes support 24-hour and 12-hour time comparisons (e.g. < 18:00 vs >= 18:00 ). Build time-variable marketing campaigns where visitors chatting before 6:00 PM receive early-bird offers expiring at 6:30 PM, while evening visitors receive offers valid until 9:00 PM.

- Platform & Device Metadata: Nodes inspect normalized incoming request metadata ( platform , channel , device , os ) to serve channel-specific answers or routing rules.

- Deterministic Flow Nodes: Trigger: Activates on events ( session.started , message.user , lead.created ). Message & Question: Sends rich markdown with multiple-choice buttons. ### Upgrade a vibe-coded site to premium with your coding agent. Motion first, then taste, checked in a real browser.

Install · Upgrade a site · Commands · The critic · Demos · FAQ · Contribute

Left: a site an agent built from a one-paragraph brief. Right: the same site after a fresh agent (Opus 5.5) ran premium-motion upgrade on it. Nothing edited by hand. All four upgrades .

Every agent-built landing page looks the same: near-black with one neon accent, a headline with an italic word, pill buttons, a bento grid, a logo marquee, and every section fading up the same way. It is not ugly. It just tells everyone a model made it, and nobody looked at it before it shipped.

Motion Debugger gives your agent two things it doesn't have:

- 🎬 A workflow that rebuilds the look and keeps the truth. The premium-motion skill runs an upgrade pipeline: it records a baseline, keeps every fact, link and form, picks a direction from the product's own world, then rebuilds the page around choreographed motion and one cinematic scroll scene. It uses a tested GSAP, ScrollTrigger, SplitText and Lenis stack, or Motion in React projects.

- 👀 Eyes. motion-debugger critique opens the local page in Chromium, records the entrance, scrolls the whole page, hovers every control, checks the phone layout and reduced motion, and hands the agent ranked fixes plus screenshots of the real frames. The agent looks, fixes and looks again, then compares against the baseline.

## Install

Every line below is one command. They work with any model and any coding agent, and the same commands run on macOS, Linux and Windows (bash, zsh or PowerShell). The CLI and npx lines need Node.js 22 or later; the git line needs only git.

The full setup (critic, skill and agent configuration). Install, then run init in your project:

npm install -g https://github.com/ShadowKingYT444/motion-debugger/releases/latest/download/motion-debugger.tgz

motion-debugger init

init detects your agent (Claude Code, Cursor, Codex, VS Code, OpenCode), installs the skill, offers to download a matching Chromium, and shows every file it would change before asking you to type yes . Nothing is written without that, and your existing settings are kept.

Just the skill, or just the critic:

For -a , use your agent's name: claude-code , cursor , codex , gemini-cli , github-copilot , windsurf , cline , roo , zed , opencode , goose , kiro-cli , amp , junie and about 70 more ( skills CLI ). An agent that can't run shell commands can still follow the skill; it just can't look at the page.

The critic uses Playwright's Chromium if you downloaded it, then CHROMIUM_PATH , then an installed Chrome, Chromium or Edge in the usual place on macOS, Windows or Linux. CI installs the packed CLI on all three and critiques a real page.

git clone https://github.com/ShadowKingYT444/motion-debugger.git cd motion-debugger && npm ci && npm run build && npm install -g . motion-debugger setup --browser # version-matched Chromium motion-debugger doctor

More options in client setup .

## Upgrade a site

Start your dev server, then tell your agent:

> Use premium-motion upgrade on this site.

What the agent does, from commands/upgrade.md :

- Baseline. Critiques the page as it is and lists its AI tells.

- Inventory. Writes down what to keep (facts, numbers, CTAs, forms, your logo and colours) and what to replace.

- Direction. Writes PREMIUM.md : audience, facts, the product's world, type, colour, imagery and one motion personality.

- First viewport. Rebuilds the hero alone and critiques it until it holds up.

- Rebuild. Works section by section, each laid out from its content instead of eyebrow, bento and marquee.

- Signature scene. Builds one scroll-scrubbed scene that tells the product's story and is finished at every scroll position.

- Polish and harden. Fixes every outlined defect, then the phone layout, reduced motion, accessibility and scroll performance.

- Verify. Critiques again and compares with the baseline side by side.

Narrow targets work too: upgrade the pricing section , signature the how-it-works section , polish the footer .

## Commands

The motion code agents copy from the skill is extracted from its Markdown and run in Chromium in CI at desktop, phone and reduced-motion sizes, so the documented snippet is the tested snippet.

## The critic

Run it yourself on anything local:

motion-debugger critique http://localhost:3000 # your dev server (Next.js, Vite, …) motion-debugger critique ./site # a folder with index.html, or one .html file

It prints findings with fixes, writes contact sheets to .motion-critique/ , and says what changed since the last run: fixed, new and remaining.

Findings come from real Chromium frames, never from reading the source. Every check and its limits .

## Four upgrades

Four landing pages that Sonnet 5.5 built from one-paragraph briefs with no plugin, the controls from the A/B study below. A fresh Opus 5.5 agent ran upgrade on each, with the same prompt. These are single runs to show the workflow, not a blinded comparison, and nobody edited the results. The prompt, the skill version and every recording are in demos/upgrades.json .

One critic run per site, made after the agents finished. The agents were working against this critic, so read the score as "the defects it can see are gone", not as a measure of taste. Judge the films.

Atelier Norr: architecture studio · film

Halo: wireless speaker launch · film

Drift: AI sleep coach · film

Ledgerline: payments API · film

Each upgraded/ folder also holds the PREMIUM.md direction file the agent wrote. Open any site live from demos/ .

## Does it work? The blinded study

Separately from the upgrades, we ran a blinded A/B test of building from scratch: same brief, same builder model (Sonnet 5.5), one fresh agent per site. One agent worked in an empty project; the other had the skill and the critic.

In the latest batch (four matched pairs, plugin v4), blinded Opus 5.5 judges preferred the plugin's site in all four pairs (8 of 8 judgments). Distinctiveness rose from 6.4 to 8.8 and overall premium from 6.9 to 8.0. The control sites shared 6.5 of 9 default-template traits on average; the plugin's sites shared none. Visual design moved least (7.8 to 8.1).

Four pairs are too few for statistical significance. The earlier 16-pair study reached it for overall premium (+1.0, p = 0.005) and motion quality (+1.34, p = 0.0004), but found no gain in visual design, which later versions were rebuilt to address. The study predates the upgrade workflow. Method, every verdict and threats to validity .

## FAQ

How is this different from Impeccable or other design skills? The skill's shape (one skill, a command vocabulary, a context file and a playbook per command) is borrowed from Impeccable , with thanks. The differences are the focus and the loop. Motion is the core: a tested GSAP and Lenis stack, signature scroll scenes, choreography and reduced-motion handling. And every command ends by recording the page in a real browser: the critic measures what actually moved and finds finish defects in the captured frames, so the agent works from evidence instead of reading its own CSS.

Will it change my content? upgrade keeps the product's facts, numbers, links, forms and anything you already own (logo, brand colours, fonts, photos). It replaces the generic look. Run audit first if you only want a report.

Does it work with my stack? Plain HTML, React, Next.js, Vite, Motion (framer-motion) and GSAP. The skill uses the animation library you already have and never adds a second one.

Does it need Claude, or a particular model? No. Nothing here calls a model API: the critic is a plain CLI with Markdown or --json output, and the skill is a standard Agent Skill in Markdown. Use it with any model your agent runs. The demos were made with Claude models because that's what we had; the workflow doesn't depend on them. init sets up Claude Code, Cursor, Codex, VS Code and OpenCode, and the skills CLI covers about 80 more agents (see Install).

Does it work on my machine? Yes on macOS, Linux and Windows with Node.js 22 or later. CI installs the packed CLI on all three and critiques a real page.

Does anything leave my machine? No. The critic only opens credential-free local pages ( localhost , 127.0.0.1 , files), never imports your browser profile, and keeps recordings in your project folder. Security model .

## Works with your agent

motion-debugger init sets these up for you; this is what it writes.

Any other agent (Gemini CLI, Aider, Windsurf, a CI job): copy the skill folder into your project and add the block printed by motion-debugger agents-md --skills-dir <folder> to the agent's instructions file ( AGENTS.md , GEMINI.md , .cursorrules , …).

MCP hosts also get motion_critique , which returns the findings and screenshots as image content. Client setup details · Native plugin packages .

For a single interaction, the MCP evidence tools record bounded journeys and compare repairs:

See Agent workflow .

## Contributing

Bug reports, false positives the critic flags, and new checks are all welcome. Browse the open issues or say hi in Discussions . Contributing guide .

# fraud-decision-lab

A vendor-neutral research benchmark of specialized AI decision models versus conventional machine learning for payment-fraud ranking . It sends the same transactions to TypeSafe Jev , OpenAI Decisions , Cloudflare Clef / Clef-flash and a structured-output LLM, then measures how much labelled fraud each one ranks into the top of an analyst's review queue , against an XGBoost baseline, at what cost and latency .

Fraud teams can review only a small share of transactions. The useful question is not "is this model clever?" but "if analysts can review only the top 1%, whose ranking catches the most fraud, and what does it cost?" This lab explores that on configured labelled tabular datasets. It runs offline by default and saves predictions and experiment metadata for local verification.

> Built and maintained by Smart Mobile House — secure AI implementation for enterprise.

## What it compares

Models use the same configured feature schema . API providers receive a shared fraud question and field descriptions through provider-specific formats; numeric payloads are rounded to four decimals. Rules and XGBoost use the original dataframe values, and XGBoost learns from labelled training history. These are intentional differences, not identical model inputs.

Metrics include average precision (labelled PR-AUC), recall at the top 1% and 5%, precision and fraud count at the top 1%, and paired bootstrap differences from XGBoost. The top 1% is 100 cases only when 10,000 cases are evaluated. Operational summaries distinguish eventual completion from earlier attempts; API costs are calculated from usage and a dated price snapshot, not invoices.

## Quick start

No API keys, no dataset downloads and no paid calls are needed.

git clone https://github.com/SmartMobileHouse/fraud-decision-lab cd fraud-decision-lab uv sync --frozen # install pinned dependencies (Python 3.12) uv run fraudlab doctor # check your setup; prints no secrets

See it work in one command (about 5 seconds, offline):

make demo # rules + XGBoost on the bundled synthetic data -> outputs/demo-report.html

Or with Docker / Podman only:

make docker container= $( docker create --network none fraud-decision-lab demo ) docker start --attach " $container " mkdir -p outputs docker cp " $container :/app/outputs/. " outputs/ docker rm " $container "

The report is saved to outputs/demo-report.html . Copying the output works with Docker and Podman VMs without sharing the host project directory. Bind mounts require that the engine can access the host path and the container user can write to it; an external drive is not automatically shared with every VM.

Then run the offline benchmark on the bundled synthetic data and build the report:

uv run fraudlab run -d configs/datasets/synthetic.yaml --providers rules,xgboost uv run fraudlab report --run-id < run_id printed above > --out outputs/report.html

Live providers need API keys, --allow-external-requests and a --max-cost-usd spending estimate; see uv run fraudlab run --help . The estimate is not a provider-enforced billing cap: tokenization, retries and uncertain billing can cause differences. Use available provider-side spending controls as well.

## Configuration

Live provider runs read credentials from a local .env file (gitignored). Copy the template and fill in only the providers you want to run:

cp .env.example .env && chmod 600 .env

The reference adapters request jev-1.14.0 , gpt-6-luna (Decisions and LLM), @cf/cloudflare/clef , and @cf/cloudflare/clef-flash . A reported identifier does not freeze a provider's server implementation; the OpenAI and Cloudflare identifiers are not immutable execution snapshots. The structured-output LLM uses reasoning effort none , a 64-token output limit, and a strict JSON score. Sampling parameters not explicitly sent are provider-controlled defaults. The fraud question is in configs/questions-v1.json ; adapters in src/fraudlab/providers/ define the request-specific wrappers.

Only the project's original synthetic data is bundled. Download third-party datasets yourself into data/external/ (see DATA_LICENSES.md ); fraudlab doctor shows what it finds.

### IEEE-CIS Fraud Detection

This repository includes optional support for the IEEE-CIS Fraud Detection dataset.

The dataset is not distributed with this project. Users must obtain it independently from Kaggle and comply with the original competition rules, including restrictions on commercial use.

The benchmark implementation is provided separately from the dataset.

The included IEEE-CIS configs are local-only ( external_processing_allowed: false ). Publication is separately disabled ( publication_allowed: false ): this includes aggregate results, plots, cached outputs and reports pending independent rights review. API-processing permission is not publication permission. The shipped ULB config allows publishing aggregate results under its ODbL/DbCL licence with attribution (see DATA_LICENSES.md ). Do not enable publication merely to bypass a report refusal.

## Development

uv sync --frozen make check # ruff, mypy, pytest (offline), license check, gitleaks secret scan make format # auto-fix lint and formatting make docker # build the offline image make help # list all targets

There is no hosted CI: run make check before every push. Tests can never reach the network; tests that call a real paid API are marked live and never run by default. See CONTRIBUTING.md .

## Results

The current source distribution contains no benchmark result files. Older Git history contains results text and screenshots, so changing the original private repository's visibility is not a source-only release. See RELEASE.md for a reviewable source snapshot without that history.

Run make demo for a synthetic offline example. fraudlab report and fraudlab export-report-data require a dataset approved for publication; they do not make a legal determination. Results from unapproved datasets remain local run artifacts. A source-only release does not provide public Level 3 verification of historical paid experiments. Retained research claims need separately reviewed prediction evidence and provenance.

## Notes & limitations

- Zero-shot vs supervised. XGBoost learns from labelled history; the AI models see each transaction cold. That is deliberate, and the report says so.

- Dataset realism. Synthetic history fields and labels are generated signals, not observed card histories or validated banking outcomes. ULB's anonymised components limit semantic interpretation by a zero-shot model. Repeated feature vectors can cross chronological splits; identical vectors alone do not prove duplicate transactions. No entity-independent evaluation is claimed.

- Uncertainty. Confidence intervals resample transactions with class counts fixed. They condition on saved predictions and ignore customer/day clustering, provider rerun variability and future distribution shift. A single saved run cannot establish a stable general ranking of vendors.

- Not a production fraud system. A fraud score is not a calibrated probability and not a decision to block a card or account. Analysts must review cases; false positives and false negatives carry different operational costs.

- Data rights are yours. MIT covers this project's code and its synthetic data only, never a third-party dataset. Some datasets (for example IEEE-CIS) must not be sent to external APIs; the lab blocks that by configuration.

- Privacy and manipulated inputs. Approved live runs transmit configured fields to providers. Confirm data rights, retention terms and privacy controls before sending real records. Transaction text can contain prompt injection; robustness against adversarial inputs has not been demonstrated. Models do not execute financial actions. Run logs support research inspection, not regulatory certification or a complete production audit trail.

- Providers change. Models, prices and APIs move; every result is tied to its run date and manifest.

- Reproducibility. fraudlab replay checks supported saved run metrics against saved labels and predictions. It does not authenticate provider execution, verify invoices, or recover missing historical load-test calls. Legacy runs may have incomplete provenance and cannot safely be resumed as new experiments. Retraining XGBoost can give slightly different numbers on another operating system or CPU; each run records its platform.

- Platforms and setup. The pinned project targets Python 3.12 on macOS and Linux. Dependency installation and Docker builds need downloads unless cached. Image tags and system package repositories are mutable; the Dockerfile is not a bit-for-bit frozen image recipe.

- This is an independent project and is not affiliated with or endorsed by TypeSafe, OpenAI, Cloudflare, Kaggle or the dataset owners.

## License

MIT © Smart Mobile House

The Smart Mobile House name is a trademark of Smart Mobile House and is not licensed under MIT. Generated reports remain subject to dataset, provider and other applicable rights; the code license does not grant publication permission.

# UniiChat

▶ Watch the announcement video

This repo is vibe-coded. AI agents wrote nearly all of it, and AI agents reviewed it. Read it, run it and fork it as such: expect bugs.

UniiChat runs a small team of AI agents, the uniis, on a computer you own. You talk to one of them, root. Each unii has one chat that never ends: you talk to the same agent for days, weeks, years, and it remembers. There is no hosted version: you run it yourself, on your own Claude subscription or API keys.

## How it works

- One chat, a memory tree. Every message is summarized into one line, and neighboring lines are merged in pairs, again and again, into a binary tree. Each call sees a view of the whole chat, up to 128 KB: recent messages one line each, older ones covered by fewer, broader lines. Detail fades with age, but nothing is lost.

- Zoom. A unii can open any line into the two it was made from, down to the original message. Its context never rots, and it never needs a compaction that throws the past away.

- Built in the background. Summaries are written as messages arrive. The view changes only at its end, so each call reads most of its input from the vendor's prompt cache.

- A tree of uniis. Root can spawn children, each owning one lasting part of your work (a project, your calendar, your infra), and they can spawn their own. A unii talks only to its parent and its children, by message; a message wakes it, and its turn ends in a reply it keeps for itself. Each works in its own git worktree, and a parent reviews and merges its children's branches. Uniis ask before spawning: nothing grows without your OK.

- Every window is a view. One process, the hub, keeps every chat. A browser tab or a terminal shows them live: the browser lists the uniis as a tree at the left; in the terminal, Tab cycles through them and /tab <name> opens one.

The design is in the header comment of each file. Start with Memory.ts (the tree and the view), Server.ts (the hub) and AskAI.ts (model calls and the cache).

## Run it

You need Bun , git, and Claude Code signed in to your Claude subscription:

git clone https://github.com/VictorTaelin/uniichat cd uniichat bun install claude # sign in, then quit mkdir -p ~/t/unii/root && cd ~/t/unii/root git init && git commit --allow-empty -m root # root's worktree cd - && bun Server.ts # the hub, on http://127.0.0.1:8788

Root works in that repo; each child works in a worktree of it beside it, ~/t/unii/<name> , on a branch of its own. Then, in another terminal:

bun Term.ts # a terminal view

or open the browser view, signed in by the hub's key ( bun Term.ts link prints the same link):

open "http://127.0.0.1:8788/auth?key=$(cat ~/.opt/key)"

The key, ~/.opt/key , is made at the first start; whoever has it reaches every unii and every command they run, so keep it private.

Every unii's chat is a dir chat/<name>/ of the hub's own worktree, ~/t/unii/.chats (branch chats , checked out at chat/ only): one JSON line per message (main/), summary (tree/) and thought (mind/). Only the hub writes them; at the end of each turn it commits that unii's chat, and merges chats into root's branch while root sleeps. They are the memory: back the repo up.

## From your phone, or anywhere

The hub listens only on 127.0.0.1. Run it on a machine that stays on, and reach it over a private network, never the open internet. With Tailscale :

tailscale serve --bg 8788

serves it over HTTPS, at your machine's Tailscale name, to your own computers and phone only. Set site (below) to that address, and open <site>/auth?key=<key> once in each browser.

To let the uniis run commands on another computer (their mac tool), link it to the hub's socket, ~/.opt/mac.sock , with ssh -W : the hub sends {"$":"job","id","unii","command"} and {"$":"stop","id"} , one JSON object a line, and the computer answers each job once with {"$":"out","id","text","code"} (Server.ts says more). Closing the link ends their access.

## Config

~/.opt/config.json (optional). Each key may also be set as the variable OPT_<KEY> :

- root : root's worktree, a git checkout you make (default ~/t/unii/root ). A child's worktree is beside it, ~/t/unii/<name> , on branch <name> , and so is the hub's, .chats .

- chats : the chats' dir in the repo (default chat ).

- site : the address you open it at (default http://127.0.0.1:8788 ).

- vendors : what the uniis may run on, comma-separated: claude-sub (your subscription, through the claude CLI; the default), claude-api ( ANTHROPIC_API_KEY ), openai-api ( OPENAI_API_KEY ).

- models : the models offered: opus-5.5 , gpt-6-astra .

- pick : what a unii runs on until you pick another, vendor:model:effort:speed (default claude-sub:opus-5.5:high:slow ).

- compactor : what writes the summaries (default the same).

- accounts : a dir of claude_<id>.token files, each a token from claude setup-token , used in order: when one reaches its limit, the next. None: the CLI's own login.

- rules : a file appended to every system prompt: who you are, how your files are organized, how you want work done.

- computer : 1 lets the uniis use the screen, mouse and keyboard of the Mac the hub runs on (it compiles Computer.swift with swiftc; macOS asks for Screen Recording and Accessibility).

API keys come from the environment, read at start and removed from it, so no command a unii runs inherits them: ANTHROPIC_API_KEY , OPENAI_API_KEY .

Other commands:

bun test # the tests

The hub builds the site's script from web/src as it starts.

# HyperFlow H3 Flash

HyperFlow H3 Flash is Video Rebirth 's compressed, few-step version of MiniMax-H3 . It generates video and synchronized stereo audio together.

Showcase · Weights (Hugging Face) · ComfyUI nodes · GGUF setup guide · 8-step LoRA for full-size MiniMax-H3

- Output: 5.2–15 s of video at 24 fps (1344×768 by default) with a 32 kHz stereo soundtrack.

- Sampling: 4, 6 (default), or 8 steps, without classifier-free guidance (CFG).

- Speed (5.2 s clip, 6 steps): 8.7 s on 4× B200, 36 s on 1× H200, 92 s on 1× RTX 5090.

- Real time on 4× Blackwell GPUs: NVIDIA SOL-H3 runs HyperFlow H3 Flash in real time on 4× B-series GPUs. SOL-H3 is our inference-acceleration partner and supports this model from day 0.

- Model size: 13.7B ( fl2va ) or 13.9B ( ref2va ) parameters, less than half of the ~31B MiniMax-H3 transformer.

- Minimum footprint: Q4_K_M is 9.1 GB ( Q8_0 is 14.9 GB). It runs on 24 GB and 32 GB GPUs in PCs with 16 GB of system RAM . 16 GB GPUs are not measured yet.

## Supported Tasks

## Choose a Runtime

Decision rule: Use GGUF on PCs with 64 GB of system RAM or less. Use INT8 convrot on data-center GPUs, or on 24 GB+ RTX GPUs with at least 69 GiB of system RAM.

All weights are in VideoRebirthAI/hyperflow-h3-flash .

## GGUF Runtimes (ComfyUI, Unsloth Studio, stable-diffusion.cpp)

Full setup guide: integrations/README.md . Quick start:

- ComfyUI ( Video-Rebirth/ComfyUI-HyperFlow-Flash ): Clone ComfyUI-GGUF and ComfyUI-HyperFlow-Flash into ComfyUI/custom_nodes/ . Download the 15.7 GB qwen3vl_32b_minimax_h3_nvfp4_awq text encoder. On 16 GB or 32 GB PCs, start ComfyUI with python main.py --fast-disk . Open Workflow > Browse Templates > ComfyUI-HyperFlow-Flash and select hyperflow_t2v , hyperflow_i2v , hyperflow_flf2v , or hyperflow_ref2v .

- Clone ComfyUI-GGUF and ComfyUI-HyperFlow-Flash into ComfyUI/custom_nodes/ .

- Download the 15.7 GB qwen3vl_32b_minimax_h3_nvfp4_awq text encoder.

- On 16 GB or 32 GB PCs, start ComfyUI with python main.py --fast-disk .

- Open Workflow > Browse Templates > ComfyUI-HyperFlow-Flash and select hyperflow_t2v , hyperflow_i2v , hyperflow_flf2v , or hyperflow_ref2v .

- Unsloth Studio ( setup guide ): Point SD_CLI_PATH at the patched sd-cli binary and run unsloth studio . Load VideoRebirthAI/hyperflow-h3-flash ( fl2va_gguf/ or ref2va_gguf/ ). Studio downloads the companion text encoder and VAEs automatically. It runs the built-in 6-step schedule at CFG = 1 .

- Point SD_CLI_PATH at the patched sd-cli binary and run unsloth studio .

- Load VideoRebirthAI/hyperflow-h3-flash ( fl2va_gguf/ or ref2va_gguf/ ).

- Studio downloads the companion text encoder and VAEs automatically. It runs the built-in 6-step schedule at CFG = 1 .

- stable-diffusion.cpp ( integrations/stable-diffusion.cpp/ ): Apply hyperflow-two-time.patch to upstream commit 3be2378 . The patch adds the two-time (t, r) embedder, low-rank linear layers, the default 6-step schedule from GGUF metadata, and 32-bit matmul token splitting for long clips.

## Python Package (INT8 convrot)

### Install

pip install git+https://github.com/Video-Rebirth/hyperflow-h3-flash pip install " hyperflow-h3-flash[hopper] @ git+https://github.com/Video-Rebirth/hyperflow-h3-flash " # H100 / H200: FlashAttention-3 pip install " hyperflow-h3-flash[fp8] @ git+https://github.com/Video-Rebirth/hyperflow-h3-flash " # --text-encoder-precision fp8

- Requirements: Python 3.10+, PyTorch 2.6+ with CUDA and Triton ( pip install triton-windows on native Windows), an Ampere or newer NVIDIA GPU, and diffusers >= 0.40 . Multi-GPU ( --gpus > 1) requires Linux or WSL2 (raise memory= in %UserProfile%\.wslconfig on WSL2).

- First-run download: ~90 GB, or ~68 GB with --text-encoder-precision fp8 . This includes the MiniMax-H3 text encoder, VAEs, and the 16 GB HyperFlow INT8 transformer for the selected task. The 62 GB base transformer is never downloaded.

- First-run compilation: Triton INT8 kernels compile on first use (~1 min).

### Command Line

Run hyperflow-h3-flash or python -m hyperflow_h3_flash :

# Text to video + audio (t2va) hyperflow-h3-flash --prompt " A chef slides a steaming bowl of ramen across a wooden counter; rain taps on the window. " \ --output ramen.mp4 # First keyframe, or first + last keyframe (fl2va) hyperflow-h3-flash --prompt " ... " --image first.png --output clip.mp4 hyperflow-h3-flash --prompt " ... " --image first.png --last-image last.png --output clip.mp4 # Reference images, videos (with soundtrack), and audio clips in prompt order (ref2va) hyperflow-h3-flash --prompt " <Picture 1> walks through the scene of <Picture 2> ... " \ --reference person.png --reference scene.png --output clip.mp4 # 15 s clip, context-parallel across 4 GPUs (or --gpus auto for up to 4 visible GPUs) hyperflow-h3-flash --prompt " ... " --num-frames 360 --gpus 4 # 4 steps (speed), 6 steps (default), or 8 steps (quality) hyperflow-h3-flash --prompt " ... " --steps 4

examples/benchmark.py times every pipeline stage and per-GPU peak memory under torchrun .

### Python API

import torch from diffusers . utils . export_utils import encode_video from hyperflow_h3_flash import load_pipeline pipe = load_pipeline ( "t2va" ) # "fl2va": pass image=... (and last_image=...); "ref2va": pass references=[...] out = pipe ( prompt = "A chef slides a steaming bowl of ramen across a wooden counter." , num_frames = 124 , num_inference_steps = 6 , # 4, 6, or 8 generator = torch . Generator (). manual_seed ( 0 ), output = [ "videos" , "audio" , "sampling_rate" ], ) encode_video ( out [ "videos" ][ 0 ], fps = 24 , output_path = "ramen.mp4" , audio = out [ "audio" ][ 0 ], audio_sample_rate = out [ "sampling_rate" ], )

- Multi-GPU under torchrun : Call torch.distributed.init_process_group("nccl") and pass device=f"cuda:{local_rank}" to load_pipeline . The pipeline shards execution across ranks and returns the full output on every rank.

- Standalone transformer ( AutoModel ): Each INT8 Hub folder ships self-contained model code. Load it without installing this package: from diffusers import AutoModel , then AutoModel.from_pretrained("VideoRebirthAI/hyperflow-h3-flash", subfolder="fl2va_int8_convrot", trust_remote_code=True, torch_dtype=torch.bfloat16) .

### Offload Modes

--offload sets GPU memory placement. auto (default) selects a mode from per-GPU VRAM:

- stream is only ~2% slower than none on the same GPU.

- model and stream keep offloaded weights in one pinned host-memory allocation.

- The loader drops unused Qwen3-VL layers above the conditioning tap. This saves ~14 GB. --text-encoder-precision fp8 saves another ~22 GiB.

- In containers, read the memory limit from /sys/fs/cgroup/memory.max , not from free .

## Benchmarks

All runs are end-to-end at 1344×768 and 6 steps : text encoding, transformer, and video and audio VAE decode. Each a / b cell is total time for a 5.2 s / 15 s clip (124 / 362 frames).

### Consumer RTX GPUs: t2va

- GGUF setup: ComfyUI, Q4_K_M , and the 15.7 GB nvfp4 text encoder. 32 GB and 16 GB PCs use --fast-disk with models on NVMe ( Host RAM ). Peak RSS is 34–37 GiB on ≥ 64 GB PCs. Anonymous RSS is ~8–16 GiB on 32 GB PCs and ~8 GiB on 16 GB PCs.

- INT8 setup: hyperflow-h3-flash --offload stream . It needs ≥ 91 GiB of system RAM with the bf16 text encoder, or ~69 GiB with fp8 . The 15 s RTX 5090 run used fp8 .

- The INT8 transformer is 10–20% faster. GGUF needs less than half the system RAM. The transformer takes over 80% of the time and is compute bound. ComfyUI dequantizes Q4_K_M weights at run time.

- Use --fast-disk on 16 GB and 32 GB PCs. It streams unresident weights from the OS file page cache. Without it, ComfyUI-GGUF copies the 9 GB transformer into pinned RAM when VRAM overflows. 16 GB PCs then run out of RAM on 15 s clips. On 32 GB PCs, the RTX 3090 and 5090 become 13% and 21% slower (text encoding takes 27–31 s instead of 7–9 s).

- 32 GB of VRAM holds both models. On the RTX 5090, the text encoder and transformer stay in VRAM together (0.8 s text encoding). On 24 GB GPUs, ComfyUI swaps them between stages (10–16 s text encoding).

- Keyframe tasks ( i2v , flf2v ): See GGUF guide: Performance .

### Consumer RTX GPUs: ref2va

- References: Two 768p stills generated with t2va (a person and a street market). Mixed is one still, one 5.2 s reference video with its soundtrack, and one audio clip.

- INT8 setup: 100–125 GB of system RAM (80–88 GiB process RSS). ¹ On 24 GB GPUs, 15 s mixed runs need --block-chunk 16384 . Without it, they run out of VRAM.

- GGUF setup: ComfyUI on ≥ 64 GB RAM, with hyperflow_ref2v_api.json and the nvfp4 text encoder. ref_image_size match (default) downscales each reference to the output's pixel area and keeps its aspect ratio. max downscales only above a 2048 short edge. The max runs used the stills upscaled to 3584×2048, the size the INT8 pipeline uses. ² max at 15 s needs python main.py --disable-cuda-malloc . The default cudaMallocAsync allocator fails with CUDA error: invalid argument .

- Each reference adds tokens to every step. At a 2048 short edge, one image adds ~14,300 tokens (about seven 768p latent frames). The clip itself is 37,710 tokens at 5.2 s and 109,062 at 15 s. Attention cost grows with the square of the token count. So at 5.2 s, the INT8 transformer takes 2.6–2.9× its t2va time with two images and 5.2–5.8× with the mixed set.

- GGUF match is the fastest image-reference path. It adds 24–36% to t2v at 5.2 s and 7–15% at 15 s. At the same reference size ( max ), GGUF is 11–25% slower than INT8 at 5.2 s and 8–9% slower at 15 s.

- --fast-disk also works for ref2v . 32 GB and 16 GB PCs ran 5.2 s and 15 s clips on all three GPUs, within 4% of ≥ 64 GB RAM at 15 s. See GGUF guide: Host RAM .

### Data-Center GPUs (INT8)

- Real-time inference: The table measures this package. For real time on 4× B-series GPUs, use NVIDIA SOL-H3 .

- INT8 GEMM backend: The 4× H200 row uses the default Triton kernel (12.6 s). int8_gemm="sgl" (CUTLASS INT8 via sgl-kernel ) measured 12.3 s.

- 4-GPU stage times (5.2 s): Text encoder 0.11–0.16 s. 6-step transformer 7.8–7.9 s on 4× H200 and 5.0 s on 4× B200. Video VAE decode 3.3–4.0 s.

- 1088p (1920×1088, 362 frames): 743 s on 1× H200 (106 GiB VRAM). 220 s on 4× H200 (68 GiB VRAM/GPU).

## Architecture and Hardware Notes

### How It Works

HyperFlow H3 Flash changes the MiniMax-H3 transformer in three ways:

- Structural pruning and low-rank factorization:

- Rotated W8A8 INT8 quantization ( convrot ): 180 linear layers are quantized to W8A8 INT8 behind a block-diagonal Hadamard rotation.

- Two-time (t, r) conditioning: Every token receives the current noise level t and the step endpoint r . This enables 4-to-8-step sampling without CFG. Conditioning tokens stay at their anchor noise level ( r = t ).

### Multi-GPU and Kernel Dispatch ( hyperflow-h3-flash )

- Sequence and VAE parallelism ( --gpus N ): Ulysses context parallelism splits the packed transformer sequence across $N$ GPUs. Ranks encode keyframes and references and decode spatial video VAE tiles in parallel. Then they all-gather and blend the tiles to match single-GPU output bitwise.

- Text encoder placement: With --offload none and the bf16 text encoder, FSDP2 shards the 50 GiB text encoder across GPUs. This cuts 4-GPU peak VRAM from 91 GiB to 59 GiB/GPU. When offloading or using fp8 , rank 0 runs the text encoder and broadcasts the embeddings (~2 MB).

- INT8 GEMM dispatch:

- Reproducibility: The same seed, GPU architecture, GPU count, and attention backend produce bitwise-identical clips. text_encoder_fsdp and vae_parallel preserve bitwise output.

# FediGoo

A Mastodon client for the Linux desktop, written in Rust with GTK 4.

Created by AI Sloperator with Claude Code.

No license is given.

## Features

- Multiple accounts, with OAuth login, switching and logout (which revokes the token)

- Timelines: home, local, federated, hashtags, lists, trending posts, bookmarks and favourites

- Notifications, mentions and private conversations

- Live updates over the streaming API, with an unread badge and a "new items" button

- Posts: content warnings, sensitive-media covers, image viewer with alt text, link cards (right-click to open the link or copy it, also as Markdown), polls (with voting), threads with indented replies, translation

- Actions: reply, boost, favourite, bookmark, edit, delete, delete & re-draft, pin, mute conversation, copy link or text, report

- Composer: character counter using the instance limit, content warning, visibility, language, media upload (file picker or paste) with alt text, polls, and Ctrl+Enter to send; if the server is slow or down, it shows that and you can cancel or try again without losing the post

- Profiles: bio, verified fields, follow or follow request, notify on new posts, hide boosts, mute, block, domain block, list membership, followers and following

- Search for accounts, hashtags and posts (URLs from other servers are resolved)

- Explore (trending posts, hashtags and news), followed hashtags, follow requests, list management, mutes and blocks, profile editing (including avatar and header)

- Keyword and hashtag filters: view, add, edit and delete them; matching posts are collapsed behind a warning or hidden, as each filter says

- Links to profiles, posts and hashtags on any server open inside the app

- The sidebar can shrink to icons only (the button at its foot), with labels as tooltips

## Keyboard shortcuts

Paging lands on the start of a post where that doesn't skip anything, and pages through posts taller than the window. Paging up twice at the top of a feed checks for new posts; paging twice past either end of a thread checks for new replies. Space and Backspace still type in text fields, and Backspace does nothing on a top-level page (there's nothing to go back to).

In the image viewer:

## Building

System packages (Debian/Ubuntu names):

sudo apt install pkgconf libgtk-4-dev libsoup-3.0-dev

Then, with a stable Rust toolchain from rustup:

cargo build --release ./target/release/fedigoo

The only crate dependencies are the GTK bindings ( gtk4 ) and the libsoup bindings ( soup3 ) plus their own dependencies. JSON handling and the HTML conversion are built in. HTTPS uses libsoup and glib-networking.

## Running

fedigoo # GTK picks the backend (honours GDK_BACKEND) fedigoo --x11 # force X11 fedigoo --wayland # force Wayland

## Installing

./target/release/fedigoo --install

This copies the executable to ~/.local/bin/fedigoo , and adds a menu entry ( ~/.local/share/applications/com.aisloperator.FediGoo.desktop ) and an icon (under ~/.local/share/icons/hicolor/ ), so FediGoo shows up in your application menu and dock. fedigoo --uninstall removes those files and leaves your accounts and settings alone.

Log in through the welcome screen. FediGoo opens your instance's authorisation page in the browser; paste the code it shows back into FediGoo.

All local data (accounts, access tokens, OAuth client registrations, preferences) is in $XDG_CONFIG_HOME/fedigoo/config.json , normally ~/.config/fedigoo/config.json . The file is created with owner-only permissions.

## Tests

cargo test # offline unit tests cargo test -- --ignored # also hits the public mastodon.social API

For testing the UI without a display, GTK's Broadway backend works, and tools/broadway-input.py sends it real pointer and keyboard input (clicks, drags, key shortcuts) in place of a web browser. Its docstring has the details.

## Code Dependencies

This section is updated before each release, from a build on the reference system: Debian 13 (trixie) on amd64 (x86_64), using Debian's own packages for GTK 4, libsoup 3 and the other system libraries.

How much of it is specific to the reference system differs by list:

- Direct crates come from Cargo.toml , so they are the same everywhere.

- Indirect crates come from the committed Cargo.lock , listed for an x86_64 Linux build. A build from the same lock file uses the same crate versions on any system, though another target may build a slightly different set of crates. A cargo update can change the versions.

- Non-crate libraries (both lists) are what the reference system's release binary links to and loads. Another distribution, distribution version or architecture may have other library versions or sonames, link a different set, or load other modules at run time.
