# AI Gude

Ei Gude is Hessian for good morning, and AI Gude sounds just like it. It is your own morning podcast.

You choose the news sources you follow and how the show should sound. At the times you pick, AI Gude reads what is new, writes a script in your style, speaks it with an AI voice and delivers one audio Episode with chapters, made for listening on your phone.

You host it yourself. AI Gude is free and open source software.

Live demo: aigude.alexdoes.dev . Sign in with the user demo and the password demo . You can browse the Episodes and play them. You cannot switch users, produce, retry or delete Episodes, and the log, the editor of the User Config and the problems of its files stay closed.

## Table of Contents

- Getting Started

- Concepts How AI Gude works Operating modes

- How AI Gude works

- Operating modes

- How-Tos

- License

In this tutorial you start AI Gude on your machine and listen to your first Episode.

- Clone the repository. git clone https://github.com/alex0ptr/aigude.git cd aigude

Clone the repository.

git clone https://github.com/alex0ptr/aigude.git cd aigude

- Install the tools with mise , which has to be activated in your shell . It installs the versions of Go, ffmpeg and task that the project pins. mise install

Install the tools with mise , which has to be activated in your shell . It installs the versions of Go, ffmpeg and task that the project pins.

mise install

- Get a key at Google AI Studio for the language model and the voice, and one at Firecrawl for reading the articles. Export both. export GEMINI_API_KEY= " ... " export FIRECRAWL_API_KEY= " ... "

Get a key at Google AI Studio for the language model and the voice, and one at Firecrawl for reading the articles. Export both.

export GEMINI_API_KEY= " ... " export FIRECRAWL_API_KEY= " ... "

- Start the service with the example configuration in hack/ . task serve:hosted It can be reached from your network, so run it on a network you trust.

Start the service with the example configuration in hack/ .

task serve:hosted

It can be reached from your network, so run it on a network you trust.

- Open http://localhost:8080 , choose the show and press "Generate now". Producing the Episode takes a few minutes. When it is done it appears in the list. Press play.

You have a running AI Gude. To follow your own feeds, continue with Configure Shows, Feeds and Schedules .

## Concepts

A User owns CastProfiles, and each CastProfile is a show. A CastProfile lists the Subscriptions it draws Content from, which are RSS feeds, a Max Lookback that says how old Content may be, and Schedules that say when an Episode is made. Content is one item that a Subscription delivers, such as an article. An Episode is one audio file with its Script and its Chapters, one Chapter for each Section of the Script.

The core flow, from a Schedule to a finished Episode:

sequenceDiagram autonumber participant S as Scheduler participant W as Worker participant DB as Database participant R as RSS feeds participant C as Crawler participant G as Gemini participant F as ffmpeg S->>W: Schedule is due, queue the CastProfile Note over S,W: "Generate now" queues the same request W->>DB: Which Content was used by this CastProfile already? W->>R: Fetch the Subscriptions, Content within the Max Lookback R->>C: Retrieve the full text of each new article C-->>R: Cleaned text, from the cache while it is fresh R-->>W: Contents alt nothing new W-->>S: No Episode, only a log line else new Content W->>G: Rules, style guide and numbered Contents G-->>W: Script with title and Sections loop every Section W->>G: Speak the Section G-->>W: Speech as PCM end W->>F: Speech joined with a pause between Sections F-->>W: One OGG/Opus file W->>W: Write the Chapters into the file W->>DB: Save Episode, Script, Chapters, sources and usage end Note over W,DB: Any failure saves the Episode as failed, with its reason

What to keep in mind:

- One Episode is produced at a time. Requests wait in a queue.

- Choose a Max Lookback that is larger than the interval between two Schedules. Content older than the Max Lookback is never considered, so a shorter one lets articles fall through the gap between two Episodes.

- A larger Max Lookback does no harm, because each Episode remembers the Content it used and no article is told twice. Deleting an Episode gives its Content back.

- A Schedule that was due while the service was not running is made up at the start, once for each CastProfile.

- A failed Episode stays in the list with its reason. You can try again or dismiss it.

- Each Section is spoken in its own call, which makes the Chapters exact, and the audio is encoded once at the end.

Behind the steps are small interfaces, and one adapter each does the work today:

flowchart LR P["Episode production"] P --> CR["ContentRepository"] --> RSS["RSS feeds"] P --> CW["Crawler"] --> FC["Firecrawl"] P --> SW["ScriptWriter"] --> GM["Gemini text"] P --> TT["TTS"] --> GT["Gemini speech"] P --> AE["AudioEncoder"] --> FF["ffmpeg"] P --> ER["EpisodeRepository"] --> DB["SQLite"] P --> AS["AudioStore"] --> FS["Files"]

The only part you can run in two ways is the Crawler, which retrieves the full text of the articles. You choose it with the setting firecrawl_url .

- The hosted Firecrawl is the default and needs FIRECRAWL_API_KEY . There is nothing to run, and it bills per page. The Getting Started uses it.

- A Firecrawl of your own costs nothing per page. Set firecrawl_url to its address. The key is then optional and is sent only when it is set. task serve starts one in Docker from hack/firecrawl/ , but that one is for development only and has no authentication, so it is not a recipe for hosting.

AI Gude keeps crawled pages for crawl_cache_ttl , which is ten days by default, and shares them between all Users. An article that is retrieved again soon costs nothing.

### Configure the Service Settings

Settings apply to the whole service. The commented example is hack/aigude.toml .

- Settings come from built-in defaults, the settings file, environment variables and flags, and each one overrides the one before it. An environment variable is AIGUDE_ plus the upper-case key, for example AIGUDE_LISTEN_ADDR . A flag is the key with hyphens, for example --listen-addr .

- The settings file is aigude.toml in the working directory of the service, or the file given with --config . It is optional. The example lists every setting with its default and a comment, and a test guards that the defaults it shows are the real ones. Copy it and delete what you do not want to change.

- A key the service does not know is an error, and so is an invalid value. The message names the setting. Changes need a restart.

- The API keys GEMINI_API_KEY and FIRECRAWL_API_KEY are not settings. A key in the settings file is rejected as an unknown key and the service does not start, so they come from the environment only.

### Configure Shows, Feeds and Schedules

Shows, feeds and Schedules belong to a User and live in that User's file. The commented example is hack/users/demo.toml , and it is the template for new Users.

- Each User has one .toml file in the folder users_dir , which is users by default. The file name is free, and the User is identified by the Id inside.

- A file holds the User, its CastProfiles, and for each CastProfile the Subscriptions, Max Lookback, language, voice, prompt and Schedules.

- The files are followed while the service runs, so an edit takes effect without a restart. A file that turns invalid keeps the last valid setup of its User, and the interface shows the problem. A deleted file takes its User away.

- A User can edit their own file in the interface with "Edit User Config". To check files without starting anything run this:

aigude validate --users-dir users

### Configure Multiple Users and Authentication

AI Gude has no sign-in of its own. Authentication is the job of a reverse proxy in front of it. The proxy tells AI Gude who is asking in a request header, and from then on each person works in their own User and cannot reach another one.

#### Start without authentication

Without the header everyone who reaches the port can switch between all Users in the interface, produce and delete Episodes and edit every User Config. At home on a network you trust that is a fine way to share one instance. It is also why the service listens on 127.0.0.1 by default. Do not leave it like this on a network that others can reach.

To add a User, copy hack/users/demo.toml into the users folder and change the [user] table and what follows. The file is picked up at once.

#### Pin each person to their User

After the proxy has authenticated a person, it sets the header X-Aigude-User to the Id of their User. Use the Id and not the display name, because only the Id never changes.

A request with this header belongs to that User. The interface offers no switch to another User, a request to switch is refused, and the person sees only their own Episodes and edits only their own User Config. A header that is empty, that names no User or that names a User without a valid setup is answered with 403 for every request.

Two things have to hold for this to be safe:

- The port is reachable only through the proxy.

- The proxy sets the header itself on every request and never passes one on from the client. A request without the header gets full rights, so a proxy that forgets it opens the service to everyone.

#### Example with Traefik and Basic Auth

Traefik asks for a user name and a password and writes the name into X-Aigude-User . So the user name of the Basic Auth is the Id of the User. Create the users file with one line for each person, for example with htpasswd :

htpasswd -nB alex >> /etc/traefik/users

Then add the route and its middleware to the dynamic configuration of Traefik. Replace the host name and the address of the service. The example assumes an entry point websecure and a certificate resolver letsencrypt . Serve it over HTTPS, because Basic Auth sends the password with every request.

http : routers : aigude : rule : Host(`aigude.example.org`) entryPoints : - websecure service : aigude middlewares : - aigude-auth tls : certResolver : letsencrypt middlewares : aigude-auth : basicAuth : usersFile : /etc/traefik/users realm : AI Gude headerField : X-Aigude-User removeHeader : true services : aigude : loadBalancer : servers : - url : http://127.0.0.1:8080

headerField makes Traefik set X-Aigude-User from the user name and replaces a value that the client sent, and removeHeader keeps the credentials from reaching AI Gude. A name in the users file that is not a User of AI Gude is answered with 403.

#### Show the demo User to visitors

The User with the Id demo is shown in Demo Mode. Whoever looks at its pages can browse and play its Episodes, and nothing can be changed. The log and the editor of the User Config are closed, and the interface leaves out what only the person running the service should see, such as problems in the User Config files. Because "Generate now" is closed too, the Episodes of the demo User come from its Schedules. Create it like any User, for example from the sample hack/users/demo.toml with the Id demo .

### Run and Maintain the Service

- Produce an Episode with "Generate now" on a CastProfile, or let its Schedules do it.

- Episodes are deleted with their audio once they are older than the Retention, the time Episodes are kept. The setting is episode_retention , it is 30 days by default, it counts from the creation of the Episode and it applies to failed Episodes too. 0 keeps them for ever. The check runs at the start and once a day, and a deleted Episode gives its Content back.

- The meter on an Episode shows what it consumed, such as tokens and crawled pages.

- GET /healthz answers 200 with ok and checks nothing behind it, not the database, not Gemini and not Firecrawl. It needs no headers of a proxy.

- Back up the data folder data_dir . I

# Skrongle

A learning app you run yourself, on a Raspberry Pi, for the people at home.

Skrongle is one small binary that teaches from courses made of JSON files: lessons, adaptive quizzes, five-minute practice sessions, games, flashcards and an AI tutor. Spanish and French courses ship with it; any subject that fits units → lesson groups → lessons can be a course, written by hand, uploaded from files, or described to an AI that writes it for you.

It is built for a handful of people who know whoever runs it: a family, a class, a few friends. Up to eight accounts, no e-mail, no outside service of any kind except the AI providers you choose to give it a key for. A Raspberry Pi Zero 2 W runs it with room to spare.

## Run it yourself

For the step-by-step path, follow the home Wi-Fi guide , written for someone who has never run a server, and the Tailscale guide to reach it away from home. The technical reference is docs/self-hosting.md . The short form:

- Download the release tarball for your machine: skrongle-<version>-aarch64.tar.gz for a Pi (64-bit Raspberry Pi OS) or -x86_64 for a PC running Linux.

- Unpack it, install the systemd unit it contains and start the service. The server writes an owner link to its log: open it to make the first account, which is the owner's.

- Everyone else joins with an invitation link the owner makes on the Manage Users page.

- Optional: paste an AI provider's API key on the same page. It serves every account, and the owner can hide the AI features for everyone with one switch.

What you get, and what you are responsible for:

A database from before version 1.0 is not upgraded; start from a fresh one.

## What it teaches with

Every feature reads the same course files:

Courses also carry music notation, clocks, protractors and algebra tiles as question types, so the format is not limited to languages.

## Courses

A course is a folder: course.json (title, units, groups, labels, an optional paradigm) plus lessons/**/*.json , one lesson per file. The format is in docs/course-format.md , with a JSON Schema at docs/course.schema.json ; a minimal course is two short files.

Ready-made. data/courses/<id>/ is loaded at start-up; the folder name must equal the manifest id . Spanish (101 lessons, CEFR A1 to C2) and French (75 lessons) ship with the app. Drop another folder next to them and restart.

Build your own. Courses → Build a course creates a starter course in the database. Edit the files in the browser or upload JSON files (or a whole folder). Every save validates the whole course and names the exact file and field that is wrong. The edit page links to the format reference, so you can also hand it to any LLM and upload what it writes.

Generate with AI. Courses → Describe a course takes a description and the number of lessons. The model plans the course and writes each lesson in turn; each file is validated against the format, with the validator's message sent back to the model when it gets something wrong. One generation runs at a time.

## Documentation

The documentation lives in docs/ and is served by the app at /docs , so a page can be handed to a person or an LLM; /llms.txt lists what an LLM needs to write a course.

- docs/getting-started.md , the user guides and the FAQ .

- docs/self-hosting.md and the self-hosting FAQ .

- docs/course-format.md : the complete course format, also the specification the AI generator follows.

- docs/features.md : what each feature does, the mastery engine, and which lesson fields each feature reads.

- docs/architecture.md : source layout, request flow, database schema, configuration, security notes.

- docs/testing.md : how to run the checks.

## Developing

./.dev-start # build + run on a free port (printed), DB in ./dev.db, debug logging ./.dev-start --release # the exact profile a release gets ./.dev-start --reset # wipe ./dev.db first ./.dev-start --lan # listen on 0.0.0.0 so a phone on your network can try it ./.dev-start --watch # rebuild + restart on changes cargo test --features dev # unit tests (without the feature, the dev-only ones are left out) scripts/smoke.sh # fresh server + fixtures: main pages and one AI generation over HTTP scripts/e2e.sh # headless browser tests (Playwright, Node 22+); see docs/testing.md cargo build --release # hardened release profile (fat LTO, 1 codegen unit, stripped, panic=abort)

./.dev-start , the test scripts and CI build with --features dev ; a release build leaves the feature out and has none of what follows. Dev mode ( SKRONGLE_DEV=1 , what ./.dev-start sets) adds /dev/login , a simulated AI provider that answers from fixtures, and seeded accounts, so every AI feature can be exercised without a key. Working on the code with an LLM? Start with CLAUDE.md .

The app itself keeps no developer keys.

### Cross-compiling and releases

brew install zig && cargo install cargo-zigbuild # on a Mac rustup target add aarch64-unknown-linux-gnu scripts/build-pi.sh # aarch64, to dist/aarch64-unknown-linux-gnu/ scripts/build-pi.sh x86_64 # 64-bit PC Linux scripts/package-release.sh 0.2.0 aarch64 # the release tarball

Release tarballs are built by CI on a v* tag ( .github/workflows/release.yml ).

## Configuration

Everything is an environment variable; all are optional. The full table with defaults is in docs/self-hosting.md , "Configuration". The ones most installs touch:

skrongle doctor prints what the server would use: version, OS, database and schema level, which secrets are set (yes or no, never their values), free disk and memory.

## On a Raspberry Pi Zero 2 W

Measured on the Pi, release build:

The limits that keep it there are in src/caps.rs : 8 accounts, 4 sessions each, 32 open connections, 2 tutor replies at once, one course generation at a time, and a course cache bounded by the account count. All state lives in SQLite, so the process has no growth path.

## Security notes

- Passwords: argon2id with a per-user salt; unknown addresses verify against a dummy hash so login timing does not reveal whether an account exists.

- Sessions: 256-bit random tokens, 30-day TTL, deleted on logout, purged hourly; HttpOnly; SameSite=Lax cookie, Secure behind TLS; at most four per account.

- Every state-changing request passes a same-origin check; the JSON API only accepts Content-Type: application/json .

- Course files are validated on every save (1 MiB per file, 400 per course). Lesson Markdown passes raw HTML through, so only load courses you trust.

- API keys are saved encrypted at rest (ChaCha20-Poly1305 under SKRONGLE_SECRET_KEY or <db>.key ) and never shown again; only owners see the page that holds them.

- The person running it secures the login: a strong password per account, an authenticator app, and the server reachable only over Tailscale or a VPN, never through a forwarded port.

## Licence

AGPL-3.0. See LICENSE .

# Character.AI export viewer

Open your Character.AI data export and read your characters and chats — in your own browser. The file is read on your device; nothing is uploaded anywhere.

Use it online, free and without an account: amavie.ai/character-ai-export . This repository is the same reader as open source, so you can check what it does with your file or run it yourself.

## What it opens

- Character.AI data export — the ZIP (or the JSON files inside it) from Character.AI's “Export data”: your characters and every chat, with dates and both sides of the conversation.

- Character cards — PNG cards with the card inside (SillyTavern, Chub, JanitorAI, RisuAI, Agnai, Backyard AI) and card JSON.

- Chat exports — SillyTavern .jsonl chats, WhatsApp and Telegram exports, plain text.

## Run it yourself

npm install npm run dev # opens the viewer at http://localhost:5173 npm test # format tests npm run build # static files in dist/ — host them anywhere

Requires Node.js 20 or newer. No server, no analytics, no network requests: the page reads the file with the File API and unzips it with fflate .

## Use the reader in your own code

import { readImportFile } from './src/lib/parse' ; const reading = await readImportFile ( file ) ; // a File from <input type="file"> if ( reading . kind === 'pick' ) { // Character.AI export: reading.pick.characters, reading.pick.chats (messages with role, name, text, time) } else if ( reading . kind === 'request' ) { // one card or one chat: reading.request.card_json, reading.request.chat }

## Where it comes from

The reader is the one Amavie uses to bring a character and a conversation over from another app; src/lib is mirrored from Amavie's codebase, so fixes land there first. Issues and pull requests are welcome.

Amavie is a universe of AI characters who remember you and live their own lives — chat with them and play roleplay scenes on the web , iOS and Android.

https://github.com/anteloc/ldraw-mecha/t.markdown:
# ldraw-mecha

Give an LDraw LEGO© model to an AI agent, get back a Blender-animated version of it.

The agent will:

- Reverse-engineer (infer) the LDraw model's mechanics from its .mpd source code file 🤓

- Study the discovered mechanisms.

- Plan the interactions between their different mechanical components.

- And finally, turn those plans into python code for Blender , that will: Create the required rigs for controlling the different mechanisms. Animate them according to plan ! 🤯

- Create the required rigs for controlling the different mechanisms.

- Animate them according to plan ! 🤯

## Installation

Note

The installation process will install every required tool and dependency locally on this project repo, in order to avoid polluting the host OS .

However, there is a requirement of setting several env vars on rc files, like e.g. .bashrc or .zshrc

The installed dependencies, like e.g. Blender, are git-ignored by default.

You'll need Python 3.12+ installed.

Start by cloning the repo and running the setup script , pick the right one for your OS:

git clone https://github.com/anteloc/ldraw-mecha.git cd ldraw-mecha ./setup-macos.sh # or ./setup-linux.sh, ./setup-win-wsl.sh

### Installed during setup

At the end of the setup process, you'll get a snippet with the env vars to be added to your shell profile ( .bashrc , .zshrc , etc.), something like e.g.:

# >>> ldraw-mecha (from setup-macos.sh) >>> export LDRAW_DIR= " /Users/me/ldraw-mecha/data/ldraw " export LDRAWDIR= " $LDRAW_DIR " export BLENDER_BIN= " /Users/me/ldraw-mecha/bin/Blender.app/Contents/MacOS/Blender " export LEOCAD= " /Users/me/ldraw-mecha/bin/LeoCAD.app/Contents/MacOS/LeoCAD " export LDRAW_XRAY_CACHE= " /Users/me/ldraw-mecha/.cache/ldraw-xray " export LDRAW_ANNOTATOR_DB= " /Users/me/ldraw-mecha/data/ldraw-info.db " # export TYPESAFE_API_KEY=... # optional: Jev semantic search (jev-rerank) # other env vars... # <<< ldraw-mecha <<<

If you're on VS Code or a terminal , restart it in order to get an updated env with the newly added env vars.

## Usage

For inspecting and selecting one pre-annotated model to animate, open the annotated models selector by running:

python3 model-selector/serve.py

Then, take a look at the Process guide for a step-by-step usage example .

## Samples

More samples available at: Gallery

Animations have been generated from original models , not from ai-generated ones.

These are some samples of animations by different agents, take a look at their Summaries for more details.

## 42043 Mercedes-Benz Arocs flatbed truck: the pneumatic crane on its own

- Agent: Claude Sonnet 5.5

- Original model: 42043-1_Flatbed-Trailer.mpd

- Context: The model was too large and complex for fully animating it, finally I accepted Sonnet's suggestion about animating the crane alone.

▶ Video · Summary

Original

## 3625 Fabuland plane: take-off, flight and landing

- Original model: 3625-1.mpd

- Context: Asked for an in-place animation, to avoid the plane moving around.

## Minifig movement catalog: ten minifigs, three moves each

- Agent: Claude Opus 5.5

- Original model: None

- Context: This one is actually a generated composition , from several different minifigs , to be used as a "howto reference" for other agents also animating minifigs.

## Agent's informational sources

## Why and How?

After publishing LDraw Nova , a sibling project for agentic generation of LDraw models , several people reached out to me asking about if models could be animated somehow.

During the development of Nova, I noticed that adding some special annotations to .mpd original model source files , and then giving those to agents , would:

- Help agents in understanding how to build other different models.

- But also, in understanding how a model was built .

Which gave me the idea that, maybe, an agent would also understand how a model would work.

### Reverse-engineering mechanisms from their sources

As a first step to it, I gave annotated models to different agents, and prompted them to infer (reverse-engineer) their constituent submodels (see Haiku 5.5. experiment below).

Results from inference experiments were both pretty good and consistent across different agents, and I also noticed the following: many of the submodels inferred were actually mechanisms.

After questioning several agents about those inferred mechanisms, regarding how would they actually work , I also got consistent results: agents would describe behaviours based on the descriptions for the parts on a mechanism! 🤯

At this point, I had the following:

- Agents would split and refine models into submodels and mechanisms.

- Agents would understand each mechanism in isolation .

- Agents would understand how individual mechanisms worked .

The result of an actual divide-and-conquer process , right? 🤓

Which would make handling individual mechanisms manageable. 🤩

### Correlating LDraw source code to a 3D model

Now, there was the matter of giving agents the means to actually animate mechanisms they already knew how they worked.

I was playing with Blender MCP at the time, and Blender looked promising as a tool that would provide agents a way to manipulate LDraw models in 3D , imported into Blender as glTF (.glb) files.

But there was still an open issue:

How to map from a refined model source code an agent would understand, to its equivalent 3D model in glTF format an agent could manipulate?

And the solution I found was:

Annotate the 3D glTF model's nodes with the same annotations as the source code, so the agent would:

- Outside Blender: plan on submodels 🤔 and parts as source code.

- Inside Blender: execute on matching nodes ✨ on the 3D glTF model.

### Putting the pieces together 😉

Now, I had a draft for a process , but no tools for the agent to use and carry it forward.

Given that the process would require a high amount of complex geometric and spatial calculations , I asked the agent to derive a new python toolset from the one created for ldraw-nova

The new python toolset I refined iteratively , by giving the agent simple models at the beginning, and increasingly complex ones each time.

And to test it, I gave an agent instructions to:

- first, plan from an annotated and refined .mpd model

- then, generate a glTF 3D version of it, with matching annotations

- then, upload it to Blender

- and then, produce the Blender python scripts that would animate the model as planned.

And it finally worked ! 🚀🚀🚀

(but not perfectly) 😜

## Experiment - Claude Haiku 5.5 reverse-engineering session

Prompt:

This is a fragment, a submodel, from an LDraw .mpd file model.

This is not an executable code fragment, but more like a 3D CAD model fragment written in LDraw language. Infer what this submodel is, and also split it into submodels (starting with: 0 FILE):

- always with relevant, semantical meaning,

- the first 0-line following every 0 FILE line is the "description line" for the submodel, according to the LDaw standard

# Umbra

An autonomous agent that lives on your Android phone. Tell it what to do; it works in the background, operates apps for you, writes and builds code in a real Linux environment on the same device, checks its own work, and asks before anything risky.

- Operates the phone. It reads the screen (accessibility tree first, screenshots when needed), taps, types, scrolls, opens apps, reads notifications and logs, and verifies that each action did what it should. Work can run in an invisible background display, so you keep using the phone.

- A Linux machine in your pocket. A Debian environment (bash, git, Python, Bun, and add-on toolchains such as C/C++, Java, Node, Android app builds and a virtual desktop) where the agent builds and tests software. Files live in workspaces both worlds can see.

- Built on omp , a coding agent with a mature tool and planning loop, extended here with Android, privileged and desktop tools. Models are yours: Anthropic, OpenAI, Google, OpenRouter, or any OpenAI-compatible server.

- You stay in control. Risky actions (payments, messages, deleting data, security settings, installing apps, passwords) always need your approval, from the app, a notification or a floating control. The agent can never operate its own app or answer its own approvals. Everything it asked and you answered is kept in a history. Settings → Stop and take back takes access back (stop everything, revoke the helpers, turn screen control off, delete the history); each of these says what it ends before it does it. The Linux side runs without privileges and cannot change its own system files or read the app's private data; the limits of that are in ADR 0010 .

- Resumable. Tasks are persistent sessions: pause, resume, stop, follow up, restart after the app or the agent crashes; terminals live in tmux and survive the app; a session may resume by itself after a restart only under a resume contract you gave it.

- Porcelain in Motion. A camera-anchored Capsule over any app (the task, approvals, a composer, and Snapshot selection: circle part of the screen and send it with its text), and the Power Studio: planning and agents, resources (requests beyond what the phone can run wait in a fair, visible queue), runners, shared services, terminals, emergency lockdown, a credential vault (git tokens used only by root for one repository, never given to an agent; a backup sealed under a recovery code), a commit gate that publishes only what you authorize and reads it back, security evidence with independent anchors, and your own computers as execution nodes ( umbra-node ), which you can revoke.

- Session files. The paperclip attaches a device file as a shortcut to its original, or mounts a device folder as the session's working directory. Git protection starts enabled: private checkpoints include ignored files and uncommitted changes without changing an existing repository's staging index. Recovery opens a separate workspace; disconnecting keeps originals and history. Direct access requires Android's file-access permission; cloud files are imported as copies.

- Personal assistants. Agents have their own assistant prompt, memory, timers, inbox and tools. They delegate implementation to separate coding sessions; tap the delegation or report event to open that work. Broad activity labels and native thinking-orbs indicators follow thinking, reviewing, writing, connecting and active work. Chats show a larger orb; headers and the Agents list keep a compact indicator visible during delegated work. Animation stops offscreen, in the background and with reduced motion. Wake digests stay out of chat, and agent turns do not send generic “Task finished” notifications. Telegram requests keep replies, reminders and approval alerts on Telegram until the user sends a new request in the app. Laya routes incoming items among agents subscribed to that source, including broadcasts when relevant to all; without a confident Laya answer, subscriptions and explicit rules remain in force.

- English and 繁體中文. The whole interface is in both; it follows the phone's language, or pick one in Android's per-app language settings.

- Updates itself. Twice a day it reads update.json on umbra-agent.pages.dev , downloads a newer APK from the site's Cloudflare R2 bucket (resumable; Wi-Fi only unless you check by hand), checks its size, SHA-256, package, version and that it is signed with the same key, and installs it when no task is running: silently through the helper or root, otherwise through Android's installer, which asks you once. Settings → About shows the state and has the switches ( AppUpdater ).

Umbra's original code is free software under the MIT License ; bundled components retain their own licenses and notices . Distribution is by sideload; there is no Play Store build. Read the privacy policy , preview use policy and public-release review and outstanding requirements .

## Requirements

## Get started

- Install the APK — download it from umbra-agent.pages.dev , or build it ( ./gradlew :app:assembleRelease , then adb install -r app/build/outputs/apk/release/app-release.apk ) — and open Umbra.

- Set up walks through what it needs: the accessibility service, the Linux environment, a model.

- Tap New task and say what you want. Watch it work, answer questions, approve what it asks.

The Linux environment is a Debian archive built by runtime-build/rootfs/build.sh and carried inside the release APK, so setting it up needs no network; a file or a URL also work. See docs/DEVELOPMENT.md .

## Your computers as nodes

umbra-node runs jobs for the phone on a computer you own (macOS or Linux, Java 21):

./gradlew :node-runner:installDist node-runner/build/install/umbra-node/bin/umbra-node serve --pair

It prints a one-time code; on the phone, Distributed Nodes → Pair a node with the computer's address and the code. Both sides pin each other's certificate; a new node gets no work until you raise its trust. A paired phone can run commands as that computer's user in the node's jobs folder, only with the files a job's manifest lists, each job for no longer than its lease ( ADR 0018 ). umbra-node phones and umbra-node unpair <prefix> manage the phones it trusts.

## What is verified

Requested feature readiness maps Laya security checks and residency, command approvals, sign-out, result history, usage limits, phone session access, and deferred voice modes.

Every part is tested against the real thing: the real omp binary, a real Android 16 emulator, a real Debian environment on it. The one stand-in is the language model in automated runs (a scripted endpoint), since a real model needs your key. docs/ONDEVICE_TEST_PLAN.md lists what was verified where, what only a real phone can show, and how to run the end-to-end acceptance task on yours. docs/traceability.md maps each requirement to code and tests, including the architecture spec's 22 acceptance criteria with their status (19 met; AC-007 partly and AC-008/009 not built: they need an Execution Halt controller this build does not have).

## Building

source scripts/env.sh scripts/verify.sh # build, unit tests, lint runtime-build/rootfs/build.sh dev # the Linux environment archive (needs Docker)

More in docs/DEVELOPMENT.md ; design decisions in docs/adr .

# Deedglass (Deed Glass) ### Check what your AI agents actually changed. An agent said it updated 1 row. Postgres changed 301. Safety for AI agents that work on databases and health records. Rules decide each AI agent tool call; Deedglass checks what really changed and seals a record. Open source, self-hosted, every feature free. ## Start in one command npx -y deedglass An app opens in your browser. It runs on your own computer, signed in, with no account, no sign-up and no Docker or database to set up, and nothing is sent to us. Choose who will use it (a clinic, hospital IT, or people building with AI), then connect Claude Desktop, Cursor, VS Code, a record system or a database. You need Node 18 or newer. Read Start here for a short tour, or try it without installing anything at deedglass.com/play . For developers , three commands: npx -y deedglass start # an agent reports 1 row, Postgres changed 301, and it's caught npx -y deedglass protect # guard Claude Code, Cursor and other coding agents npx -y deedglass help # the eight everyday commands; "help all" lists every command Without Docker, start plays the same scene inside the binary, every line labelled live or replay , in under 30 s. More: Quickstart · Docs · Policy Generator · Healthcare · Benchmarks · Security · deedglass.com Found it useful? A star helps other people find Deedglass. To hear about new releases, use Watch › Custom › Releases . ## What it does Deedglass sits between AI agents and the systems they change. Rules decide each tool call, a check compares what the system really changed with what the agent reported (Claimed, Checked or Proven; Matches, Doesn't match or Can't check), and each result is sealed as a signed record anyone can check offline. It can undo the rows an action changed. A real run of make demo-hero (commit 97a524c, 2026-10-14), each line shown at the time it printed. Source: docs/assets/demo-hero.cast.json , recorded by scripts/demo/capture.mjs and drawn by scripts/demo/cast2svg.mjs ( make demo-svg ). ## Install curl -fsSL https://deedglass.com/install.sh | sh # macOS and Linux: checks the sha256, copies deedglass into ~/.local/bin npx -y deedglass help # or run it with no install (Node 18 or newer) npm install -g deedglass # or install it from npm The install script downloads the release archive for your platform, checks its sha256 against the release's checksums.txt (and the signature, when cosign is installed), and copies deedglass into ~/.local/bin ; read it first: scripts/install.sh . It downloads from a copy of the release on deedglass.com and falls back to GitHub: about 7 s on one network in India, where the GitHub-only install took 81-119 s. A public container image is coming; until it's published, build the image locally as above. Checksums, signatures and SBOMs: docs/INSTALL.md . ## Who it's for - Developers with agents on databases. Claude Code, Cursor or your own agent writes to Postgres. Your rules decide each call first, Postgres's change log shows what really committed, and the rows one action changed can be undone after a person countersigns. MySQL and other databases can be checked from a Debezium change feed ( docs/WITNESS_DEBEZIUM.md ). - Health-tech teams and hospitals on FHIR. The FHIR connector (beta) puts a FHIR R4 server behind Deedglass with SMART Backend Services, reads each write back at the version the server reported, and checks Proven on HAPI FHIR JPA 8.x and Medplum 5.x running on Postgres. See deedglass.com/healthcare and the FHIR benchmark . To see it on synthetic data first, with no Docker and no server, run npx deedglass health pilot ( the 15-minute hospital pilot ). - Security teams. Lockdown makes every agent write wait for a person, needs two people for high-risk writes and for turning lockdown off, and keeps each agent to one connector ( docs/LOCKDOWN.md ). Records are signed and anyone can check them offline with deedglass verify . ## Project status - Pre-1.0. Every release is in CHANGELOG.md and on the releases page . The deed format is a versioned public spec ( spec/ ), so old records keep verifying. - One maintainer. Deedglass is built by Arjun Prabhakaran in India ( GOVERNANCE.md ). Replies are best effort ( SUPPORT.md ). - Free and self-hosted. Every feature is free while we grow, including ee/ , and it runs on your machines with your own Postgres. Nothing checks a licence and nothing is sent to deedglass.com ( Security ). - Not yet: no SOC 2 report, no outside penetration test and no SSO. Known limits are in docs/LIMITATIONS.md and KNOWN_ISSUES.md . ## How it works flowchart LR A["AI agent
Claude · OpenAI · Cursor · any MCP client"] -->|tool call + agent key| R subgraph D["Deedglass · one binary + Postgres"] R["1 · Rules
allow · deny · ask a person"] --> X["2 · Run
with credentials from the vault"] X --> C["3 · Check
what really changed"] --> S["4 · Seal
a signed record"] end X --> T["Tools
Postgres · FHIR · GitHub · Slack · Stripe · MCP servers"] T -->|change log or read-back| C S --> U["Undo
Postgres rows, after a person countersigns"] H[People] -->|approve · stop| R Every tool call passes through Deedglass with the agent's key. Your rules (policies) decide allow , deny or require_approval ; Deedglass runs the call with credentials the agent never holds; the check compares what happened with what was asked; and the outcome is sealed as a record in the org's chain. ## How sure each check is Each record claims one level and one result: Matches , Doesn't match or Can't check . When Deedglass can't tell whether a tool ran, the result is Can't check, never Matches. The API keeps the short names ( L0 / L1 / L2 , VERIFIED / MISMATCH / UNVERIFIABLE ); the glossary maps them. ## The 301-row scene What an agent reports is not always what the system stored, and a log the agent writes itself can't show the difference. An agent was asked to mark order 42 as shipped. It ran one UPDATE and its tool reported 1 row. A legacy trigger shipped 300 more orders in the same transaction. This is the real output of the Quickstart's last step on 2026-10-14 (shortened where you see … ): $ npx -y deedglass init --trigger … ✕ UPDATE order 42 Proven · Doesn't match · Postgres changed 301 rows in public.orders. The agent reported 1. expected UPDATE 1 row in public.orders where id = 42 · sets status observed UPDATE 301 rows in public.orders · 300 outside id = 42 … ✓ Trigger off orders_ship_open_batch dropped ✓ Undo preview Undo available · 301 rows in public.orders · 301 updates policy undo-needs-approval · a person countersigns first The agent's log says 1 row. Deedglass read Postgres's own change log for that transaction, found 301, sealed the difference as a record, and planned an undo from those rows that runs only after a person countersigns. ## Quickstart Docker running with about 2 GiB of free disk, Node 18 or newer, and macOS or Linux, then (from the tested Quickstart ). On Windows, npx deedglass runs the native Windows binary, no WSL needed; deedglass init uses Docker on macOS and Linux, so on Windows start with npx deedglass app , which needs no Docker: mkdir acme-agents && cd acme-agents npx -y deedglass init --yes npx -y deedglass doctor npx -y deedglass init --trigger deedglass init starts two Postgres 18.6 containers in Docker (Deedglass's own database and a demo database), runs deedglass serve on 127.0.0.1:8080 , creates an org, an agent and the postgres-check policy (reads and writes run, every write is checked at Proven, DROP and TRUNCATE never run; use postgres-safe in production, where writes wait for a person), and ends with a blocked DROP TABLE and an UPDATE checked at Proven. deedglass doctor runs seventeen read-only checks, each with its fix. deedglass init --trigger turns on the demo database's legacy trigger, sends the same one-row UPDATE , and ends on the 301-row mismatch and the undo preview shown above. Its last line is the undo run command; the undo waits for a person, and undo run prints the approve link. Port 8080 or 55432 taken? npx -y deedglass init --yes --listen 127.0.0.1:8090 --pg-port 55440 ( --listen is where deedglass serve listens; --pg-port is Deedglass's own Postgres, and the demo database takes the port 10 above it). Every later command run in that directory finds the ports in .deedglass/stack.json . npx -y deedglass init --purge removes the containers, the volumes and the files in .deedglass/ when you're done. Protect every agent in one command: npx deedglass protect adds the shell guard to Claude Code, Cursor, Codex CLI, Gemini CLI and GitHub Copilot CLI, so a command such as railway volume delete , supabase db reset --linked or terraform destroy waits for your yes (Codex and Gemini CLI deny it instead). It backs up each file first and --undo puts them back: a second check, not a sandbox ( docs/protect.md ). Then put your own Postgres behind it (Supabase, Neon or any Postgres 16 to 18): npx -y deedglass connect "$DATABASE_URL" runs read-only checks and prints a plan; --apply sets it up ( guide ). ## Four ways in When a scan finds a trigger or a cascade on a table your agent can write, it says so and points to the 301 scene. Observe mode is below . ## Observe mode: nothing to rewire deedglass observe run --connector pg-demo -- ./agent.sh # open a watched session, run the agent, close it deedglass observe show obs_01k… --undo-sql # the undo as SQL you review and run (free) deedglass observe run --connector dev --undo-sql ~ /deedglass-undo -- claude # watch a Claude Code session, shell included Turn it on with witness.observe.enabled: true in the connector's config. Observe mode reads only Postgres's change log, through the role and replication slot that deedglass connector postgres init creates, so it works beside any gate you already use, or none. It shows every row committed on the watched tables while the session was open and seals the session as a record. It can't tell which program wrote a row, so a session gets no Matches or Doesn't match verdict; row images are kept 30 days; a TRUNCATE can't be undone from the record. Undo SQL is free, and so is a one-step undo through Deedglass: every feature is free while we grow. Details: docs/OBSERVE.md . ## Add it to your agent client Install in VS Code · LM Studio · Goose · Claude Desktop · Every client claude mcp add --scope user deedglass -- npx -y deedglass mcp serve No link holds a key. Run npx deedglass init first; each client asks Deedglass for the key it wrote. Claude Code plugin (the MCP server, the /deedglass:scan , /deedglass:wrap and /deedglass:watch commands, and skills for reading a scan and for giving an agent Postgres access safely), from this repo's own marketplace: /plugin marketplace add deedglass/deedglass /plugin install deedglass@deedglass Every format, with its source: docs/INSTALL_CLIENTS.md . ## SDKs and clients - TypeScript: @deedglass/sdk , with adapters for the AI SDK, the OpenAI Agents SDK, LangChain and the Claude Agent SDK. - Python: deedglass , with LangChain and Claude Agent SDK adapters. It isn't on PyPI yet; install it from this repo or from a release's wheel ( docs/SDK_PYTHON.md ). - Go: github.com/deedglass/deedglass/pkg/deedglass . - MCP: deedglass mcp wrap governs any stdio MCP server; deedglass mcp serve governs remote ones for Claude Desktop, Claude Code, Cursor, VS Code and Windsurf. ## Connectors Postgres (Proven), REST, GitHub, Slack, Stripe (test mode only), Gmail drafts, Notion and remote MCP servers. Credentials live in an encrypted vault; every outbound call goes through one egress door. See docs/CONNECTORS.md . ## Benchmarks Each benchmark publishes what Deedglass misses next to what it catches. Every scenario, with the misses named: corpus/BENCHMARK.md , corpus/fhir/BENCHMARK.md and deedglass.com/benchmark . Speed: How they were measured, and the misses: docs/BENCHMARKS.md . ## What it doesn't do - Proven checks cover Postgres only, and ne [truncated]

https://github.com/francescobianco/aiquo.markdown:
# AIQuota

See what's left of your AI subscriptions every time you open a terminal.

ChatGPT nearly out until 3 pm? Open Claude instead. AIQuota tells you before you start the coding agent, not halfway through a task.

- A status band when a terminal opens : one section per account, with a green, yellow or red dot showing how close it is to its limit

- In the title bar , always visible and refreshed in the background

- Your accounts, your order : only the ones you list are shown or queried

- Instant : opening a terminal never waits for the network

- Tiny and portable : one POSIX sh script that needs only awk and curl

## Install

List your accounts in the order you want them:

curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/francescobianco/aiquota/main/install.sh | sh -s -- --display=codex,claude,copilot,freebuff

Then open a new terminal. This installs the script to ~/.local/bin and adds one line to your shell's startup file. To change the accounts or their order, run it again; the line is replaced, not duplicated:

aiquota install --display=claude,codex

Prefer to do it by hand? Put bin/aiquota in your PATH and add this as the last line of your startup file:

## Usage

### The band

● ChatGPT Plus [5h 12% ↻1h48m] [7d 61%] ┃ ● Claude Max 5x [5h 99%] [7d 92%] ┃ ● Freebuff Free [day 100%]

- The dot is a traffic light for the account's tightest window: green from 50% left, yellow from 20%, red below that. Grey means no data, for example after a login expires.

- [5h 12%] is one window and the share left. An account can have several.

- ↻1h48m is the time until that window resets, shown when less than half is left.

An empty line separates the band from your first prompt. To remove it, add --no-blank-line to aiquota install or to your startup line.

The band always stays on one row. On narrower terminals it gives up detail in this order:

It uses 256 colors where available and falls back to 16 colors and plain ASCII.

### Short names

Add --short-names to aiquota install or to your startup line to always use short names in the band and the title:

● GPT Plus [5h 12% ↻1h48m] [7d 61%] ┃ ● Cld Max 5x [5h 99%] [7d 92%] ┃ ● Fbf Free [day 100%]

The full aiquota view keeps the complete names.

### The title bar

Title bars only show plain text, so this is a shorter summary with no colors or plan names:

ChatGPT 12% 1h48m │ Claude 92% │ Freebuff 100%

For each account you get the share left in the window that will stop you first. The time until it resets appears when less than half is left.

A ~ before a value means it may be out of date: the login expired, the network failed, or the window has reset since the last successful check.

To use it in a tmux status bar:

set -g status-right ' #(aiquota line --plain --display=codex,claude) '

## Accounts

Note

These are mostly undocumented endpoints , the same ones the agents use for their own usage screens. They can change without notice. When one does, AIQuota keeps showing the last known values, marked ~ .

### Flat subscriptions only

This is a deliberate limit, not a missing feature. AIQuota answers one question: which of the agents I already pay for can I still use right now? That means quota measured in time and resources until the next reset. API keys and metered, usage-based plans are never queried or shown, even if they are on your machine.

## Good to know

Logins expire while you're away. AIQuota reads each agent's credentials but never refreshes them, because refresh tokens can rotate and using one could log you out of the agent. So after a long break an account may show login expired , or its last known values marked ~ , until you next open that agent. For example, the Claude access token lasts for hours and the ChatGPT one for days.

It replaces your title. If your title bar normally shows the current directory, that's what you give up. Set AIQUOTA_TITLE=0 before the startup line to keep your title and only get the band when a terminal opens.

IDE terminals show the band, not the title. The band appears each time a terminal opens, in any terminal. JetBrains IDEs use their own fixed tab names, so the title summary doesn't appear there. In VS Code, set "terminal.integrated.tabs.title": "${sequence}" to see it in the tab. In either IDE, run aiquota for the full view.

Gemini is limited by Google. Since June 2026, Gemini CLI login has only been served for Standard and Enterprise seats, so personal accounts show no flat subscription found .

## Settings

Set these as environment variables before the startup line, or in ~/.config/aiquota/config :

## Privacy and security

AIQuota has no server and no telemetry. Each token goes only to the service that issued it.

- Credentials are read-only, and are never copied to the cache or passed on a command line.

- The cache in ~/.cache/aiquota holds only plan names, percentages and times, and only you can read it.

- Text from the network is stripped of control characters before it can reach your terminal.

- Redirects are not followed, so a token can't be forwarded to another host.

## Compatibility

Runs anywhere with a POSIX shell, awk and curl .

## Contributing

New accounts are welcome as long as they are flat subscriptions. See CONTRIBUTING.md .

## License

MIT

https://github.com/gethardcount/hardcoun.markdown:
Usage billing for AI products, on your own servers. Price tokens per model, sell prepaid credit, and see what each customer costs you. Hardcount makes the invoices, and Stripe charges the card. Your billing data stays in your own Postgres. An open-source alternative to Stripe Billing and Lago: no Stripe Billing fee, no paid edition, and light enough to run yourself. Why Hardcount → ## What it looks like One month of AI usage for one customer, from the demo in test mode: one invoice line per model and token type, $5.73 due. Your margin on it is 51.9% (Sonnet 67.1%, Haiku 20.0%), shown only to you. ▶ Watch the 65-second walkthrough , narrated, with captions. ## Quick start Try Hardcount on your own computer. It runs in test mode, where no real money moves. You need git and Docker 24 or newer with the Compose plugin. On Windows, run it inside WSL. 1. Start Hardcount git clone --branch v0.9.2 https://github.com/gethardcount/hardcount.git cd hardcount/deploy/compose ./quickstart.sh You see: "Hardcount is running.", then your dashboard address, email, password and a test API key. The password is shown only once; the script also saves all four in deploy/compose/quickstart-credentials.json . Open http://localhost:8080 and sign in. Hardcount opens in test mode, and it is empty. 2. Run the demo ./quickstart.sh demo The demo sets up AI token prices, creates a customer and sends token usage the way a LiteLLM proxy would. Then it moves the customer's test clock (a pretend clock for test customers) to the end of the month, and Hardcount makes the invoice, its PDF and the margin report shown above. You see: nine steps, each ending in a green ✓, then links to the invoice and the customer. Home still reads $0, because its totals leave out test-clock customers; use the links instead. Each demo step, and where to click 3. Stop or remove it ./quickstart.sh stop keeps your data. ./quickstart.sh destroy deletes it, and cannot be undone. If port 8080 is taken, start with HARDCOUNT_PORT=9000 ./quickstart.sh . Next: send your own usage and get a first invoice · run it for real on one VM · change Hardcount itself ## How it works flowchart LR A["Your app or LiteLLM"] -->|"usage events"| B["Hardcount
counts and prices"] B -->|"month ends"| C["Invoice + PDF"] C -->|"saved card"| D["Stripe charge"] D -.->|"card declined"| E["Retries and emails"] Your app tells Hardcount what each customer used. Once the customer and its prices exist, one usage event looks like this: curl -X POST http://localhost:8080/v1/usage-events \ -H " Authorization: Bearer $HARDCOUNT_KEY " \ -H " Content-Type: application/json " \ -d ' {"event_name": "tokens", "external_customer_id": "acme", "quantity": 1200, "dimensions": {"model": "claude-sonnet-4.5", "token_type": "input"}, "idempotency_key": "req-42:input"} ' external_customer_id is your own ID for the customer. The dimensions pick the price: here, Sonnet 4.5 input tokens. If you send the same idempotency_key again, Hardcount counts the event once. Already run a LiteLLM proxy? It sends these events for you. Your first invoice, step by step ## Why Hardcount The gaps Hardcount is built for: Stripe still charges its normal card fee, and Stripe Tax's fee if you use it. Every claim above has a source in Why Hardcount exists , and How it compares lists where the other projects are ahead. ## Is Hardcount right for you? Pre-1.0. Hardcount is young: one maintainer, Stripe and cards only, no SDKs yet, no production users yet. Until 1.0.0, a minor release can break the API, and a patch release can change something you rely on ( versioning before 1.0 ). A good fit if: - You charge by usage, most of all an AI product that prices per token, by model and token type. - You want billing on your own servers. Usage and invoice records stay in your own Postgres. Stripe sees each charge, and the invoice lines too if you use Stripe Tax. - You are a small or mid-size team. One engineer can run it, on one server or several. - Your volume is up to about a million usage events a day. A €6.49-a-month server took that rate for 20 minutes with no errors (measured on v0.8.0). Plan 15 to 18 GB of database disk a month at that volume. How we measured Not a fit if you need: - Simple per-seat pricing paid by card. Stripe Billing already does that well. - Automatic charging through a processor other than Stripe. Stripe is the only one built in today. Tell us which one you need . - A marketplace that splits payouts between sellers (Stripe Connect). Hardcount bills your own customers. - Revenue recognition or accounting reports. Export the data to your own warehouse. - Quotes or multi-phase contracts for sales-led deals. ## What's inside - Pricing: per-unit, graduated and package prices; rates per model and token type on one meter; a base fee plus usage on one invoice; prepaid credit that later usage draws down. AI pricing - Billing you can trust: Hardcount never bills the same period twice, because the database refuses a second invoice for it. Every usage line on an invoice links to the events behind it. How Hardcount keeps a bill right - Getting paid: cards through Stripe, with automatic retries and emails when a payment fails. # gethome hub The local brain of your home. Matter, Zigbee and MQTT devices in one app. An assistant you can talk to, and rules you write by describing them. It runs on a small computer at home, on your own Wi-Fi — with your own AI key and no cloud account. Get started · What it does · Hardware · Docs · gethome.me The app a hub is lived in: gethome for iPhone, free on the App Store. ## What is a hub? Most smart-home gear belongs to an account: pair a lamp with one phone and it answers to that phone, and to nobody else. A hub turns that around. It is one small box on your shelf that owns your devices , so everyone you invite — each with a role of their own — sees the same home, and your rules keep running while every phone is out of the house. One hub is one home. There is no account to create. Nothing about your home leaves your network unless you give the hub an AI key — and then only what the AI feature you use needs ( what goes where ). In one line: your devices talk to the hub, and your phone talks to the hub over your own Wi-Fi. flowchart TB APPS["gethome apps
iPhone · Mac"] <--> HUB["gethome hub
at home"] AI["Optional AI
on your own key"] <-.-> HUB HUB <--> DEV["Your devices
Matter · Zigbee · MQTT"] ## What it does - Every device, one app. Matter devices, Zigbee devices (through Zigbee2MQTT and a USB stick) and your own MQTT hardware all speak one typed schema — 27 capabilities across 16 kinds of device — so each gets controls that fit it. → Zigbee · Matter · the schema - Ask the house. An assistant answers questions about your home, works your devices and presses your scenes — typed, or spoken. It runs on your own Anthropic or OpenAI key; the spoken version needs an OpenAI key. → The assistant - Rules in plain words. Describe what you want and an agent writes the rule, shows it back to you as a flow and saves it switched off until you turn it on. Scenes are rules you can press. Rules keep running with no AI key at all. → Automations - Devices it has never seen. Pair a Zigbee device the hub doesn't know and an agent works out what it is, so it gets real controls instead of a blank tile. It needs your AI key; without one the device still appears, flagged needs review . → AI device recognition - A home for everyone in it. Invite family with a short-lived code. Owner, Member and Guest come built in, you can add roles of your own, and the same person can sign in on a second device as themselves. → Roles and sharing - What happened, and when. Temperature, humidity, air quality and power are kept in five-minute steps for a week, and an activity feed shows what was asked of the home, and by whom. → History - Build your own. Anything that can publish JSON over MQTT can be a device, with no hub-side code. Your own scripts, dashboards and AI agents use the hub's local REST and WebSocket API with an API key — narrowed to what you give it, and taken back with one tap. → Building on a hub · Agent skills · The MQTT convention · The API - Private by default. No cloud account, and your AI key stays on the hub. → Private by design Also: AI portraits of your devices, drawn on the hub with your OpenAI key and shared by everyone in the home ( portraits ) — and pictures of your rooms, drawn from a few photos as an isometric cutaway with every device marked where it stands ( room pictures ). ## The gethome family - gethome hub (this repository) — the brain: talks to your devices, runs your rules and agents, and serves your apps. Public, and installs today — see Get started . - gethome for iPhone — the everyday app: rooms and devices, the assistant, rules, history and widgets. Free on the App Store . - gethome studio for Mac — guided setup: prepares the SD card or finds a Pi on your network, installs and claims the hub, and keeps it updated — then shows the broker's live traffic, the device-schema library and the AI's run log. The way we recommend setting a hub up — download it from gethome.me . - gethome.me — the website: changelog, privacy policy and terms. ## Get started Three steps: get a small computer, install the hub on it, then open the app. ### 1. Get the hardware - A small computer running 64-bit Linux , such as a Raspberry Pi. → Choosing hardware 2 GB of memory or more runs Matter and Zigbee together and never has to choose. 1 GB or less runs one radio at a time by default. You can switch both on, and it works while your Zigbee network is small — as that network grows, the hub hands a radio back and says so. - 2 GB of memory or more runs Matter and Zigbee together and never has to choose. - 1 GB or less runs one radio at a time by default. You can switch both on, and it works while your Zigbee network is small — as that network grows, the hub hands a radio back and says so. - Raspberry Pi OS Lite (64-bit) for its card. Lite, not the desktop edition that Raspberry Pi Imager shows first: it is one level down, under Raspberry Pi OS (other) . - A USB Zigbee stick , if you want Zigbee. We develop against the SONOFF ZBDongle-E, which needs a one-minute firmware update when new. Without a stick you get Matter, Wi-Fi and MQTT devices. ### 2. Install the hub Pick one way. Both run the same installer. #### The easy way: gethome studio (recommended) On a Mac with macOS 14 or later, download gethome studio and follow it. It prepares the SD card or finds a Pi already on your network, installs the hub and tells you if anything goes wrong, then claims it for you — no terminal, and no pairing code to type. Afterwards it shows what the iPhone app doesn't: the broker's live traffic, the device-schema library and every AI run with what it cost. #### By hand, with one command No Mac, or prefer a terminal? - Write Raspberry Pi OS Lite to the card with Raspberry Pi Imager, and switch SSH on as you do. - Start the Pi and log in to it . - Run: curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/gethome-inc/gethome-hub/main/deploy/install.sh | bash Run: curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/gethome-inc/gethome-hub/main/deploy/install.sh | bash It downloads a prebuilt hub for your machine, installs Node.js 22 and Mosquitto, sets everything up to come back by itself after a power cut, picks up a Zigbee stick on its own and prints a pairing code — you'll use it in step 3. → The full install guide ### 3. Get the app Install gethome for iPhone , free on the App Store. It finds the hub on your Wi-Fi. - Installed by hand? Claim the hub in the app with its pairing code. Whoever claims it first becomes its owner, and the owner invites everyone else. - Set up by gethome studio? The hub is already yours — studio claimed it as your Mac. In studio's People tab, press Add device on your own row, then enter the code it shows in the app: your iPhone joins as you, not as somebody new. ### Getting a shell on the hub Everything on this page that runs on the hub needs a login first: ssh < user > @ < address > is the account you set in Raspberry Pi Imager ( pi unless you changed it).
is the Pi's IP or its .local — the same host the apps show for the hub, without the :8420 , which is the API and not SSH. If gethome studio set the hub up, it never asked you for that password — it authorizes its own key on the Pi instead — so the key is usually the shortest way in, and on a card install it may be the only one you still know: ssh -i " $HOME /Library/Application Support/gethome-studio/id_ed25519_gethome " pi@192.168.0.200 The quotes are load-bearing: the path contains a space. Use "$HOME/…" rather than '~/…' — a tilde inside quotes is not expanded, and ssh will report a key that isn't there. ## Everyday commands sudo gethome-hubctl status # every service, and what the API says sudo gethome-hubctl logs 100 sudo gethome-hubctl pairing-code # the code, until the hub is claimed sudo gethome-hubctl update # install the latest build (`rollback` goes back) The API answers at http://:8420/api/v1/hub . An update keeps the running build until the new one answers its health check, and flips back by itself if it doesn't — from the command line, or from an app (Owners and Members can). → Installing and running a hub ## Private by design - No cloud account, relay or tunnel. The hub opens nothing through your router, and your home lives in one file on its own card. Don't forward port 8420 (the API) or 1883 (MQTT) — both are plain connections meant for your home network, and your router is the boundary. - Your AI key stays on the hub , encrypted, and the API never returns it — not even to your phone. AI is optional, and what each feature sends is written down. - Every request but three needs a token or an API key (the hub's public description, the claim, and the hub proving it is itself to an app that already has one), and the hub refuses any request addressed to a public domain name, which stops a web page from reaching it through your browser. - The installer checks what it downloads against published checksums, and leaves your running hub alone if anything doesn't match. → Privacy and network security , including the short, honest list of what does leave the hub. ### Good to know - On your own Wi-Fi only, for now. Controlling the home from away is not built yet — a relay is planned. Your rules keep running while you're out. - Zigbee needs a USB stick. Without one: Matter, Wi-Fi and MQTT. - AI features need your own Anthropic or OpenAI key. Without one the hub works, and devices it can't place are flagged needs review . - One radio at a time on 1 GB or less , by default — what that costs . ## Build with an AI agent Two agent skills teach Claude Code, Codex, Cursor and the other coding agents that read Agent Skills to build on a hub, and the agent picks the right one by itself when a task fits: - gethome-hub-api for software that uses your home — a script, a dashboard, a bridge, an agent of your own — through the API and an API key. - gethome-mqtt-device for hardware that is a device — ESPHome, Arduino, MicroPython or Python on a board of your own — joining over MQTT. npx skills add gethome-inc/gethome-hub That needs Node.js and no copy of this repository: it asks which of your agents to install for, copies in just the two skill folders, and nothing else stays on your machine. For the API one, make an API key and give it to the agent through its environment, never in the conversation. → The skills · Building on a hub ## Documentation Use it - Choosing hardware — what to buy, and why memory decides - Installing and running a hub — install, update, roll back - Privacy and network security - Zigbee · Matter · MQTT for your own hardware - Automations · The assistant · AI device recognition · Device portraits Build on it - Building on a hub — API keys and your own software, and the agent skills for Claude Code, Codex and others - The API · The device schema · Architecture · The gethome family ## For developers cp .env.example .env npm install npm run dev # tsx watch npm test # vitest — no services needed Node.js ≥ 22. There is no cloud: everything runs from this repo. The hub is deployed on Linux only, but it develops and tests fine on macOS — the suite needs no radios and keeps its database in a temp file. HUB_TEST_MQTT=1 npm test adds the end-to-end broker round trip (it needs Mosquitto). Read CLAUDE.md , the engineering guide, before changing code, and Architecture for the module map. ## License - Source-available. The code is public under the PolyForm Noncommercial License 1.0.0 : read it, change it, share it. - Free for personal and noncommercial use — your home, hobby projects, evaluation, research. - Commercial deployments — hotels, property management, paid installations — need a separate license: see COMMERCIAL-LICENSE.md . This is a source-available license, not OSI open source: the open-source definition doesn't allow restricting commercial use. The Terms of Use and the Privacy Policy on gethome. [truncated]

# Zipzi 2D

English · 简体中文 · 日本語

An open-source 2D modeling and animation tool for creating alongside AI.

You shape the artwork. Your AI agent helps with the modeling work. Zipzi connects a visual desktop editor with a Python API, so you and your agent can inspect and edit the same model, share undo history, and build on each other’s changes.

Zipzi 2D is an open-source alternative to Live2D Cubism Editor, built with Rust and GPUI. Its name comes from Cantonese 摺紙 ( zip3 zi2 ), meaning “origami”.

Download Alpha · Python SDK · Report an issue · Contribute

> Early development: There is no stable release yet. APIs and file formats may change. The editor supports macOS and Windows.

- Open source and commercial friendly — Create, refine, and use your models commercially with an open-source editor and an MIT-licensed SDK.

- Native and high performance — Built with Rust and GPUI for low memory usage and responsive editing, even with complex models and dense meshes.

- Agent-ready — Create from scratch, collaborate with AI, or import an existing model for further refinement.

## Your editor. Your AI agent. One model.

Describe what you want to your AI coding agent. It uses the Python SDK to inspect models, view rendered images and make edits you can review and undo in the editor. You and your agent work on the same document, with shared undo history.

Bring your own Python-capable agent and point it to the SDK guide .

### First code: let AI give every mesh a meaningful name

You describe the task; your AI agent writes and runs the code. The examples below were generated by an AI coding agent and tested against a running Editor. They show how the agent works through the Python SDK—you do not need to write these scripts yourself. Your role is to explain what you want and review the results in the editor.

Ask your agent: “Look at every mesh and give it a meaningful name.”

Install the Python client (CPython 3.14), start a compatible Editor with GPU observation support, and open one model. An image-capable coding agent can run the following two steps.

1. The agent observes every mesh. Its generated script exports one image per mesh, with its wireframe highlighted over the textured model, plus a JSON naming worksheet. observe supplies visual evidence; the agent supplies the semantic interpretation.

View ( width = 768 , height = 768 , roi = ( x0 - margin , y0 - margin , x1 + margin , y1 + margin ), topology = observation . Overlay ( targets = ( observation . Have the agent open each exported PNG , identify the highlighted mesh in context, and edit only new_name in names.json . Keep IDs and old_name intact. The overlay selects diagnostic geometry, not isolated artwork: surrounding textures remain visible, and hidden or occluded artwork may still be ambiguous. Keep the original name for uncertain or image-less entries, or inspect additional poses before naming them.

2. The agent applies the semantic names together. After you review the proposed names, the agent writes and runs the following script with the path to names.json . You do not need to copy the code or run a terminal command. Keep the same model open and unchanged between inspection and application.

SessionId ( ** review [ "session_id" ])) # All renames commit together as one undo step. A missing mesh or changed # original name aborts the edit instead of leaving a partly renamed model. with session . edit ( "AI: semantic mesh names" ) as edit : for row in rows : current = edit . meshes . get ( row [ "id" ]). value if current . name != row [ "old_name" ]: raise RuntimeError ( "Mesh changed; inspect the model again." ) if row [ "new_name" ] != row [ "old_name" ]: edit . meshes . rename ( row [ "id" ], row [ "new_name" ], expected_name = row [ "old_name" ], ) print ( "Review the names in the editor. Undo to revert, or save to keep them." )

No project save happens automatically. The name check detects renamed or removed meshes, not every possible geometry or texture change; repeat the inspection if the model has changed. For more workflows, see the capability guide .

## Built for hands-on creation, too

Work with meshes, parameters, deformers and BlendShapes, then bring them together in the animation workspace. Generate mesh geometry or refine it by hand. Mesh Edit lets you work on the posed model or switch to the source image, while resampling stored shapes as the geometry changes.

Python scripts can also run independently with a local Runtime for automation outside the editor. Explore the Python SDK for modeling, animation authoring, previews and inspection.

## Try Zipzi 2D

- Use the editor: Download an Alpha build from GitHub Releases . Check the release notes for the available platform builds and requirements.

- Automate with Python: Follow the installation and connection guide . The SDK currently requires CPython 3.14.

- Build your own tools: Explore the Rust SDK for programmatic authoring.

### Current capabilities

See the SDK capability guide for details. GPU inspection requires a compatible host and usable GPU. Format support does not imply lossless round trips for every model.

## Contributing

Try an Alpha build and tell us what gets in your way . For bug reports, include the build version, platform and steps to reproduce; share model assets only when you have permission to do so.

For code contributions, start with the repository map , editor guide or Python SDK guide . The documentation index covers deeper references. Development commands and focused test selection are below.

## Development

Use Rust 1.95 or newer, uv 0.10.7 or newer, and CPython 3.14. The macOS Editor requires Xcode Command Line Tools and a Metal-capable GPU. The Windows Editor requires MSVC, the Windows SDK and a usable GPU. Run these commands from the repository root:

uv sync --locked python3 tools/workspace/cargo_domain.py --check # Focused SDK development cargo test --locked -p zipzi-sdk --test integration physics_editing:: # Native Editor (macOS) cargo run --locked -p zipzi-editor ./tools/test-editor.sh fast timeline:: # Repository tooling tests; no native application build uv run --locked python tools/test_tools.py

For the Python SDK, ./tools/test-sdk.sh python refreshes its native adapter and runs Local/Connected behavior and static types. python-connected installs the pure wheel and validates real subprocess host discovery and session binding; add --editor-host /absolute/path/to/zipzi-editor for the current desktop host. Root pyproject.toml and uv.lock manage development tools.

## Tests

Choose the smallest gate covering the change, then broaden when needed. Run commands from the repository root; inspect available modes with ./tools/test-sdk.sh --help , ./tools/test-editor.sh --help or uv run --locked python tools/test_tools.py --help .

Filters and filenames are placeholders; omit them to run the selected gate. For a crate's integration targets, inspect its README and tests/ , or list cases with cargo test --locked -p <crate> --test <target> -- --list . Editor shell gates clear ZIPZI_DEV_SESSION_DIR ; clear it explicitly when running Editor Cargo tests directly.

Full coverage, prerequisites and CI define regression, stress, native acceptance and packaged-wheel gates. Both domain scripts default to expensive full runs when no mode is supplied. Plain cargo test selects only zipzi-core , zipzi-project and zipzi-sdk . Tooling tests belong in tools/tests/ , crate tests stay with their crate, and shared data belongs in fixtures/ .

All owned crates share the root Cargo workspace and lockfile. Local models belong in models/local/ ; see the model inventory . Source archives, Python wheels and macOS app bundles have separate distribution checks .

## License and third-party rights

SDK components use MIT ; Editor components use GPL-3.0-only . LICENSING identifies scopes and shared-file origins; third-party notices retain dependency and benchmark exceptions.

Live2D, Cubism, the Live2D Cubism SDK, Cubism Core, Cubism Native Framework, and associated sample data are owned by or licensed through Live2D Inc. and/or their respective rightsholders. This project is independent and is not affiliated with, authorized by, endorsed by, or sponsored by Live2D Inc. The names “Live2D” and “Cubism” describe interoperability only.
