### Fast, high-density, scalable orchestration with Rivet Actors. Built on S3 at SSD speeds.

4.99 ms p99 cold starts, 72 KB RAM per Actor, scales to billions

Quickstart • Documentation • Blog • Discord • X

## What is Rivet?

Rivet Actors are long-lived processes with in-memory state, a SQLite database, WebSockets, and scheduling. You can create one for each agent, user, session, or tenant.

- 72 KB per Actor : Actors share a node process instead of each booting a sandbox, so one server holds hundreds of thousands.

- 4.99 ms p99 cold starts : No image pull and no VM boot.

- Built for scale : All data lives in S3, so a cluster scales to billions of Actors.

- Hibernates when idle, wakes on demand : Idle Actors cost nothing and wake on the next request with nothing lost.

- SQLite backed by S3, at SSD speeds : 1.07 ms durable writes and 1.36 ms reads at p99, for about 10.4× less than replicated SSD storage.

### Use cases

- Durable & multiplayer AI agents : memory that survives restarts, shared live with every client

- Workflows : multi-step operations that replay instead of starting over

- AI-generated apps : run the apps and Actors your agent generates

- Collaborative editing : one Actor per document, synced to every editor

### Example

A minimal agent written from scratch. For a ready-made agent, use Pi Durable .

// server.ts import { actor , setup } from "rivetkit" ; import { db } from "rivetkit/db" ; import { streamText } from "ai" ; import { openai } from "@ai-sdk/openai" ; // One Actor per agent, created on first use: agent.getOrCreate(["agent-123"]) export const agent = actor ( { // 1. SQLite: every agent has its own database, so history survives restarts db : db ( { onMigrate : async ( db ) => { await db . execute ( "CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS messages (role TEXT, content TEXT)" ) ; } , } ) , // 2. In-memory state: plain variables that live with the Actor, with no database round trip createVars : ( ) => ( { online : new Map < string , string > ( ) } ) , // 3. WebSockets: each client holds a live connection, and the Actor pushes to all of them onDisconnect : ( c , conn ) => { c . vars . online . delete ( conn . id ) ; c . broadcast ( "online" , [ ... c . vars . online . values ( ) ] ) ; } , actions : { join : ( c , user : string ) => { c . vars . online . set ( c . conn . id , user ) ; c . broadcast ( "online" , [ ... c . vars . online . values ( ) ] ) ; } , sendMessage : async ( c , text : string ) => { // Save the message await c . db . execute ( "INSERT INTO messages VALUES (?, ?)" , "user" , text ) ; const messages = await c . db . execute ( "SELECT role, content FROM messages" ) ; // Stream tokens to every connected client const response = streamText ( { model : openai ( "gpt-5" ) , messages } ) ; for await ( const delta of response . textStream ) { c . broadcast ( "token" , delta ) ; } // Save the response await c . db . execute ( "INSERT INTO messages VALUES (?, ?)" , "assistant" , await response . text ) ; } , } , } ) ; export const registry = setup ( { use : { agent } } ) ;

// client.ts (frontend or backend) import { createClient } from "rivetkit/client" ; import type { registry } from "./server" ; const client = createClient < typeof registry > ( ) ; // Open a WebSocket connection to the agent const agent = client . agent . getOrCreate ( [ "agent-123" ] ) . connect ( ) ; // Listen for realtime events agent . on ( "online" , users => console . log ( "online:" , users ) ) ; agent . on ( "token" , delta => process . stdout . write ( delta ) ) ; // Call actions on the Actor await agent . join ( "nathan" ) ; await agent . sendMessage ( "how many r's in strawberry?" ) ;

### Why run agents on Rivet Actors?

Each Actor gives the agent a long-lived process for long agent turns, in-memory state for context, a WebSocket server for multiplayer, durable SQLite storage for session transcripts and agent artifacts, and hibernation when idle.

Most of an agent's time is spent waiting on inference . When the agent loop runs inside a sandbox, you pay for a whole VM that sits mostly idle with low CPU usage.

Rivet Actors run the agent loop outside of the sandbox instead, often called "separating the head from the hands." The agent's state, memory, and context live in the Actor, and it reaches the sandbox through tools only when it needs to run code. This uses a fraction of the memory and limits the blast radius and trust boundary of the code it runs. Read more about running the harness outside of the sandbox .

### Do I need a sandbox with a Rivet Actor?

Often not. An agent needs a sandbox only to run code it writes. Developers on Rivet use three patterns:

- Agents with tools : Many agents only need tool calls, MCP, and APIs, such as customer support or personal agents. No sandbox needed.

- Agents with a lightweight sandbox : agentOS provides Linux-compatible sandboxing for JS and Python using V8 and WebAssembly, with full POSIX filesystems, networking stacks, and process trees. It covers most workloads, like data analysis, file processing, evals, and code mode.

- Agents with a full sandbox : Keep your existing sandbox provider and expose its shell and filesystem to the agent as tools, such as a bash tool that runs commands in the sandbox. The Actor reattaches to it across sleeps and restarts. See the sandbox coding agent example .

## Getting Started

### Use with your coding agent

Paste this prompt into Claude Code, Cursor, Codex, or any coding agent:

Run npx skills add rivet-dev/skills, then ask me what to build and run it locally.

### Start from scratch

Rivet ships libraries built on top of Actors for common use cases.

- Actors : Long-lived processes with state, realtime, and scheduling built in.

- Agents : Durable agents built on Actors, with memory that survives restarts.

- Workflows : Multi-step operations built on Actors that replay instead of starting over.

- agentOS : Run the code your agent writes, securely, with granular control over network access, filesystem access, and resource limits.

- Dynamic Apps (preview): A backend per user, deployed the moment it is generated.

## How Actors compare to sandboxes

- Rivet numbers come from the published Rivet Actors vs Cloudflare Durable Objects benchmark , run on Rivet 3.0.3. Its repository has the raw samples and the scripts to reproduce them.

- Sandbox numbers are for E2B : 512 MiB is its default memory allocation from E2B's billing documentation as of November 4, 2026, and 1.70 s is the p99 cold start from ComputeSDK's October 30, 2026 sandbox benchmark .

- Storage cost compares S3 Standard with three Amazon EBS gp3 copies at AWS list prices.

- Sources, dates, and the full method are at rivet.dev/docs/benchmarking .

## Features

- Fault tolerance : If a node goes down, its Actors move elsewhere with their state intact.

- HTTP & WebSocket networking : Call an Actor over HTTP or hold a live WebSocket to it.

- End-to-end type safety : Typed clients for your backend and React hooks for your frontend.

- Cron & scheduling : Wake an Actor on a schedule or at a time it sets for itself.

- Actor-to-Actor calls : Actors call each other by key across the cluster.

- Scoped JWTs : Give each client a JWT scoped to the Actors it may reach.

- OpenTelemetry : Traces, metrics, and logs in OTel format.

## Deployment Options

Every option runs the same control plane, from local dev to production. Talk to an engineer →

## Works with the tools you already use

Typed SDKs for your backend and React hooks for your frontend. Rivet runs on native Node.js and Bun with no custom runtime, so your existing packages, tooling, and tests work unchanged.

Deploy nodes on : Docker Compose • Kubernetes • VM & bare metal • Hetzner • AWS ECS • Railway • Render

Frameworks : React • Effect

Runtimes : Node.js • Bun • Rust

Tools : Vitest • OpenTelemetry • Pino • AI SDK • OpenAPI • AsyncAPI

Request an integration →

## FAQ

Yes. Rivet deploys into your own cloud account, including air-gapped environments: the control plane and storage run inside your VPC while Rivet operates them. See the BYOC docs .

Yes. Rivet Cloud runs fully managed, dedicated clusters on AWS or GCP in any region. It can run your app's Docker image as nodes on Rivet Cloud , or you can bring your own nodes .

Yes. Rivet is fully self-hostable; see the self-hosting docs . The control plane runs anywhere a container runs, with guides for Docker Compose, Kubernetes, VMs and bare metal, Hetzner, Railway, Render, and AWS ECS. For enterprise support with a self-hosted deployment, contact us .

No. An object storage bucket is the only dependency: there is no database to run and no message bus, and control plane instances find each other through the bucket. Rivet works with Amazon S3, Google Cloud Storage, Azure Blob Storage, and any S3-compatible store such as MinIO, Cloudflare R2, or Hetzner Object Storage. A local filesystem backend is available for trying Rivet on one machine.

Yes. Rivet is open source under the permissive Apache 2.0 license. You're looking at it.

No. Rivet is a general actor platform at its core, with nothing specific to agents. For agents, you can use the optional agent library , which runs Pi Durable on Rivet Actors, or write your own agent from scratch.

A sandbox boots a VM or container per agent, which is slow to start and sits mostly idle. A Rivet Actor runs inside a shared node process: 72 KB and 4.99 ms p99 to start, versus 512 MiB and 1.70 s for a sandbox, and it hibernates when idle. To run untrusted code your agent writes, use agentOS .

Rivet is often used as an open-source alternative to Cloudflare Durable Objects that is easy to self-host and scales. It also fixes many of the constraints of Durable Objects: no 128 MB memory cap, bottomless storage instead of a 10 GB SQLite limit, Actors are not randomly evicted, and you control the runtime because Actors run on vanilla Node.js or Bun instead of a custom runtime. Rivet also adds built-in connection handling, event broadcasting, durable scheduling and cron, full Vitest support, lifecycle hooks for draining, and control over Actor upgrades. See the Cloudflare Durable Objects comparison .

No. Rivet runs on native Node.js and Bun, so your existing packages, tooling, and tests work unchanged.

Rivet implements the virtual actor pattern, which is closest to Orleans, but focuses on what modern workloads need: SQLite persistence instead of simple JSON stores and support for modern runtimes. Erlang and Akka do not provide virtual actors out of the box, though ecosystem packages exist that offer functionality comparable to Rivet Actors.

No. Rivet only needs a standard process that connects to the control plane over WebSocket. That process can be Node.js, Bun, Rust, or anything else.

# Pair Flow

### AI that cannot code faster than you can understand.

Plan together. Review one small change. Apply only when you are ready.

AI coding agents are fast. Sometimes too fast: they generate hundreds of lines, touch several files, and leave the developer reviewing code they never really owned.

Pair Flow changes the unit of collaboration. It pauses before the plan and before every code change, so you stay inside the reasoning loop instead of cleaning up afterward.

Your goal │ ▼ Understand and propose a plan │ you approve ▼ Explain one small code chunk │ you inspect the diff ▼ Apply / Ask or revise / Reject │ └──────── repeat, one understood change at a time

## The contract

- No hidden workspace edits. Proposed changes are stored only in workspace-local extension storage for restart recovery, and no source file changes until you approve them.

- No giant hand-off. Each chunk is one coherent change across at most three files.

- No escaping the workspace. Absolute paths and path traversal are rejected.

- No stale overwrites. Source hashes stop a preview from replacing a file that changed afterward.

- No mystery key storage. API keys live in VS Code SecretStorage.

- No mandatory backend. Connect any OpenAI-compatible API endpoint.

## Try it

Install Pair Flow from the VS Code Marketplace when the Preview listing is available, or download the latest VSIX from GitHub Releases , then:

- Open VS Code → Extensions → … → Install from VSIX .

- Open a disposable project folder for your first test.

- Run Pair Flow: Set API Key from the Command Palette. After the key, it asks for an optional base URL (press Enter on the empty box to use the provider's default address) and then lets you pick a model.

- To switch provider or model later, run Pair Flow: Choose Model . It lists suggested models, the models your key can use, and an Other model… option for any model id.

- Run Pair Flow: Start Session .

- Ask for one real change and inspect every decision boundary.

Or install from the command line:

code -- install-extension .\pair - flow - 0.4 . 0. vsix

## A good first prompt

> Add input validation to the signup handler. Explain the approach first, then keep every proposed change small enough for me to understand without scrolling.

Pair Flow returns an ordered plan. After plan approval it prepares only the first chunk, explains why it exists, and opens the current and proposed code side by side.

## Build from source

Requirements: Node.js 20+ and VS Code 1.95+.

git clone https: // github.com / roee030 / pair - programming - with - ai.git cd pair - programming - with - ai npm install npm test npm run typecheck npm run package

The packaged extension is written to pair-flow-0.4.0.vsix . Press F5 in VS Code to run the extension in an Extension Development Host while developing.

## AI providers

Choose pairFlow.provider in VS Code Settings. Pair Flow supports each provider through its native API:

Set pairFlow.model when you want a different model or when your Ollama installation does not contain the default local model. Use pairFlow.baseUrl for proxies, self-hosted gateways, or a remote Ollama instance.

## What is tested

The automated suite currently protects the highest-risk boundaries:

- plan approval is required before chunk generation;

- chunk approval is required before file mutation;

- reject and revise never write the pending proposal;

- malformed model responses fail safely;

- unsafe paths and binary-like content are rejected;

- unknown webview messages are ignored.

Run the complete gate with:

npm run package

## Privacy

Pair Flow has no hosted service and no product analytics. While a session is active or paused, its transcript, plan, and unapproved proposals are stored in workspace-local extension storage so VS Code can safely resume after a restart. Completed and canceled sessions retain only their lightweight summary. To create plans and chunks, selected text files from the open workspace are sent directly to the model endpoint you configure. API keys use VS Code SecretStorage and are never written to session JSON. Do not use a provider that is not approved for your codebase. Shell commands are never executed automatically in this release.

## Settings

## Getting an API key

Run Pair Flow: Set API Key after choosing pairFlow.provider . The key must come from the API console of that provider. A ChatGPT Plus or Claude Pro subscription does not include an API key.

Leave pairFlow.baseUrl empty unless you use a proxy or gateway. It is the API address, not a website or dashboard link.

## Troubleshooting

- No workspace: open a folder before starting Pair Flow.

- "returned a non-JSON response … HTML page": the error shows the URL Pair Flow called. If you set pairFlow.baseUrl , clear it. If it is already empty, a proxy, VPN, or network filter is intercepting the request; check VS Code's http.proxy setting.

- "model … is not recognized" / "does not exist": the model id is wrong for that provider (for example gtp 5 mini instead of gpt-5-mini ). Click Choose model on the error card, or run Pair Flow: Choose Model , then Try again . The session is kept.

- Coming back later: leaving a session, starting a new story, or closing VS Code keeps the session saved. Open the Pair Flow panel and click Resume under Pick up where you left off or Recent sessions .

- Authentication error: run Pair Flow: Set API Key again and confirm the selected provider.

- Ollama connection error: start Ollama locally and verify the configured model exists.

- A request takes too long: use Stop and keep session , then Resume or change the timeout setting.

- A proposed file changed after preview: Pair Flow intentionally refuses the stale apply; request a fresh chapter.

## JetBrains IDEs

A JetBrains version (IntelliJ IDEA, WebStorm, PyCharm and the rest, 2025.1+) is on JetBrains Marketplace (in review) and its source lives in jetbrains/ . It reuses the same panel UI and ports the core logic to Kotlin.

## Status

This is an early public preview. Pair Flow now lives in a persistent Activity Bar side panel with larger, accessible typography, a conversation timeline, resumable workspace-local sessions, and safe pause/resume controls. Every proposed file opens as a native VS Code diff with previous/next navigation. The current release supports one workspace root and whole-file text proposals. The next milestones are VS Code Extension Host integration tests, selective context controls, checkpoints, and Marketplace publishing.

Found a rough edge? Open an issue with the smallest reproduction you can share.

## Contributing

Small, reviewable pull requests fit the project philosophy best. Read CONTRIBUTING.md , start with an issue, keep behavior changes covered by tests, and run npm run package before opening a PR. Security issues should follow SECURITY.md , not a public issue.

# samir-vllm

> Teaching LLM inference from first principles by building a small engine in C++ and CUDA.

The series follows what happens between a prompt and a generated token, from loading model weights to running each part of the transformer on the GPU.

## My inference notes

Read Inference from Scratch (PDF) for 80+ pages of my handwritten notes and diagrams. I developed all of the writing in this PDF myself, with NO AI writing .

## Build series | 6+ Hours of footage

Companion notes for every video are in the study-notes index , with separate Markdown and PDF folders. You can also read the complete PDF collection .

## What works so far

- A C++17 / CUDA project, built with CMake and linked with ICU for Unicode-aware tokenization.

- Direct model.safetensors loading: parse metadata, validate tensor offsets, and copy the raw BF16 weights to GPU memory. There is also a memory-mapped loader implementation to avoid an extra CPU-side copy.

- A fixed Llama 3.2 1B Instruct weight layout, with direct pointers to the embedding, normalization, attention, and MLP tensors across all 16 layers.

- A local BPE tokenizer that supports Unicode, special tokens, encode/decode, and the Instruct chat prompt format; its expected output is covered by a dedicated test executable.

- A CUDA embedding-gather kernel and prefill path that copies prompt token IDs to the GPU and allocates activations.

- A CUDA RMSNorm kernel for the 2,048-wide hidden state: it reduces in FP32 and applies the learned BF16 weights throughout the forward pass.

- Dense causal prefill now runs all 16 layers: Q/K/V projection, RoPE, grouped-query attention, output projection, the attention residual, post-attention RMSNorm, SwiGLU MLP, and the MLP residual.

- The final RMSNorm and tied embedding/LM-head projection produce FP32 logits; GPU argmax selects each next token.

- A shared BF16 KV page pool with a block table per sequence and layer. Each physical page holds 16 tokens of K and V; prefill fills prompt pages and decode appends one new token at its absolute RoPE position.

- Greedy response generation with Instruct chat formatting, end-of-turn/end-of-text stopping, and configurable output length within the 2,048-token context.

- Persistent scratch buffers and one cuBLAS handle shared by prefill and decode. Q storage is reused for output/MLP projections, and normalization storage is reused for attention output.

- Batched decode with runtime-sized buffers, packed projections, and separate KV page mappings and attention lengths per sequence. Request count does not enlarge the KV pool.

- Static batching and a continuous scheduler that admit queued prompts according to available page budgets, then return their pages and budgets on completion.

- Direct paged decode attention with FP32 online softmax. Each query head streams its sequence's cached pages and accumulates weighted values without gathering a contiguous prefix or storing attention scores.

Part 8 explains Prefill, Decode, and the KV Cache . Part 9 follows with Static and Continuous Batching , including the current paged cache and online-softmax decode attention.

## Current scope

The Llama 3.2 1B inference path includes dense causal prefill, paged decode attention, and static or continuous batching. Model dimensions and the 2,048-token context remain fixed for this learning engine. The KV pool defaults to 128 MiB and can be set with --kv-cache-mib N ; active request capacity follows the workload's page budgets rather than a fixed two-request limit.

Admission guarantees room for each request's maximum processed prefix: prompt_tokens + allowed_new_tokens - 1 , rounded up to 16-token pages in each of the 16 layers. The allowed output budget is clamped to the context limit, and the final predicted token is returned without being processed again. These admission credits are separate from physical pages, which are assigned lazily. Early completion releases both the assigned pages and the remaining credits.

Requests wait in FIFO order when their budgets cannot fit alongside active requests. Active requests have room to finish, so future page-boundary growth cannot exhaust the pool or deadlock generation. A request whose budget exceeds the entire pool is rejected with a clear error. This conservative policy avoids preemption and recomputation; a large requested output budget can limit concurrency even if the model eventually stops early.

--stats reports the pool size, peak active requests, largest decode batch, peak assigned pages, admission waits, and final free-page count. Prefill still processes one prompt at a time between decode iterations.

BF16 computations can round differently at different batch sizes. When vocabulary logits are nearly tied, greedy output tokens can therefore differ between individual and batched runs. Bitwise output equality across batch sizes is not guaranteed.

## Build

### Requirements

- A CUDA-capable NVIDIA GPU and CUDA Toolkit

- CMake 3.24+

- A C++17 compiler

- ICU development libraries

- The nlohmann/json header

- Model weights at models/llama-3.2-1b-instruct/model.safetensors

- The matching tokenizer at models/llama-3.2-1b-instruct/tokenizer.model (copy it from models/Llama-3.2-1B-Instruct/original/tokenizer.model )

mkdir -p models/llama-3.2-1b-instruct cp models/Llama-3.2-1B-Instruct/original/tokenizer.model models/llama-3.2-1b-instruct/ cmake -S . -B build cmake --build build -j ./build/samir-vllm " Explain the KV cache in two sentences. " 128 # Continuous batching (default): admit requests whose page budgets fit. ./build/samir-vllm " Say hello. " 64 " Explain the KV cache. " " What is RoPE? " # Static batching: wait for the current group before admitting more. ./build/samir-vllm --static " Say hello. " 64 " Explain the KV cache. " " What is RoPE? " # More than two requests share the same default 128 MiB pool. ./build/samir-vllm --stats " Explain paging. " 64 " Explain GQA. " " Explain RoPE. " " Explain softmax. " # A smaller pool queues requests when their declared budgets cannot fit together. ./build/samir-vllm --kv-cache-mib 8 --stats " Explain paging. " 64 " Explain GQA. " " Explain RoPE. " ./build/tokenizer-test models/llama-3.2-1b-instruct/tokenizer.model

After optional --static , --continuous , --kv-cache-mib N , and --stats flags, the first argument is a prompt and the second is max_new_tokens (default: 128). Any remaining arguments are additional prompts; the token budget applies to each request. Every prompt is formatted as an Instruct user message. Generation stops independently at EOS, EOT, or EOM, or the output/context limit, and each completed response is printed with its token IDs and request number.

Prompts are prefilled one at a time, pausing decode. Each decode step packs one token from every active sequence into the shared buffers. Attention reads only that sequence's cache; requests can have different prompt and output lengths. Continuous batching admits waiting requests when page credits become available, while static batching admits the next group after the current group finishes.

# Current

Change control for AI agents

Agents propose changes. Current validates them, waits for your approval, applies them, and records every step in a tamper-evident log.

The Elevator Pitch · See it in action · Quickstart · How it works · Provenance · Reproducibility · Verifiability · Architecture · Intents · CLI · HTTP API · MCP · Configuration · Security · Status · Roadmap

## The Elevator Pitch

Why not just use Claude Code or Codex? You can. But there, the agent acts and you approve step by step as it goes. In Current, the agent can’t act at all. It hands over a complete proposal, and nothing happens until that proposal is approved and applied.

- Safety : The agent is limited to doing just one thing -- producing proposals . It sees only the files it asks for that Current's read policy permits, and can only propose changes from nine typed intents. Nothing touches your project until you approve it, and only allowlisted commands can run.

- Verification : You don’t take the agent’s word for it. You review the exact proposal, or have other agents review it, before anything happens, and Current checks the agent’s claims against what actually ran.

- Provenance : As agents write more of the code, someone will ask why was this changed, and who approved it? Current answers from a commit log: the oldest, best-tested idea in systems.

That log is hash-chained, so changes to past history are detectable, and the full state can be rebuilt from it on another machine.

> Status: early. Single node, local projects. Current is not a sandbox or an authentication system: approved commands run with the runtime's privileges. See Security and the threat model .

## See it in action

Ask Current to add CSRF protection to the included Next.js example:

current run " add CSRF protection to this app " \ --dir examples/nextjs-auth \ --model openai:gpt-5.6-sol

The model never gets the repository. It sees the layout and asks for what it needs, and Current fetches each file:

… round 1: the model asked to see 8 things ✓ read_file app/api/login/route.ts 769 B ✓ read_file lib/auth.ts 626 B ✓ read_file lib/rate-limit.ts 2.4 KB ✓ read_file tests/login.test.ts 847 B ✓ read_file tests/rate-limit.test.ts 2.3 KB ✓ read_file package.json 343 B ✓ read_file tsconfig.json 221 B ✓ read_file .gitignore 83 B

Reads are confined to the project. Dependencies, build output, .git and .env* files are never shown to the model, and every read is recorded.

Then it returns a proposal:

Agent produced proposal proposal sha256:672c4973787b… The login route already invokes a missing CSRF validator before parsing credentials. Implement that validator with fail-closed same-origin Origin checking and add focused coverage for accepted and rejected origins. PROPOSED 1 WriteFile lib/csrf.ts 2 WriteFile tests/csrf.test.ts 3 RunCommand npm test 4 Report Add fail-closed same-origin CSRF validation for the login route and unit tests covering valid, absent, malformed, and cross-origin headers. ✓ Proposal decoded ✓ Proposal validated Waiting for approval. Nothing has been applied.

The agent has proposed a change. Your project is untouched.

Review the exact files and commands, or pass the machine-readable version ( --json ) to another agent for a second opinion:

current review sha256:672c4973787b

Then decide. Send it back with feedback, and the model reads more and returns a new proposal:

current revise sha256:672c4973787b -m " add a test for a missing Origin header "

Or approve it. Approval is recorded, but nothing runs yet:

current approve sha256:672c4973787b -m " LGTM "

✓ Approved sha256:672c4973787b message LGTM Nothing has been applied. Apply it with: current apply sha256:672c4973787b

Applying is its own step. Current, not the agent, writes the files and runs the command:

current apply sha256:672c4973787b

✓ Proposal approved ✓ Workflow completed MODE: APPLY 4 effects executed. Inspect current events sha256:1429719b7546 current proposal sha256:672c4973787b current artifact sha256:fb30687f1722 (raw model output)

Every step above, from the request and each file the model read to its raw reply, the approval and each effect's output, is now part of the workflow's record. current events prints it.

## Quickstart

### Requirements

- Elixir 1.19 on Erlang/OTP ( mise.toml pins OTP 28.5 and Elixir 1.19.5; run mise install if you use mise )

- git , make , and bash

- An OpenAI or Anthropic API key

### 1. Get the code and build

git clone https://github.com/santosh79/current.git cd current mix deps.get mix compile make client

### 2. Start the runtime

In one terminal, export a key and start the server. It listens on 127.0.0.1:4000 and prints every request and commit as it happens.

export ANTHROPIC_API_KEY= " ... " # or OPENAI_API_KEY export CURRENT_ALLOWED_COMMANDS=npm # commands are denied unless allowlisted bin/current-server

### 3. Make a request

In another terminal, from the repository root:

export PATH= " $PWD : $PATH " # puts the local `current` CLI on PATH current models # the models your keys give you MODEL= " openai:gpt-5.6 " # replace with a model listed above current run " add CSRF protection to this app " \ --dir examples/nextjs-auth \ --model $MODEL

run stops when the proposal is waiting for review. Output varies between models and runs. Use plan instead of run for a proposal that can be reviewed but never applied.

### 4. Review, decide, apply

current review < proposal-id > current revise < proposal-id > -m " keep the route check, add edge cases " current approve < proposal-id > -m " reviewed " current apply < proposal-id >

Or current reject <proposal-id> -m "..." to end the workflow. A revision produces a new proposal ID, which must be reviewed and approved in turn; the earlier one is stale. IDs can be shortened to a unique prefix of at least four hex characters.

### 5. Trace it

current events < workflow-id > # the full chain, in log order current proposal < proposal-id > # intents, claims, and what the model read current artifact < artifact-id > # exact bytes: a file, command output, a raw reply

## How it works

In a typical agent, a tool call is the action: the file is written the moment the model decides to write it. In Current, the model's output is a proposal , a list of typed intents:

> "in lib/signup.ex , replace this text with that"; "run mix test "; "claim the tests pass, because that command exits 0"

A proposal does nothing on its own. Between it and your project, the runtime:

- decodes the model's reply, which is untrusted bytes, into a closed set of intent types. Anything outside it is rejected, not interpreted;

- validates it: paths confined to the project, files exist, every edit matches exactly, claims cite earlier intents they can be checked against;

- waits for a decision. A proposal is reviewed as a unit and approved, rejected, or sent back with feedback. The reviewer can be a person or another agent: each decision is an API call, recorded as its own event with the reviewer's metadata. A decision must name the workflow's latest proposal, and revisions are bounded (10 by default);

- applies it, in a separate step, with a small trusted interpreter that re-checks every path immediately before touching it and records every result;

- checks the outcome itself. Claims are evaluated against recorded results, and a claim that doesn't hold fails the workflow.

Every step is an event. Rounded boxes are where a workflow ends.

### Producing a proposal

- A task is submitted with a prompt, a project directory and a model. The directory is resolved once to its real path and recorded.

- The model is given the project's layout : paths and sizes, no contents. Dependencies, build output, VCS directories and .env* files are left out.

- The model may reply with an observe request: up to 20 read_file , glob or grep intents, each with a reason. The runtime runs them read-only, under path confinement and the read policy, and asks again with the results. Up to 8 rounds, 400 KB of results in total, 200 KB per file.

- The model replies with a proposal . Its exact reply is stored as an artifact, whatever it contains.

- The proposal is decoded into typed intents ( wire contract ), every path is made absolute against the project, and it is validated .

Validation answers "is this well-formed and in bounds right now?", not "will it apply cleanly?". The project can change before apply, and those failures are caught and recorded then. Producing a proposal is bounded by llm_proposal_timeout_ms per call and the task's --timeout-minutes (default 10) overall.

### Applying it

apply starts the interpreter. It re-checks every path against the filesystem as it is now (following symlinks), then carries out the intents in order. The first failure, or the first claim that doesn't hold, stops it and fails the workflow. Effects are not rolled back. The re-check narrows the window for a path to escape the project but doesn't close it (T2 in the threat model ).

### Lifecycle

created → planning → validating → waiting_for_approval plan mode: → planned apply mode: → approved → applying → assembling_result → completed → rejected → revision_requested → planning → validating → waiting_for_approval (bounded; each pass adds a proposal to the workflow) any stage: → failed (production, validation or an effect failed) → abandoned (no further automatic progress is possible) planning: the model sees the layout, may ask to read files, then returns a proposal

### Three primitives

> Intents propose change. Artifacts hold bytes. Events record fact. State is derived from the event log.

## Provenance: from a change back to the request

Because the runtime is the only thing that acts, and records each step before taking the next, every change sits at the end of an explicit chain:

TaskCreated the request: prompt, model, project, submitted_at └─ WorkflowCreated └─ ProposalProduced intents, what the model read first, its raw reply └─ ProposalValidated ├─ ProposalRevisionRequested who asked for what change; loops back to │ └─ ProposalProductionStarted → ProposalProduced (revision 1, revises │ the one above) → ProposalValidated → ... up to the bound └─ ProposalApproved who, when, with what message └─ EffectApplicationStarted ├─ EffectApplied an edit: file before and after ├─ EffectApplied a command: exit code, stdout, stderr ├─ EffectApplied a claim: verified, and against what └─ WorkflowCompleted

So for any change you can answer, from the record alone and without the model:

Authorization is recorded, not enforced by identity. Current guarantees that nothing is applied without an approval event in the chain, followed by a separate apply, and the reducer enforces that at commit time. Who may approve is for a layer in front of it: approvals enter through one route ( POST /v1/proposals/:id/approve ), where a gateway can authenticate the caller and write verified identity into the approval's metadata. Today reviewed_by is whatever the client sends.

## Reproducibility: replay the record anywhere

The commit log and the artifact store are the whole of Current's state. Nothing else is persisted, and everything the runtime shows you (tasks, proposals, workflows) is rebuilt from them. So the record is portable: copy the data directory to another machine, and replaying it gives the same history.

There are two levels of replay, and it matters which one you mean.

Replaying the record (works today). Every workflow state is a pure function of its events (see the reducer ). Every piece of content those events refer to is an immutable artifact named by its SHA-256. Replaying the same log, anywhere, gives the same states, the same accepted transitions and the same rejections, and every artifact can be checked against its own name. Point CURRENT_DATA_DIR at a copy and the runtime rebuilds it on start. (Starting the runtime also resumes or fails workflows that were still in progress, which appends new events. # 🗣️ FAAAH (Filesystem As An AI Handler)

The simplest OpenAI-compatible LLM proxy you will ever need.™️

FAAAH allows you to reuse your AI Agent subscription as a generic OpenAI-compatible local server.

FAAAH is dependency-free, implemented as a plain-text file protocol (UNIX-philosophy certified) :

- Instead of sending your prompts to cloud LLM APIs, send them to FAAAH, which reads OpenAI-compatible requests and dumps them into a folder as .txt files.

- Then, tell your existing AI coding agent (Claude Code, opencode, etc) to read the files and write responses to other .txt files.

- FAAAH then packages the responses into OpenAI-compatible JSON, and returns them to your app.

## Why?

Because you already pay for an AI coding assistant. Stop paying for API keys just for your weekend side projects! faaah!

It's also an agnostic proxy between any OpenAPI-expecting tool, and any LLM.

As an example, check GraphRAG fully driven through FAAAH .

## Video Demo

## Is This Allowed?

It is my understanding that local, non-commercial use of this tool doesn't break the existing ToS of any AI agent provider.

But if any lawyer disagrees, kindly send me a message. I would then introduce you to a friend of mine: Miss Barbra Streisand.

Be cautious about using FAAAH to process massive datasets. Some providers (you know which ones ) might do some Kafkaesque interpretations of their ambiguous ToS, and deploy Orwellian telemetry to detect infractions (hasn't happened to me yet, YOLO!)

## Features

- Zero Dependencies: Uses Python's http.server . That's it.

- 308 lines of code: Have you seen the bloat of other tools in this space? Yuck.

- Unix Philosophy: Everything is a file. Do one thing well. Keep it KISS, ya YAGNI.

- Universal Compatibility: If a tool supports the de-facto OpenAI API format (GraphRAG, LangChain, LlamaIndex, LiteLLM, the openai SDK), it supports FAAAH.

- Agent Agnostic: Due to the agent entrypoint being a prompt , it's not tied to any specific agent provider/version. Future-proof.

- Human-in-the-loop Fallback: If the AI agent gets stuck or hits usage limits, you can literally open the current response file (say response-0004.txt ), type the answer yourself (or copy-paste the request to your favorite web chatbot), and hit save. FAAAH will succeed.

## Usage

### 0. Install

Install with uv , from inside this repo:

uv tool install . # installs the `faaah` command on PATH uv tool install .[embeddings] # with the local embeddings extra (see later)

Or straight from the git repository:

uv tool install git+https://github.com/sebastiancarlos/faaah

### 1. Start the server

faaah # listens on 127.0.0.1:8000, queue ~/.cache/faaah/queue faaah --port 8080 # override port faaah --queue /tmp/q # override queue directory faaah --log-dir /tmp/logs # override session log root (see below) faaah -c # also copy the agent prompt to the clipboard

Each run creates a session-log dir ( ~/.cache/faaah/sessions/<TIMESTAMP>-<RANDOM> by default) that mirrors every queue file written or answered during that run, so you can debug a session even after the queue is wiped on restart:

- prompt-<id>.txt , response-<id>.txt — same files as the queue

- request-<id>.json , response-<id>.json — the raw OpenAI request/response

- embed-<id>-request.json , embed-<id>-response.json — embeddings traffic

- session.log — plain-text copy of all log lines

Pass --log-dir "" to disable session logging.

### 2. Point your agent at the queue

The agent prompt is printed on startup. To grab it again:

faaah --agent-message

Paste it into your coding agent, which then starts a FAAAH coordinator loop :

- Call faaah --watch to obtain the next request (blocks until one exists).

- Delegate the request to a worker subagent (to prevent accumulating context).

- Repeat. If a worker leaves no response file, faaah --watch simply returns the same path again, so the coordinator retries it.

Note: FAAAH uses subagents to prevent exhaustion of context on multiple requests. Thereby, your AI Agents must support creation of subagents on request by prompt .

### 3. Send a request

You can use curl , for example:

curl http://127.0.0.1:8000/v1/chat/completions \ -H " Content-Type: application/json " \ -H " Authorization: Bearer anything " \ -d ' { "model": "faaah", "messages": [{"role": "user", "content": "Write a haiku."}] } '

Or any OpenAI-API shaped client:

from openai import OpenAI client = OpenAI ( base_url = "http://127.0.0.1:8000/v1" , api_key = "anything" ) response = client . chat . completions . create ( model = "faaah" , # this field is ignored anyway messages = [{ "role" : "user" , "content" : "Write a haiku." }], timeout = None , # agents can be slow ). choices [ 0 ]. message . content print ( response )

A dependency-free example lives in examples/chat.py .

For an advanced usage, GraphRAG fully driven through FAAAH , see graphrag-faaah .

### Tool calling

FAAAH supports the OpenAI tools parameter, including multi-turn tool loops. Send a non-empty tools array and the prompt tells the agent which tools exist and how to request them. Without tools , the classic text-only behavior is unchanged.

The agent requests tool calls by committing a JSON object whose only key is tool_calls :

{ "tool_calls" : [{ "name" : " get_weather " , "arguments" : { "city" : " Lisbon " }}]}

FAAAH mints the call ids, returns finish_reason: "tool_calls" , and expects the client to execute the tool and send the result back as a tool message. On the next request, tool results are rendered as <tool_result> blocks and the agent answers in plain text with finish_reason: "stop" .

Supported tool_choice values are auto (default), none , required , and a forced function. parallel_tool_calls: false limits the reply to one call. Malformed tool replies are retried up to twice with the error fed back to the agent; after that FAAAH returns 502 .

Streaming is not supported; requests with stream: true get a 400 .

A dependency-free example lives in examples/tools.py :

./examples/tools.py " What's the weather in Lisbon? "

### Embeddings

FAAAH stays dependency-free by default, but can serve local embeddings via the optional embeddings uv extra (Installs a spaCy model, en_core_web_md ):

uv tool install ' .[embeddings] ' # global tool with embeddings (from inside this repo) uv sync --extra embeddings # or just the dev environment

When installed, POST /v1/embeddings returns OpenAI-shaped vectors computed locally. Without the extra dependencies, the endpoint just returns 503 .

curl http://127.0.0.1:8000/v1/embeddings \ -H " Content-Type: application/json " \ -d ' {"model": "en_core_web_md", "input": ["hello world"]} '

## CLI usage

usage: faaah [-h] [--host HOST] [--port PORT] [--queue QUEUE] [--log-dir LOG_DIR] [--timeout TIMEOUT] [--agent-message] [-c] [-d] [--watch] Filesystem As An AI Handler: an OpenAI-compatible proxy backed by an AI agent working over text files. options: -h, --help show this help message and exit --host HOST Address to bind (default: 127.0.0.1). --port PORT Port to listen on (default: 8000). --queue QUEUE Directory where prompt/response files live (default: ~/.cache/faaah/queue). --log-dir LOG_DIR Parent dir for per-session logs (default: ~/.cache/faaah/sessions). A new <TIMESTAMP>-<RANDOM> subdir is created each run; pass empty string to disable. --timeout TIMEOUT Abort each call after N seconds. 0 (default) waits forever. --agent-message Print ONLY the agent prompt and exit (it's also printed on launch). -c, --copy Copy the agent prompt to the system clipboard on startup (uses wl-copy, xclip, xsel, pbcopy or clip.exe if available). -d, --debug Print the full request/response flow for each call once it completes. --watch Block until a pending prompt exists, print its path.

## Protocol (The "Filesystem API")

The protocol relies on files on the queue directory ( ~/.cache/faaah/queue by default).

Each request produces a prompt-<id>.txt file, where the first one's ID will be 00001 and increase monotonically.

FAAAH then expects the agent (or anything really) to generate a corresponding response-<id>.txt .

The subagent workers are prompted to write a first pass as response-<id>.txt.draft , which they may revise, before renaming it to the final response-<id>.txt they consider final .

Retry is automatic: a prompt with no response file is simply re-offered by faaah --watch to the coordinator until one appears. Tool-call validation retries also use a fresh prompt id, with the rejected reply and the reason included in the new prompt.

If the client disconnects, or the server-side --timeout fires, faaah removes the prompt so --watch does not keep re-offering work nobody is waiting for.

## Prior art

Other projects put an API in front of a CLI subscription:

- CLIProxyAPI is a Go proxy that exposes several CLI providers such as Claude Code, Codex, Gemini, and Grok through OpenAI, Gemini, Claude, Codex, and Grok compatible endpoints. It handles OAuth, streaming, multimodal input, tool calling, and multi-account load balancing.

- opencode2api is a Go gateway for OpenCode Zen and Zen Go.

Unlike the above, FAAAH doesn't talk to a provider at all: FAAAH tells you how to prompt the model you already have to act as an OpenAI API , so in principle any model that you can prompt locally works.

## License

MIT

# linkedin-ops

High-reliability, multi-agent-safe LinkedIn automation engine and CLI built on Chrome DevTools Protocol (CDP).

> Disclaimer & Responsible Use : linkedin-ops is an independent open-source tool built for developer automation research, testing, and workflow automation via local Chrome DevTools Protocol (CDP). This project is not affiliated with, endorsed by, or sponsored by LinkedIn Corporation. Automated interaction with LinkedIn must comply with applicable platform terms and policies. Always maintain realistic human delays and respect LinkedIn rate limits to safeguard account health.

## Quickstart (<30s Setup)

### 1. Install dependencies

npm install

### 2. Run automated setup

node index.mjs setup

The setup wizard automatically:

- Locates your Google Chrome binary (macOS, Linux, Windows).

- Discovers your existing Chrome profiles from system User Data so you can pick your logged-in account (or create a dedicated project session).

- Saves settings to .linkedin-opsrc (no manual path pasting required).

- Generates a one-click launcher ( start-chrome.command / start-chrome.bat ).

### 3. Verify session & connection

npm run doctor # or: node index.mjs doctor

Checks CDP port 9222 reachability, browser version, user agent, and verifies an authenticated LinkedIn session.

### 4. Run your first dry run

node index.mjs connect --profile= " https://www.linkedin.com/in/username " --note= " Hi, loved your post on distributed systems... "

(Dry-run mode navigates and fills the note without submitting. Add --send only when ready to live submit).

## Architecture Guarantees

- Automated Runtime Fallback : Daily commands ping port 9222. If Chrome is closed, linkedin-ops automatically launches it using your configured profile. If Chrome is already running without remote debugging enabled, it detects the profile lock and prompts to restart cleanly.

- Cross-Process Mutex Locking : Serializes execution across concurrent agents and processes ( linkedin.lock ). Prevents session collisions, focus-stealing, and rate-limiting.

- Isolated Ephemeral Tabs : Each operation spawns its own dedicated Chrome tab via PUT /json/new and connects directly via target ID.

- Auto-Cleanup : Guarantees tab destruction ( /json/close/<targetId> ) in a finally block on success or failure, eliminating zombie tab leaks.

## CLI Usage

# Automated setup wizard node index.mjs setup # Pre-flight health check node index.mjs doctor # Connection invitation with personalized note (dry-run) node index.mjs connect --profile= " https://www.linkedin.com/in/username " --note= " Hi, loved your post... " # Live connection invitation node index.mjs connect --profile= " https://www.linkedin.com/in/username " --note= " Hi, loved your post... " --send # Direct message to 1st-degree connection node index.mjs dm --profile= " https://www.linkedin.com/in/username " --message= " Checking in on our conversation. " --send # Comment on a LinkedIn post node index.mjs comment --url= " https://www.linkedin.com/posts/... " --text= " Great insights on distributed systems! " --send # Company people search (e.g. recruiters) node index.mjs search --company= " Google " --keywords= " recruiter " --limit=10 --json # Inspect or force-release active mutex lock node index.mjs lock node index.mjs lock release

## Programmatic Library Usage

import { withLock , withDedicatedTab , sendConnectionInvite } from 'linkedin-ops' ; await withLock ( 'outreach-task' , async ( ) => { await withDedicatedTab ( { port : 9222 } , async ( cdp ) => { const result = await sendConnectionInvite ( cdp , { linkedinUrl : 'https://www.linkedin.com/in/username' , note : 'Hi, loved your work on distributed systems.' , send : true } ) ; console . log ( result ) ; } ) ; } ) ;

## Batch Campaigns

For multi-profile outreach and candidate sweeps, see campaigns/batch-connect.example.mjs :

# Copy template to your personal user campaigns folder cp campaigns/batch-connect.example.mjs campaigns/my-outreach.mjs # Run the campaign safely with mutex locking and isolated tab lifecycles node campaigns/my-outreach.mjs

(User campaigns and harvested datasets in data/ and campaigns/ are gitignored and never committed to source control).

- Architecture Blueprint : Deep dive into CDP socket lifecycle, locking mechanisms, and tab management.

# Loose Ends

Graph-powered liveness checks for AI-written code.

> Every change should lead somewhere.

Coding agents write code fast, and they leave things behind: a helper that is never called, a UserServiceV2 sitting next to the UserService it replaced, a route that was unregistered while its handler stayed. Loose Ends checks every change before merge and reports, with evidence, whether the code it added or touched is still reachable from a real entry point.

$ npx loose-ends check Loose Ends · check main (dc9af08) → working tree 4 files changed ✖ error orphaned-addition src/lib/pagination.ts:1 File added in this change is not reachable from any entry point. Import it from live code, add it to `entries`, or mark it with `// loose-ends-file: dormant <reason>`. ✖ error superseded src/services/users.ts:1 src/services/users.ts appears to have been replaced by src/services/users-v2.ts#listUsersV2 but was not removed: its callers now use the new code (src/routes/users.ts); the names match; 100% structural similarity. Delete it, or mark it dormant with a reason. edge removed: src/routes/users.ts → src/services/users.ts was reached via: src/server.ts → src/routes/index.ts → src/routes/users.ts → src/services/users.ts root: entry point "src/server.ts" of express-api-example related: src/services/users-v2.ts#listUsersV2 Summary: 2 errors, 0 warnings, 0 info Files: 6 live, 0 test-only, 2 orphaned, 0 uncertain, 0 dormant Result: fail (2 findings in failOn: orphaned-addition, superseded)

That is the express-api example after an agent-style change: a v2 service was added and wired in, the original was left behind, and an unused pagination helper was added.

## What it checks

- Added code must be reachable from a recognized product entry point.

- Changes must not orphan existing code by removing the edges that kept it alive.

- Replaced implementations must be removed or explicitly justified.

Loose Ends builds a Liveness Graph of TypeScript, JavaScript, Python, and Java code: imports, exports, re-exports, references between top-level declarations, dynamic imports, and package dependencies. It finds roots in package manifests, scripts, framework conventions (Next.js routes, Vite entries, browser extension manifests, serverless functions, tool configs, Django apps, pyproject entry points, server commands in Dockerfiles and Procfiles, Spring and Jakarta annotations, Android manifests and layouts), config, and tests. It analyzes the base and head revisions and reports only what the change did. Existing dead code never blocks a pull request.

It is not an LLM guessing whether code looks unused, a general code reviewer, a formatter, or a security scanner. It does not claim that unobserved code is safe to delete, and it never deletes anything without deterministic evidence and a passing verification run.

bench/RESULTS.md has the results on public repositories, including about 700 Python and Java commits replayed through check and a sweep of 30 popular repositories.

## Install

npm install --save-dev loose-ends

Requires Node.js 20 or newer and git.

Python and Java projects need no package.json . With Node installed, run npx loose-ends check from the repository root.

The npm packages are published from GitHub Actions with provenance , so each version links back to the commit it was built from.

## Usage

npx loose-ends check # working tree vs. merge base with the default branch npx loose-ends check --base origin/main --head HEAD npx loose-ends check --format markdown # also: json, sarif npx loose-ends scan # whole-project report of existing debt npx loose-ends explain src/lib/format.ts#formatUser npx loose-ends roots # what counts as an entry point, and why npx loose-ends fix --verify --patch cleanup.diff npx loose-ends init # starter loose-ends.config.json

check exits with 0 on pass, 1 on blocking findings, and 2 when it could not run.

### Findings

scan reports existing code instead of a change, so it uses orphaned (nothing reaches it) and test-only (only tests reach it), plus unused-dependency and uncertain . It exits 0 unless you pass --fail .

See docs/findings.md for what each kind means and what to do about it.

### Configuration

Every option is optional. npx loose-ends init writes a starter loose-ends.config.json :

{ "$schema" : " https://raw.githubusercontent.com/sid732/loose-ends/main/schema/config.schema.json " , "entries" : [ " src/jobs/*.ts " , " src/events/handlers.ts#onInvoicePaid " ], "extendExclude" : [ " src/generated/** " ], "languages" : [ " javascript " , " python " ], "failOn" : [ " orphaned-addition " , " newly-orphaned " , " superseded " , " invalid-suppression " ], "checks" : [ " npm run typecheck " , " npm test " ] }

- entries adds roots the graph cannot see, such as files a job runner loads by name.

- extendExclude adds to the default excludes ( node_modules , build output, virtualenvs, …).

- languages limits analysis to some of javascript , python , and java .

- failOn picks the finding kinds that fail check .

- checks are the commands fix --verify runs.

All options, dormant rules, and suppressions are in docs/configuration.md .

### Intentionally unused code

// loose-ends: dormant v1 webhooks still arrive until the March cutover export function handleV1Webhook ( ) { }

# loose-ends: dormant v1 webhooks still arrive until the March cutover def handle_v1_webhook (): ...

Java uses // like TypeScript. A loose-ends-file: comment applies to the whole file instead of the declaration below it.

Dormant markers and suppressions need a reason. Without one, they become findings themselves. See docs/configuration.md .

## In CI and on pull requests

# .github/workflows/loose-ends.yml name : Loose Ends on : pull_request permissions : contents : read pull-requests : write # for the PR comment jobs : liveness : runs-on : ubuntu-latest steps : - uses : actions/checkout@v5 with : fetch-depth : 0 # the base commit must exist locally - uses : sid732/loose-ends@v1

- GitHub Action (no server, free on public repos): adds inline annotations on the diff, keeps one PR comment up to date, writes the report to the job summary, and fails the job on blocking findings. It works for Python and Java repositories too, with no Node setup step.

- GitHub App: the same report as check runs, for people who prefer to host a server and install once across many repositories.

Inputs ( working-directory , fail-on , comment , sarif , …) and App setup are in docs/github.md .

## For coding agents

- MCP server: npx -y @loose-ends/mcp exposes check_changes , scan_project , explain , list_roots , and plan_cleanup . All of them are read-only.

- Skills: skills/ has two short SKILL.md files that tell an agent when to run the check and how to respond to each finding.

{ "mcpServers" : { "loose-ends" : { "command" : " npx " , "args" : [ " -y " , " @loose-ends/mcp " ] } } }

## Cleanup

npx loose-ends fix --verify --patch cleanup.diff

fix turns blocking findings into file deletions and declaration removals and applies them to a scratch copy of the project. Then it runs your configured checks ( npm test , npm run build , …) there and writes a patch. Anything that would leave a dangling import is skipped, with the reason listed. --apply writes the change to your tree, and only after verification passes.

## Coverage as evidence

npx loose-ends check --coverage coverage/coverage-final.json

Runtime hit counts from istanbul or lcov reports are attached to findings. Coverage never overrides the graph. It explains it: code the graph considers unreachable that still ran points to a loader the graph cannot see.

## Scope

- TypeScript and JavaScript: Node.js, React, Next.js, Vite, Express, NestJS, React Router framework mode, Vue, Svelte and SvelteKit, Astro, Nuxt, VitePress, npm/yarn/pnpm workspaces, browser extensions, and common test runners.

- Python: packages and src layouts, relative and namespace imports, __init__.py re-exports and __all__ , scripts, notebooks, pyproject/setup.py entry points, Django, Flask, FastAPI, Celery, Alembic, Airflow, Streamlit, pytest, and dependencies in requirements*.txt , pyproject.toml , setup.py , setup.cfg , and Pipfile .

- Java: top-level classes, interfaces, enums, and records; imports, same-package and fully qualified references; main methods; Spring, Jakarta EE, CDI, JAX-RS, Quarkus, Micronaut, MyBatis, MapStruct, Dagger/Hilt, and Android; class names in resource files; Maven and Gradle (including version catalogs) dependencies; and Java code used from Kotlin.

A repository can mix all of them. How it works is described in docs/architecture.md .

### Limits

- Tracking stops at top-level declarations. An unused method inside a used class, or an unused property on a used object, is not reported.

- Code reached only through dependency injection by name, string-based plugin registries, or reflection is invisible to the graph. Add it to entries or mark it with loose-ends: entry .

- Java classes with framework annotations ( @Service , @Controller , @Entity , …) count as entry points, so they are never reported as unused.

- Kotlin and Groovy are only scanned for the Java names they use. Their own code is not analyzed.

- Python getattr with a computed name and modules found through sys.path changes are not followed.

- Other languages are not analyzed.

## Contributing

Setup, pull request rules, and the release process are in CONTRIBUTING.md . To report a vulnerability, see SECURITY.md .

# simba-skills

Six skills that stop your AI coding agent from hurting production, and keep its own setup clean.

Made for people who run their apps on their own server (Docker, Postgres, a VPS) and use an AI agent such as Claude Code on that same machine. That setup is convenient, but it means one wrong test run, repro loop or deploy can hit live data. These skills put guard rails around exactly those moments.

## Quick start (Claude Code)

1. Add this repo as a plugin source and install it:

claude plugin marketplace add simbaTmotsi/simba-skills claude plugin install simba-skills@simba-skills

2. Restart Claude Code. That's it. The skills now work in every project.

3. Try one: type /simba-skills:server-maintenance in any session, or just ask Claude to run your tests and watch production-safe-loops check where they will write first.

> Using Cursor, Codex, Copilot or another agent? Run npx skills@latest add simbaTmotsi/simba-skills instead. Pick one install method, not both, or you'll get every skill twice.

## What's inside

There are two kinds of skill:

- Automatic : the agent uses it on its own when the situation fits. You can also type it.

- You type it : only runs when you type /simba-skills:<name> . Everything that deploys, deletes, or changes settings is in this group, so the agent can never start it by itself.

## Examples

- You: "fix the failing signup test." Agent: notices your .env points at the production database, and runs the test against a throwaway test database instead.

- You: /simba-skills:safe-deploy . Agent: finds how this project deploys, lists the commits and migrations going out, asks you to confirm, takes a backup, deploys, checks the logs and health page, and saves a rollback note.

- You: "why isn't my deploy skill showing up?" Agent: finds it was saved as deploy.md instead of deploy/SKILL.md , and offers to move it.

- You: /simba-skills:audit-claude-settings . Agent: backs up your settings, lists the risky rules with secrets hidden, removes what you approve, and reminds you to change any password that was stored there.

## Keeping it up to date

Turn on auto-update once and new versions arrive whenever Claude Code starts. Add "autoUpdate": true to this marketplace in ~/.claude/settings.json :

"extraKnownMarketplaces" : { "simba-skills" : { "source" : { "source" : " github " , "repo" : " simbaTmotsi/simba-skills " }, "autoUpdate" : true } }

Or update by hand at any time:

claude plugin update simba-skills@simba-skills

To remove it: claude plugin uninstall simba-skills@simba-skills .

## Tested

The repo includes an eval suite in evals/ that runs Claude Code on the same scenarios with and without the plugin:

It's a small suite (Claude Code 2.1.323, November 2026), so treat it as a sanity check rather than a benchmark. Run it yourself with claude plugin eval . from the repo root.

## Good to know

- Nothing risky happens silently. Every step that deletes, deploys, pushes or installs a scheduled job asks you first.

- Secrets stay hidden. Skills mask passwords and tokens in their output. If one was ever stored in plain text, they tell you to change it, because deleting it is not enough.

- Works on its own. You don't need Matt Pocock's skills. If you have them, production-safe-loops also guards the loops his tdd and diagnosing-bugs skills build.

- Built for Linux servers running Docker. The server and deploy skills assume Docker Compose and Postgres, and adapt to whatever deploy scripts your project already has.

## Contributing

Contributions are welcome when they are useful and safe. Read SCOPE.md for the bar and CONTRIBUTING.md for how. In short:

- A skill did the wrong thing? Open a bug report with what you asked, what the agent did, and what you expected.

- Hit a gap in real use? Open an idea before writing code.

- Found a security problem? Report it privately, as described in SECURITY.md .

Every pull request is checked automatically and reviewed by the maintainer before it can merge.

# Skylands

Once developers get past the initial adoption stage and start using AI assistants and harnesses for real work (aka "in anger"), their needs change. Managing multiple agents working in multiple repositories from different locations and apps becomes a real pain and slows down the work. Developers end up herding terminal sessions and VPNs more than they orchestrate agents.

You can use any agent you like, or mix and match however you choose. Skylands supports Claude Code , Gemini , Codex , and Goose , with more to come.

Skylands solves that problem by giving you a single interface through which you can dispatch agent work to any machine you have access to, from any browser you like. Tell your agents to start working on your dev box from your laptop and approve permission requests from your phone, all with a fun 3D interface that also supports a unified inbox for all your work.

Skylands gives you a secure , signed log of everything your agents do and every approval or rejection you provide, no matter where the agent's running or what it's doing. Conversation history is available through a central inbox rather than hidden deep within some obscure sub-directory.

If you want to use Skylands in your agentic development workflow, then check out the documentation at docs.skylands.ai .

The rest of the information in this README applies mostly to those looking to contribute to Skylands.

## Quickstart

Install Skylands with Homebrew on macOS or Linux:

brew tap skylands-ai/tap brew trust skylands-ai/tap brew install --cask skylands

The installation page has the other ways to install it. Then start a world on this machine:

skylands devworld up

devworld up runs an embedded NATS server, a citadel, and a daemon for this machine in one process, so you get the castle and one island. The first time, it prints a link to set the world up:

Set up this world. Open this link in a browser: http://127.0.0.1:8080/setup#...

Open it and set the world up. After that, the world is at http://127.0.0.1:8080 , and that browser opens it as a valid approver.

# spar

two AIs. one ball. no mercy.

Make Claude and ChatGPT argue until the answer is actually right, using the plans you already pay for.

npx spar-ai " should I lease or buy my next car? "

New here? Run npx spar-ai doctor first: it checks that Claude Code and Codex are installed and signed in.

## Why

You ask Claude. You paste its answer into ChatGPT: "what's wrong with this?" You paste that back into Claude. Again. And again.

spar does the copy-paste for you. One serves, the other returns, back and forth, until one of them looks at the other's answer and can't find anything to fix. You can step in on any turn.

Works for anything you'd ask an AI: questions, decisions, plans, emails, essays, research, code.

## Install

You need Node.js 18+ and at least one of these, signed in with your own plan:

- Claude Code (Claude Pro, Max, Team): npm i -g @anthropic-ai/claude-code

- Codex (ChatGPT Plus, Pro, Team): npm i -g @openai/codex

- Or no subscription at all: an OpenRouter key for any model, pay as you go

npm i -g spar-ai spar doctor

No account with us. With your plans, your prompts go only to Anthropic and OpenAI, through their own official tools. With an OpenRouter key, they go to OpenRouter and you pay them directly.

## Play

spar " what should I name my dog? " # you steer between turns spar --auto " explain mortgages like I'm 12 " # no pauses, play to the end cat draft.md | spar " make this cover letter land " # pipe in material spar -f contract.pdf.txt " anything risky in here? " # or hand them files spar --swap " ... " # ChatGPT serves first spar --left-model opus --right-effort high " ... " # pick models and effort spar " ... " > answer.md # only the final answer goes to stdout spar --save " ... " # keep the whole rally as markdown

They behave the way their own apps do:

- Each side keeps its own conversation. Claude continues one Claude conversation and ChatGPT one ChatGPT conversation, so each remembers what it said and only gets what's new.

- You see what each one is doing as it happens: "Searching the web for…", "Running npm test", "Writing · 212 words", next to a little animated mark for each side.

- If one asks you a question, your answer goes back to it , not to the other side.

While they play:

### Any model: Claude vs Gemini, GPT vs DeepSeek…

export OPENROUTER_API_KEY=sk-or-... # your own key from openrouter.ai spar --right openrouter:google/gemini-2.5-pro " ... " # Claude (your plan) vs Gemini (your key) spar --left openrouter:deepseek/deepseek-chat --right openrouter:x-ai/grok-4 " ... "

Any model on openrouter.ai/models can play either side. spar shows roughly what a turn costs before it starts and what the match cost at the end. You pay OpenRouter directly; spar never touches the bill. Web search is off for OpenRouter sides unless you pass --web , since it costs extra there.

### Code matches

spar --code " the date parser fails on leap years. fix it and add a test "

They take turns in your repo: one edits, the other reads the diff, runs the tests and fixes what's wrong. Every turn is a commit on its own spar/… branch, so nothing touches your work until you merge it.

## How a match ends

- Someone concedes. A side says VERDICT: PASS and changes nothing: the other side's version stands.

- You call it with d .

- Turn limit: --turns n (default 6 with --auto ).

## House rules

Both sides get the same short rules: be right, not agreeable. No flattery. If the other answer is good, say PASS instead of changing things to look busy. Mark anything uncertain [CHECK] and never invent sources. (Read them in lib/prompts.js .)

## FAQ

Is this allowed on my Claude and ChatGPT plans? spar doesn't touch your login. It runs the official Claude Code and Codex command-line tools on your computer in their documented non-interactive modes ( claude -p and codex exec ), exactly as you could from a script, and they count against your plan's usage like any other session. It never reads, copies or sends your tokens anywhere. Each provider's terms are theirs to set and can change, so check your plan's terms if you're unsure. If you'd rather use API keys, pass --use-api-keys , or use an OpenRouter key.

Why two models instead of one good one? A model reviewing its own answer tends to agree with itself. A different model, from a different company, trained differently, misses different things, and in spar it has to say exactly what's wrong before it can change anything. It's not magic: sometimes the first answer is already right, and then the other side says so and the match ends in one turn.

Won't they just agree with each other to be polite? Both get the same short house rules: be right, not agreeable; no flattery; say PASS rather than make busywork changes; mark anything uncertain [CHECK] ; never invent sources.

What does it cost? Nothing extra with your Claude and ChatGPT plans: each turn is one normal Claude Code or Codex request. A match is usually 2 to 6 turns. With OpenRouter, spar shows roughly what a turn costs before it starts.

How is it different from other "make the models debate" tools? It's a single npx command, it runs on the subscriptions you already have (no API keys needed), each side keeps its own real conversation, it works for everyday questions as well as code, and in code mode every turn is a git commit on its own branch. Apache 2.0.

Something's not working. Run npx spar-ai doctor . Most problems are a tool that isn't installed or isn't signed in, and doctor says which. Otherwise, open an issue .

## Want more?

spar for desktop adds projects, your imported Claude and ChatGPT history (each side gets its own), attachments and images, Gemini and OpenRouter, pay-as-you-go spar credits for hundreds of other models, saved matches, and a safe code mode with one-click undo. → Join the desktop beta

## License

Apache 2.0. See LICENSE and NOTICE . "spar" is a trademark; forks need their own name.

Not affiliated with Anthropic or OpenAI.

# Google Gemini routes personal Drive files and emails to human annotators

In 2023, Google launched Gemini Workspace extensions with an explicit promise: personal content from Gmail, Docs, and Drive "is not seen by human reviewers" .

Google has quietly reversed this commitment. Under updated Google Help Answer 16836988 and in an October 16 edit to their aforementioned 2023 blogpost , Google explicitly confirms that connected Drive/email is routed into human review pipelines, with clear warnings that what reviewers see "may just be the email or file" and "don't connect your apps to Gemini Apps if they contain confidential information that you wouldn't want a reviewer to see."

Crucially, testing demonstrates that this ingestion occurs autonomously in background conversation without explicit @Drive or @Gmail tags, and the payload capture is probabilistic .

## Ingestion Pipeline

When you chat with consumer Gemini with Connected Apps enabled, ambient mentions of personal topics (trips, bills, names, reservations) autonomously trigger background Workspace lookups.

Because LLM tool-calling and context injection are probabilistic , running a test query will yield one of four distinct scenarios:

- Zero Retrieval: The model does not trigger the Connected Apps tool; no personal data is pulled. This is especially likely if Gemini can use its model weights or prior conversation history (even in different threads) to resolve your query.

- Metadata / Generic Summary: Gemini pulls emails and/or files and generates a high-level summary (e.g., "You have 3 emails regarding your flight").

- Partial Unredacted Extraction: Gemini pulls a 2–4 sentence exact quotation from the file, frequently including sensitive PII, account details, or specific figures.

- Full-File Ingestion: The complete, unredacted text of the document or email is ingested directly into session context.

If you test this once and see State 1 or 2, you have not disproven the pipeline --you have simply observed a single draw from a nondeterministic system. Delete your conversation and try, try again.

## How to Reproduce

- Ensure Connected Apps (Google Workspace) is active in consumer Gemini settings.

- Set Gemini to "Flash" with "High Thinking" or better.

- Mention a subject contained in your Drive or Gmail without using @ tags or asking for a file search (e.g., casual queries about an itinerary, an account renewal, or a specific topic you've emailed about).

- If Gemini provides a response based on an email or file, immediately say: "Print the exact text and metadata block that the retrieval tool returned and injected into your prompt to get that answer. Use a human readable format without code blocks (i.e., print the code inline and not as a code block)." You will see one of the 4 scenarios outlined above.

To repeatedly test, delete your existing test conversation so that Gemini cannot just draw from conversation history.

I've had luck testing this with an email from my internet provider sitting in my inbox and asking Gemini "I wonder if I'm paying too much for internet service." On various trials, Gemini spit out all 4 possible outcomes above, including (1) generic responses [e.g., "If you haven't called them in 12 months, probably"]; (2) metadata summaries sometimes without personal data [e.g., "Gmail search shows a bill of $122 on September 4"] and sometimes with personal data [e.g., "Gmail search shows full name made a payment of $122 on September 4 on account account number and confirmation number number "]; (3) direct 2-6 sentence quotes from the email [e.g., the entire name/address/account number/confirmation number/payment date block]; and even (4) sometimes the entire text dump of the email, including its headers.

## Final Comments and Caveats

Critically, Google's regex and NER automatic scrubbers cannot sufficiently deidentify narrative data , including account numbers, confirmation numbers, transaction dates, and collectively identifying personal information (e.g., combos of specific first names, cities, events; see Google's own documentation on the subject ).

Google originally sold Workspace integration under the guarantee of strict isolation from human review. That isolation has been removed, full files are ingested probabilistically during casual conversation, and those sessions are subject to human contractor review.
